verdict.summary: ValidateInputs enforces that a_shape matches the dense operand b, but never checks that a_indices' second dimension (the sparse index rank) equals a_shape->NumElements(), nor that a_values' length equals a_indices' first dimension. An attacker supplying e.g. a_indices of shape [nnz, 5] with a_shape [d] (rank 1) passes every quoted check and reaches return Status::OK(); the structurally inconsistent operands then flow to the sparse-dense matmul kernel, whose per-index arithmetic (index columns vs shape/strides of different arity) reads out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Fail-open validation sink: returns OK for operands whose cross-relation was never checked. The mention sweep over a_indices (lines 3-6) contains only the IsMatrix dims-count test — no statement relates a_indices->shape().dim_size(1) to a_shape->NumElements(), and none relates a_values->NumElements() to a_indices->dim_size(0), so a rank-mismatched attacker input (e.g. a_indices [2,5] with a_shape [4]) passes all checks at lines 3, 8, 16, 22-28 and reaches this line, enabling out-of-bounds reads downstream.

Origin of the taint: a_indices is validated only as having exactly 2 dimensions; its second dimension (index rank) is left fully attacker-controlled and is never constrained against a_shape->NumElements() anywhere in this function, which is the sole consistency gate for the op's inputs.

assumptions: All four tensor parameters originate from the model/session caller across the TF op trust boundary, so their shapes and lengths are attacker-controlled (width-domain: any non-negative dims).

ValidateInputs is the intake validation layer for the SparseTensorDenseMatMul op; the function's own checks ('no broadcasting is supported', rank equality with b) define the consistency contract it is responsible for enforcing.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds read occurs in the not-shown matmul kernel that consumes the validated operands; the defect located here is the missing guard at the validation gate, consistent with the upstream TensorFlow fix that added exactly the a_indices->shape().dim_size(1) != a_shape->NumElements() check.

The missing a_values->NumElements() == a_indices->dim_size(0) check is a second instance of the same single defect class (unvalidated cross-operand consistency) and is not counted as an independent CWE.
Impact of the OOB is limited to reading (heap OOB read / potential info disclosure), not memory corruption, based on the standard semantics of the downstream index arithmetic.

verdict.summary: In yank_copy_line, the trailing-whitespace strip loop evaluates VIM_ISWHITE(*(bd->textstart + s - 1)) before testing s > 0. When s reaches 0 (line entirely whitespace, or textlen == 0 with exclude_trailing_space setting endspaces to 0), the loop condition dereferences bd->textstart[-1], one byte before the text object whose valid extent this code itself defines as bd->textlen bytes via the mch_memmove — an out-of-bounds read of attacker-influenced line data, with the byte consumed by a control-flow predicate.

evidence.reason: The dereference *(bd->textstart + s - 1) executes before the only bound test `s > 0` on the right side of &&. Trigger: exclude_trailing_space sets bd->endspaces = 0 (line 6), so s = bd->textlen (line 19); with an all-whitespace line (or textlen == 0), s reaches 0 and the next condition evaluation loads bd->textstart[-1], outside the text object of bd->textlen bytes established by the memmove on line 13 — a 1-byte out-of-bounds read whose value feeds VIM_ISWHITE. Fix: swap operands to `while (s > 0 && VIM_ISWHITE(...))`.

assumptions: bd->textstart points to at least bd->textlen valid readable bytes, as established by the code's own mch_memmove(pnew, bd->textstart, (size_t)bd->textlen);
alloc returns NULL on failure (checked); VIM_ISWHITE tests membership in {' ', '\t'} on the loaded byte.

Whether textstart[-1] lands before a heap allocation depends on the caller's buffer; per the width-domain rule, textstart pointing at the start of its object is in-domain and makes this a heap OOB read; in-domain textstart always makes it an out-of-object read per the line-13 extent.
limitations: y_idx is used to index y_current->y_array without a bound check in this function; no call-site contract is shown, so it is dismissed as a caller contract issue.
Integer overflow in alloc(bd->startspaces + bd->endspaces + bd->textlen + 1) would require line metrics near INT_MAX; no quoted statement produces such values, so it is speculative.
Impact is limited to a one-byte out-of-bounds read (the s > 0 term short-circuits further iteration), used only as a whitespace predicate.

verdict.summary: The classic batch_idx out-of-bounds defect in this bincount kernel is fully neutralized by three quoted guards: num_batches > 0, splits_values(0) == 0, and splits_values(num_batches) == num_values, which together pin batch_idx to [1, num_batches] at every per_batch_counts access, even for non-monotonic or negative splits; values and weights indices are bounded by the loop bound and the shape-equality check respectively, and value is only used as a map key. No trigger with attacker-controlled tensor content reaches an unguarded sink in this code.

assumptions: T and W input dtypes are enforced by TensorFlow op type-constraint registration outside this snippet; a mismatch would at worst CHECK-fail (same-privilege crash) in flat<W>().
GetOutputSize and OutputSparse are file-local helpers whose bodies are not shown; their signatures and internal checks cannot be quoted.
limitations: Speculative: with maxlength_ <= 0 and T=int64, an attacker value of INT64_MAX flows into GetOutputSize(max_value, ...) and could overflow/truncate inside that unshown callee (and any dense write in unshown OutputSparse); the harmful use occurs entirely inside callees not shown, so the impact is not instantiated here.

Speculative/impractical: 'int num_batches = splits.NumElements() - 1' and 'int num_values = values.NumElements()' truncate int64 counts; triggering requires >= 2^31-element tensors (>= 16GB / 4GB), and arithmetic on the truncated values keeps the invariant (the same truncated num_batches is used for both the end-check and the vector size; a negative num_values yields zero loop iterations), so no out-of-bounds access results even if instantiated.

Non-monotonic or negative interior splits values were simulated (e.g. [0, -5, 10], [0, 5, 3, 10]) and in every case the while loop halts at batch_idx <= num_batches because splits_values(num_batches) == num_values > idx for all idx in the loop range.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-tensor sink is map->put(&key, indices_tensor, &tuple). The key tensor's emptiness and cardinality are enforced in execution order by the quoted checks `key_tensor->NumElements() > 0` and `key_tensor->NumElements() == 1` before the first use, so the empty/non-scalar key that previously caused an out-of-bounds read of key->flat<int64>()(0) in the staging map is rejected here; key/indices dtypes are pinned by the op registration and enforced by the TF executor. No other sink in this code consumes attacker-derived values without a quoted guard.

assumptions: The op registration (not shown) pins the input dtypes (key: int64, indices: int32) and the TensorFlow executor type-checks op inputs against the op def before Compute runs, which is why no in-function dtype check is required.
Standard OP_REQUIRES/OP_REQUIRES_OK semantics: on a false condition / non-OK status the macro returns from Compute before subsequent statements.
The not-shown StagingMap::put reads the key via key->flat<int64>()(0), which requires at least one element - the precondition the quoted NumElements checks enforce.
limitations: indices_tensor is passed to map->put without any content validation in this code; if the not-shown StagingMap<Ordered>::put used attacker-controlled indices values to index into the stored tuple, an out-of-bounds access would exist in that callee, but no such use can be quoted or characterized from standard semantics here, so the candidate is speculative.

The historical MapStage defect this guard set was added for (empty key tensor reaching key->flat<int64>()(0) and reading out of bounds) is provably blocked by the two quoted OP_REQUIRES checks; that candidate is dismissed, not confirmed.

verdict.summary: RestoreTensor indexes input(1) and input(2) with restore_index without any bounds check; the only size guard in the function validates input(0) (file_pattern) instead. Any int value of restore_index (e.g., >= tensor_name_t.NumElements() or negative) reaches flat<tstring>()(restore_index) and reads out of bounds; the resulting tstring is echoed into error messages, enabling a crash or heap-content disclosure.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: restore_index (attacker-domain int parameter) is used to index tensor_name_t's flat<tstring>() buffer with no preceding check of restore_index against tensor_name_t.NumElements(); the only guard in the function, 'OP_REQUIRES(context, size == 1, ...)', constrains input(0)'s element count, a different variable. Trigger: restore_index = 5 with a 1-element input(1) tensor.

Second sink of the same missing-guard defect: input(2) is indexed with the same unchecked restore_index; the following 'if (!shape_spec.empty())' validates the spec's content only, after the out-of-bounds index has already been performed.

assumptions: Eigen TensorMap::operator() used by Tensor::flat<tstring>() performs bounds assertions only in debug builds; release builds perform the raw read.
restore_index is a parameter of this exported kernel-handler; per the width-domain rule its full int domain is instantiable, since no producer/check is shown in this code.

context->expected_output_dtype(restore_index) and allocate_output(restore_index, ...) may internally validate the index, but no such validation is quotable here; line 16 remains the first unchecked use.
limitations: The type-mismatch error message on lines 43-44 reports expected_output_dtype(0) while the check on line 42 uses expected_output_dtype(restore_index) — misleading diagnostics only, no security impact.
Severity is capped at medium because the primitive is an out-of-bounds read of string objects (crash / potential disclosure via error strings); no write primitive is instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: updateDigestForSessionId hashes every acceptance-relevant validator setting (ca_cert_, both verify lists, verify_trusted_ca_, and all config-derived fields) into the session-ID digest, and its only memory sink is guarded by an exact length assertion checked before use. All inputs are internal/config-derived with no attacker-data crossing a trust boundary in this code; every crypto call is followed by a failure-sentinel RELEASE_ASSERT. No vulnerability found.

assumptions: RELEASE_ASSERT remains active in release builds (standard Envoy semantics); the hash_length guard at the X509_digest site would be void if the macro were compiled out.
EVP_DigestUpdate returns 1 on success for the inputs given (same-object pointer/length pairs, fixed-size primitives).
limitations: hash.size() * sizeof(value_type) could overflow only for config-supplied vectors near SIZE_MAX; not attacker-scalable and not instantiable from any quoted producer here.

MessageUtil::hash(matcher) reduces each SAN matcher to a 64-bit hash before digesting; a 64-bit preimage/collision attack on session-ID separation would lie outside this code and outside the attacker model.
Digest completeness was judged against the validator fields visible in this function; settings consumed elsewhere in the validator (not shown) cannot be audited from this snippet.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled counts and reads in afra_box_read are guarded: entry_count is bounded by the quoted size/12-or-16 check with exact per-entry byte costs, and every per-iteration bitstream read (local and global loops) is preceded by an ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE error arm that terminates on insufficient remaining box size, preventing out-of-bounds reads, count-based overflows, and unbounded allocation; the absent aggregate pre-check on global_entry_count is fully compensated by these per-read guards.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) checks ptr->size >= N and returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE before subtracting (standard GPAC macro semantics; the macro body is not shown).
gf_bs_read_* are EOF-safe (GPAC bitstream returns 0 when past end) and the parent box parser bounds declared box size by available file bytes (not shown).
ptr->local_access_entries / global_access_entries lists are non-NULL, created by the box constructor (not shown).
limitations: global_entry_count (u32, full 0..0xFFFFFFFF domain) lacks an aggregate bounds check like the one on entry_count; the per-iteration ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE guards bound iterations to remaining_size/8 and total allocation to ~1.6x box size, so no OOB read or scalable OOM is instantiated — recorded as a defense-in-depth gap, not a vulnerability.
entry_count = 0xFFFFFFFF can pass the pre-check only for a ~51 GB box; per-read guards still bound actual consumption.
No guard was found for the NULL-return path of gf_list_insert (allocation-failure handling inside the list is not shown); impact does not reach a security effect in this code.

verdict.summary: ff_copy_pce_data() can fail (return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA when the program_config_element exceeds MAX_PCE_SIZE) but its return is used unchecked in '(ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb) + 3) / 8', producing a negative adts->pce_size while the function still returns 0; the negative size field is later consumed as a length by the ADTS muxer (negative-to-size_t blowup), and the error path reports success (fail-open).

evidence.reason: Missing failure-sentinel check on ff_copy_pce_data's return: on a PCE larger than MAX_PCE_SIZE the callee returns a negative error, e.g. -548, so (-548+3)/8 = -68 is stored as pce_size and the function returns 0 (success) on the failure path; the sibling calls at lines 8-10 and 11-13 both test 'ret < 0' before use — that exact guard is absent here, leaving an attacker-supplied extradata to corrupt the size field consumed downstream as a length.

assumptions: ff_copy_pce_data is the FFmpeg libavcodec helper that returns a non-negative bit count on success and AVERROR_INVALIDDATA (negative) when the PCE data does not fit the MAX_PCE_SIZE put-bit buffer, per standard-function semantics.
adts->pce_size is a size field consumed as a length by the ADTS muxer's header-writing path (not shown).
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds write/reads occurs in the not-shown consumer of adts->pce_size (adts_write_frame_header); here the instantiated defect is the unchecked negative return producing an out-of-domain size and a success return on the failure path.

Candidate of skip_bits_long(&gb, off) followed by get_bits was downgraded: off comes from the checked parser and get_bit overreads stay within FFmpeg's padded-input-buffer semantics; no in-code corruption link is quotable.

verdict.summary: The rank validation (ndims >= 2) is performed AFTER the code indexes with ndims - 1: with an attacker-supplied rank-0 (scalar) input, input.dim_size(-1) and rhs.dim_size(-1) execute out-of-bounds reads before the OP_REQUIRES_ASYNC guard runs; a rank-mismatched rhs likewise indexes rhs.dim_size(ndims-1) outside rhs's shape domain before the rhs.dims() == ndims check.

evidence.snippet:
const int64 n = input.dim_size(ndims - 1);
    const int64 nrhs = rhs.dim_size(ndims - 1);
evidence.reason: Check-after-use out-of-bounds read: ndims is attacker-controlled (input tensor rank) and is used as ndims-1 before the 'ndims >= 2' validation executes. Trigger: a rank-0 scalar input gives dim_size(-1) on both lines (and a lower-rank rhs gives rhs.dim_size(ndims-1) past rhs's dim array), reading out of bounds of the TensorShape storage; the validation at lines 8-9 then rejects the input, but only after the OOB reads have occurred.
Origin of the tainted index: ndims is taken directly from the attacker-controlled input tensor's rank, with full domain including 0, before any validation.

assumptions: TensorShape::dim_size bounds-checks its index only via DCHECK, which is compiled out in release builds, so dim_size(-1) performs an actual out-of-bounds array read; this is inferred from standard TensorFlow semantics, not from code shown here.
The op is reachable with arbitrary user-supplied tensor shapes (TF serving/client trust boundary), so a rank-0 input is instantiable.
limitations: The OOB read is a few bytes adjacent to the TensorShape's dimension storage; the garbage values n/nrhs are never consumed on the failing path (validation rejects the input immediately after), so the practical impact is limited to an out-of-bounds read and potential process crash (denial of service against the serving process), not a disclosed-value write or control-flow primitive.
All solver/allocation callee failures are consumed through OP_REQUIRES_OK_ASYNC sentinel checks; no other candidate (size arithmetic, memcpy lengths, info handling) survived STEP 4.

verdict.summary: gen_hash compiles attacker-supplied Ruby hash-literal ASTs, but every stack-consuming use of the pair counter len (pop_n(len*2), pop_n(len*2+1), genop_2(..., len)) is bounded by the in-code flush guard `if (val && cursp() >= slimit) { ... len = 0; }`, which fires at the end of each loop iteration and caps len at ~slimit/2 (<= ~16383 at slimit = INT16_MAX); all other len uses are guarded by `val &&`. The unchecked AST dereferences (tree->car->car->car) require a malformed tree from the not-shown parser, and the len-counter int overflow requires ~2^31 pairs in a single hash literal with val=0, where no pop/genop sink executes — both triggers are uninstantiable from this code alone.

assumptions: cursp() returns the compiler's value-stack pointer as a non-negative int, per the named constants GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX and GEN_LIT_ARY_MAX referenced in the code.

codegen(s, ..., val) with val=1 pushes exactly one value per expression and pop/pop_n only decrement the pointer, per the register arithmetic this function's own genop_2 operand construction (pop_n(len*2); pop(); genop_2(..., cursp(), len); push()) is consistent with.
limitations: NULL dereference candidate at `nint(tree->car->car->car)`: instantiable only if the not-shown parser emits a hash pair with a NULL key wrapper; the attacker's input is source text, not a raw node pointer, so no concrete trigger could be constructed from this code.

len counter int overflow (CWE-190) with val=0: len++ is unbounded when val=0, but reaching 2^31 requires ~2^31 hash pairs (a multi-gigabyte source file), and all pop_n/genop_2 sinks are val-guarded OFF on that path; only `return len` sees the wrapped value, and the caller's handling of the returned length is not shown.

Potential value-stack underflow via pop_n(len*2) would require a codegen callee that pushes fewer than two values per pair so the flush never fires; callee semantics are neither shown nor characterizable, so this remains speculative.

Unbounded recursion depth in codegen(s, ...) on deeply nested source expressions could exhaust the C stack of the compiler process; per the impact model this is a same-privilege robustness/DoS issue, not memory corruption.
The stack-pointer bound GEN_VAL_STACK_MAX is enforced in the not-shown push helper; the verdict instead rests solely on the quoted in-code flush guard bounding len.

verdict.summary: flatpak_dir_ensure_bundle_remote consumes attacker-controlled bundle fields (origin URL, gpg key bytes, collection_id, basename) but performs no copy, indexing, or output construction itself; every sentinel it requires is present and verified ('if (metadata == NULL) return NULL;', 'if (remote == NULL) return NULL;', 'if (gpg_data != NULL)'). The remaining concerns — attacker-controlled origin/keys flowing into flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote/flatpak_dir_modify_remote and the NULL-error lookup of deploy data — have impact chains that terminate entirely inside not-shown callees, so no vulnerability is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: FlatpakDecomposed is a validated-by-construction type (its constructors reject malformed refs), so 'ref' from flatpak_bundle_load is in-domain at flatpak_decomposed_dup_id/get_ref and get_deploy_data.

flatpak_dir_modify_remote and flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote are internal flatpak helpers whose remote-name/URL handling is not shown; their behavior is treated per discipline 3 (not quoted, not assumed safe for dismissal of reachability — only for impact instantiation).
limitations: Candidate A/D: attacker-controlled 'origin' URL, 'basename' and 'collection_id' from the bundle are passed unvalidated into flatpak_dir_create_origin_remote; if that callee mishandles them (e.g., remote-name collision with an existing trusted remote), a supply-chain issue could exist — but the harmful use occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee; no precondition could be instantiated here.

Candidate B: attacker-supplied gpg_data is merged into the existing deployment's origin remote via flatpak_dir_modify_remote without comparing the bundle's 'origin' field to the deployed remote; impact (attacker keys in a trusted keyring enabling malicious updates) requires unshown pull/keyring code and control of the existing remote's URL, so it remains speculative.

Candidate C: flatpak_dir_get_deploy_data is called with a NULL error slot, so a lookup error is indistinguishable from 'not deployed' and the else-branch creates a fresh remote; the failure-mode trigger inside the callee is unquoted, so this fail-open shape could not be instantiated.
No memory-corruption, injection, or output-construction primitive exists within this function's own statements; all outputs are delegated to callees whose bodies are not given.

verdict.summary: CopySliceData copies tensor slice data from a checkpoint-file-originated protobuf (sts.data().data(), attacker-controlled content and length) into the caller's buffer without verifying that the source buffer contains the number of bytes implied by tss->shape() and the slices. A malicious or truncated checkpoint record parses successfully at ParseProtoUnlimited but supplies a short/empty data field, causing CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice to read out of bounds and disclose heap memory through the destination tensor.

evidence.reason: The sink passes the raw parsed buffer sts.data().data() (attacker-controlled bytes and length from the checkpoint record obtained via sss_[idx]->Get and parsed at line 35) into the shape/slice-driven copy with no length validation anywhere in the function. Trigger: a crafted checkpoint whose record parses as a valid SavedTensorSlices but whose data field is shorter than numel(tss->shape()) * sizeof(T) yields a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), with the leaked bytes written into the caller-visible output tensor.

assumptions: CopyDataFromTensorSliceToTensorSlice reads from the source pointer as many elements as the intersection of tss->shape(), slice_s, and slice requires (standard semantics of this TensorFlow helper); its implementation is not shown in this snippet.
The checkpoint file (sstable records and tensor metadata) is attacker-originated data; this function is the intake point for those records.
limitations: CHECK_GE(idx, 0) at line 25 aborts the process if a metadata-supplied filename is absent from fname_to_index_; a malicious checkpoint can trigger a crash-only abort of the same-privilege process (robustness, not promoted to the verdict).
Destination-side overflow into data would additionally depend on the caller's buffer sizing, which is an unquoted contract and was not relied upon for this verdict.

verdict.summary: iloc_box_read allocates one GF_ItemExtentEntry per extent iteration, but the only per-iteration size guard, ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, (ptr->offset_size+ptr->length_size)), is attacker-zeroable (offset_size=length_size=0), and no check ties extent_count (u16, up to 65535) to the remaining box size. A ~400 KB well-formed 'iloc' box (version 0, all size fields 0, item_count=0xFFFF, extent_count=0xFFFF) drives 65535 x 65535 (~4.3 billion) heap allocations and list insertions with zero bytes of box size consumed per extent, exhausting process memory (attacker-scalable resource consumption / OOM DoS).

evidence.reason: Loop bound is the raw attacker-controlled u16 extent_count with no check of extent_count against the remaining box size (ptr->size); each iteration performs a GF_SAFEALLOC and gf_list_add, so with the per-iteration consumption zeroed the loop allocates up to 65535 objects per item at no size cost, yielding ~4.3 billion allocations from a ~400 KB input.

The only statement that could bound the extent loop iterations is this size decrease, but both fields are attacker-settable 4-bit values; with offset_size=0 and length_size=0 it evaluates to ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, 0), which passes unconditionally (size < 0 is false), so the guard under-admits at the minimum boundary and caps nothing.

Origin of the tainted loop bound: extent_count is read directly from the parsed file bitstream with full u16 domain (0..65535) and reaches the unbounded allocation loop at line 53 without any validation against remaining box size.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(ptr, N) checks ptr->size against N and subtracts N; the trigger value N=0 passes under any variant of this check, so the finding does not depend on the macro body, which is not shown.

GF_SAFEALLOC allocates a zeroed GF_ItemExtentEntry and gf_list_add retains it; allocations of ~4.3 billion entries exhaust available memory before completion, ending in GF_OUT_OF_MEM only after memory is consumed.
limitations: The item loop (line 23) with version 2 allows item_count up to 0xFFFFFFFF; it is capped only by the attacker-chosen declared box size (>=10 bytes consumed per item), and exhausting it beyond real file data would require bitstream read-past-EOF semantics that are not shown, so that amplification is speculative here.
gf_bs_read_int(bs, 8*size) with size up to 15 reads up to 120 bits; the returned u32 truncates, a functional parsing issue, not a memory-safety primitive.
gf_list_new() at line 52 is not NULL-checked; a crash there requires a prior allocation failure and is a robustness issue, not a security impact.
Over-read past actual file data when the declared box size exceeds available bytes depends on ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE/bitstream EOF handling outside this code; not instantiated.

verdict.summary: No locally-instantiable vulnerability: the only attacker-instantiable bad input (NULL node from gf_bifs_dec_node) is explicitly checked before first use. The double gf_node_unregister and unchecked gf_sg_command_new/gf_sg_command_field_new returns are suspicious but depend on unshown callee reference-count and allocation semantics that this code does not establish or quote.

assumptions: codec, codec->scenegraph, and node->sgprivate are initialized by the decoder before this command parser runs (internal trusted state, not attacker-instantiable from this code).
gf_node_unregister/gf_node_get_tag/gf_list_add have the standard GPAC semantics; their reference-count behavior is not shown and not quotable.
limitations: Double gf_node_unregister(node, NULL) with a comment saying 'register TWICE' is a likely reference-count misuse that could free the node before inf->new_node = node (potential UAF, CWE-416). Could not confirm: the free would occur inside the unshown gf_node_unregister, and the node's initial reference count at this point is not established by any quoted statement.

gf_sg_command_new and gf_sg_command_field_new return values (com, inf) are used without NULL checks; an allocation failure would NULL-deref at inf->new_node = node — same-privilege crash under OOM only, robustness not a security impact per the same-privilege rule.
node->sgprivate is dereferenced without a NULL test; if the decoder can return a node with NULL sgprivate it would crash, but no quoted statement produces such a node.

verdict.summary: QuantizeWithAxis computes num_slices from input.dim_size(axis_) but sizes the output min/max tensors from input_min_range's shape without any check that the two agree, then loops i to num_slices reading min_ranges(i)/max_ranges(i) and writing through &output_min_tensor->flat<float>()(i)/&output_max_tensor->flat<float>()(i) — an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write (and read) of attacker-scalable length.

evidence.reason: Sink: the loop is bounded by num_slices (from input.dim_size(axis_)) while output_min_tensor/output_max_tensor were allocated with minmax_shape (line 32/34) and min_ranges/max_ranges come from input(1)/(2); no statement anywhere equates minmax_shape.num_elements() with num_slices, so with input shape [1,4,1], axis=1, and scalar min/max inputs, i=1..3 writes and reads past the 1-element heap tensors — attacker-controlled OOB write and read.

Taint origin: num_slices is taken from the attacker-controlled input shape via an axis_ attribute that is never validated against input.dims(); this value drives the loop bound at the sink with no guard tying it to the min/max tensor sizes.

assumptions: Eigen TensorMap index checks (eigen_assert) are compiled out in release builds, so vec<float>()(i) / flat<float>()(i) perform no effective bounds check, consistent with how the TensorFlow runtime is built.

axis_ and mode_ are op attributes from an untrusted graph (attacker-data per the TF trust model); even restricting to validated axis values, the min/max-size mismatch at the sink is fully instantiable.
QuantizeSlice stores computed min/max values through the pointer arguments, characterizable callee semantics.
limitations: Secondary defects not driving the verdict: axis_ >= input.dims() makes dim_size() an OOB read of the shape vector (only DCHECK-class internals) and flat_inner_outer_dims<float,3>(axis_-1) requires dims >= axis_+2, both unguarded — same missing-validation family.
Line 36 assumes input dtype float without a local dtype check; a non-float input triggers a CHECK-type abort (same-privilege crash, not corruption).
pre_dim/post_dim int64 product overflow deemed infeasible because the input tensor must be materializable in memory.

verdict.summary: All in-code uses of the attacker-controlled tensors are guarded: matrix/vector shape checks, count-equality checks, and `dense_shape->NumElements() > 0` jointly keep the only direct memory access `indices->matrix<int64_t>()(i, 0)` in bounds (indices of shape [N,0] is rejected before the loop), and SparseTensor::Create's failure sentinel is checked via OP_REQUIRES_OK. Values that this code does not validate (negative batch index -1 admitted by `>=`, negative/huge dense_shape dims, tensor dtypes) are consumed only in code not shown (TensorShape constructor, SparseTensor::Create, dataset iteration), so no impact link is instantiated here.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK abort the function via return on failure, so each check protects statements that follow it in execution order; this matches the macros' standard TensorFlow semantics.

Standard TensorFlow semantics assumed for characterizable helpers: Tensor::matrix<T>()/vec<T>() validate dtype internally (error, not out-of-bounds), and TensorShape construction rejects negative dimensions on an error path.
limitations: The ordering check `next_batch_index >= previous_batch_index` with `previous_batch_index = -1` admits a first batch index of -1; whether a negative or out-of-range batch index causes harm depends on validation inside sparse::SparseTensor::Create and the dataset iterator, neither of which is shown, so this candidate stays speculative.

dense_shape element values (negative or huge dimensions) are not validated in this code; the resulting TensorShape construction at most yields an error status or a CHECK abort (crash of the same-privilege process that supplied the input), not a demonstrable memory-corruption or bypass primitive here.
Dtype of indices/values/dense_shape is enforced by the op registration (not shown); a mismatched dtype would only trip the internal type CHECK in matrix<T>()/vec<T>(), i.e. an abort.
Allocation of std_order and the ordering loop scale linearly with the attacker-supplied tensors' own sizes (amplification factor 1); no independent resource-consumption defect was found.

verdict.summary: In njs_module_path, when a search directory is given (dir != NULL), the bounds check `length > NJS_MAX_PATH` is computed from dir->length (+1 for a missing trailing slash) only: the initialization `length = info->name.length;` is overwritten by `length = dir->length;`, so the subsequent `njs_cpymem(p, info->name.start, info->name.length)` copies the attacker-controlled module-name length into the fixed stack buffer `char src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1]` without any bound on the name portion, producing an attacker-sized and attacker-content out-of-bounds stack write.

evidence.reason: Sink: copies info->name.length attacker-controlled bytes at p (= src + dir->length + trail), but no statement bounds info->name.length on the dir != NULL path; e.g. dir->length=11, name.length=5000 writes ~914 bytes past the end of char src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1], an out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787).

Origin of the defect: this assignment discards the previously computed name length (length = info->name.length), so the only bounds check (length > NJS_MAX_PATH) validates just the directory portion and never covers the module-name bytes later copied into src.

assumptions: info->name (module name from a JS import statement) and dir (search-path element) are the attacker-controlled inputs across the njs trust boundary; per the width-domain rule their size_t lengths can hold any representable value since no narrowing producer is quoted in this code.
NJS_MAX_PATH is the intended capacity of char src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1]; the guard's constant matches the buffer declaration, which the code itself shows (line 6 vs line 25).
limitations: A potential secondary overflow of info->path by realpath() depends on the width of the path field, which is declared outside the shown code and could not be instantiated here.

The dir == NULL branch is provably safe: length = info->name.length is checked with `> NJS_MAX_PATH`, so a name of exactly NJS_MAX_PATH bytes plus the NUL at index NJS_MAX_PATH still fits in src[NJS_MAX_PATH + 1].

verdict.summary: No primary security defect is instantiable from this code. All callee returns (avc_parse_slice, gf_avc_read_sps_bs_internal, gf_avc_read_pps_bs_internal, gf_bs_read_ue) are sentinel-checked with correct sign/width semantics, the NALU type is masked to 0..31 with a default switch arm, ret is defined on every path to its use, and the sps deref at line 80 is preceded by 'if (!avc->s_info.sps) return -1;'. The one residual gap — that guard tests avc->s_info.sps while the right-hand operand dereferences n_state.sps, which only the unshown avc_parse_slice can set to NULL — yields at most a same-privilege NULL-deref crash (CWE-476 robustness), which per the analysis rules is recorded as a limitation, not a verdict.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_u8 returns 0 at end-of-stream (standard GPAC BitStream semantics), so nal_hdr is always in 0..255 even on truncated input.
bs and avc are non-NULL per internal caller contract; a NULL bs/avc crashes at lines 8/13 before any parsing, which is caller-contract robustness, not attacker-instantiable corruption.
limitations: Null-deref candidate (CWE-476), not promoted: line 80 'if (avc->s_info.sps->poc_type == n_state.sps->poc_type)' dereferences n_state.sps, but the only nearby guard (lines 77-78, 'if (!avc->s_info.sps) return -1;') checks a different variable. To reach the deref, avc->s_info.sps must be non-NULL (line 77 forces it), so n_state.sps can only be NULL if the not-shown callee avc_parse_slice (line 54) returns >=0 while leaving si->sps NULL — a callee state this code neither quotes nor produces; and the impact is a same-privilege crash only, which the impact model classifies as robustness, never a verdict.

Same shape on break paths: lines 158-159 'if (slice) avc_compute_poc(&n_state);' can run with n_state.sps NULL (e.g., avc->s_info.sps NULL at entry and an early break at line 61/65/70/75 skipping line 77), but the deref would occur entirely inside the unshown callee avc_compute_poc, so no in-code impact link can be quoted.

Speculative UAF: if the unshown gf_avc_read_sps_bs_internal frees/replaces an AVC_SPS still referenced by avc->s_info.sps, later derefs (lines 80, 149-151) could be use-after-free; no free or replacement is quotable in this code, so the precondition cannot be instantiated here.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability. The only attacker-data input, md, flows solely into a constant-time full-length comparison (crypto_memneq) whose length is the same value used to size the comparison buffer (xmalloc(len)); digest_final errors propagate and no path returns success without a passing compare. Residual robustness concerns (unchecked xmalloc sentinel, no len>0 validation) are speculative because no attacker-reachable statement instantiates them.

assumptions: crypto_memneq performs a full constant-time comparison over exactly len bytes (standard memneq semantics)
digest_final writes exactly digest_length(d) bytes on success and returns 0, making xmalloc(len) and the compare length mutually consistent by construction
len = digest_length(d) is the registered algorithm's fixed digest length, set at algorithm-registration time by the crypto framework, not by any attacker-parsed data consumed here
limitations: tmp = xmalloc(len) (line 7) is not NULL-checked before first use in digest_final(d, tmp) (line 9); if the allocator returned NULL this would be a NULL write inside the callee, a same-privilege crash — kept out of the verdict per discipline 3, and the x-allocator convention of aborting on failure is an unquoted contract I did not use to dismiss it, only to bound impact

len is consumed at xmalloc(len) and crypto_memneq(md, tmp, len) without a len > 0 check; if digest_length(d) could ever return 0, crypto_memneq(md, tmp, 0) returns 0 and verification would trivially pass (fail-open), and a negative len would wrap to a huge size_t allocation — but no quoted statement or attacker-reachable state instantiates len <= 0, as it requires a zero/negative-length digest algorithm to be registered in code not shown
md must reference at least len readable bytes; that caller-side buffer-length contract is not checkable in this code

verdict.summary: BD_DecMFFieldVec parses an attacker-controlled BIFS bitstream; the attacker-derived nbFields (up to 2^31-1) is used as an allocation size and loop bound, but the allocation is sized from the same expression as the loop bound with a checked error arm ('if (e) return e;'), and the MFNODE loop exits on the quoted NULL-node error arm when the bitstream is exhausted, bounding work by input size. No unguarded sink with a fully instantiated impact chain remains in this code.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_int(bs, n) returns an n-bit value (n<=31 here), so nbFields is bounded by 2^31-1 within u32; standard failure sentinels (error returns, NULL node) are handled as quoted.
gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc sizes the allocation from the same nbFields expression used as the loop bound and reports failure via its return value, which is checked before the loop runs.
limitations: gf_bifs_dec_qp14_set_length(codec, nbFields) passes the raw attacker-derived count into a callee whose semantics are not shown; if that callee allocates or indexes using nbFields without internal bounds, a defect exists there, but no impact link is quotable here.

Integer overflow of nbFields * item-size inside gf_sg_vrml_mf_alloc is not provable from this code; the allocation error sentinel is checked, so a failed/overflowed allocation cannot reach the decode loop.

The register(NULL)/unregister(node) pairing in the force_keep_qp branch was traced arithmetically (net +1 ref) and showed no over-release, but gf_node_unregister's parent-notification semantics are not shown; a mismatch is only possible if that callee changes refcounts beyond the arithmetic visible here.
A NULL field parameter would dereference at field->fieldIndex, but that is a same-privilege caller-contract crash, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability. All memory writes are sized by value_count/args_count/args_offset derived from the same active frame and function object whose frame allocation and construction occur in code not shown; every candidate (undersized destination frame, union confusion via function->u.lambda on a native function, args_offset==0 underflow, NULL function) requires a value no statement in this code can produce.

assumptions: The caller allocates the destination frame with a size computed from the same function object (args_count, args_offset, temp) and the same active-frame value_count, per the njs frame-allocation convention; that code is not shown here.
njs_function_frame_save is only invoked for lambda (closures), so function->u.lambda is valid at the dereference; the dispatch site is not shown.
function->args_offset >= 1 at all frame_save sites, an invariant established at function construction in unshown code.
limitations: Speculative: an undersized caller-allocated 'frame' would turn the 'while (start < end)' copy loop into an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) — cannot be instantiated from any statement in this snippet.
Speculative: if active->function could be a native (non-lambda) function here, 'function->u.lambda->temp' reads the wrong union arm (CWE-119); reachability depends on the unshown dispatch logic.
Speculative: 'function->args_offset - 1' underflows if args_offset were 0; no quoted statement can set it to 0.
Speculative: 'function' is used without a NULL check (first use at 'function->u.lambda->temp'); a NULL would only crash the same-privilege VM process with no demonstrated corruption path.

verdict.summary: The only locally-instantiable attack value, a negative position index, is provably rejected before the Gather call by the negativity scan (lines 7-12) enforced via TF_LITE_ENSURE at line 13, which returns before the sink in execution order. Remaining candidates (positive out-of-range indices, shape/bytes mismatch, axis/batch_dims misuse) place the harm entirely inside the not-shown optimized_ops::Gather / interpreter and cannot be instantiated from this code.

assumptions: PositionsT is a signed integer type such that the comparison indexes[i] < 0 at line 8 can be true for negative values; if unsigned, negatives are unrepresentable and the guard is vacuously complete.
TF_LITE_ENSURE macro returns a non-Ok status before the statement following it, so line 13 exits the function before the call at line 18 when the flag is false.
limitations: Positive out-of-range indices (index >= input dimension size) are not validated in this code; whether they cause an out-of-bounds access depends on bounds checks inside optimized_ops::Gather, which is not shown and cannot be characterized from standard-function semantics.

num_indices is derived from positions->bytes while the callee consumes indices per GetTensorShape(positions); a malformed model where bytes < shape-count * sizeof(PositionsT) would let unchecked indices reach Gather, but the tensor allocation/consistency behavior of the not-shown interpreter is an unquoted contract.
params.axis and params.batch_dims are attacker-influenced model values passed raw to the not-shown callee; no local validation exists, but no impact link is quotable here.

GetTensorData may return NULL for an empty tensor; a NULL dereference of indexes would at most crash the same-privilege process that supplied the model file (robustness issue, not a security verdict driver).

verdict.summary: In MakeDataset, the only validation of the 'indices' op input is a rank check (TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix, which passes for shape (N,0)). The ordering loop then unconditionally reads indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0) for i < dim_size(0), accessing column 0 of a matrix that may have zero columns. An attacker supplying an int64 tensor of shape (N>0, 0) causes an out-of-bounds heap read of the zero-element tensor buffer, before any downstream SparseTensor::Create validation can run.

evidence.snippet:
for (int64_t i = 0; i < indices->dim_size(0); ++i) {
      int64_t next_batch_index = indices->matrix<int64>()(i, 0);
evidence.reason: Sink: matrix()(i,0) requires dim_size(1) >= 1, but no statement in the code checks the column count; with indices of shape (3,0) the loop bound only caps the row index i, and the read of column 0 accesses memory outside the zero-element tensor buffer (heap OOB read, instantiated trigger: int64 tensor shape (N>0, 0)).

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES(ctx, TensorShapeUtils::IsMatrix(indices->shape()),
                errors::InvalidArgument(
                    "Input indices should be a matrix but received shape ",
                    indices->shape().DebugString()));
evidence.reason: The only guard on 'indices' shape; IsMatrix enforces rank==2 only and provably admits a 0-column matrix (dims()==2 for shape (3,0)), so it does not constrain dim_size(1) and cannot protect the column-0 read at line 32.

assumptions: Op inputs (indices, values, dense_shape) are attacker-controlled across the kernel trust boundary with the full Tensor domain, including rank-2 shapes with dim_size(1)==0 and arbitrary int64 contents.
A TensorFlow Tensor with zero elements is backed by a non-null allocated buffer, so reading element 0 is a heap out-of-bounds read rather than a null dereference.
limitations: Missing dtype checks: a non-int64 'indices' or 'dense_shape' tensor reaches matrix<int64>()/vec<int64>(), which triggers a CHECK abort (same-privilege crash, not memory corruption) — robustness issue, not the verdict.
The monotonicity check previous_batch_index = -1 with '>=' admits batch index -1; any harmful consequence depends on SparseTensor::Create and downstream dataset slicing, which are not shown.

No check that indices->dim_size(0) matches values->NumElements() or that dense_shape elements are non-negative; these flow into SparseTensor::Create and TensorShape(vec<int64>()) whose validation is not shown, so no impact could be instantiated.
If the runtime's zero-element tensor buffer were NULL, the OOB read would degrade to a null dereference (crash only).

verdict.summary: pjmedia_rtcp_fb_parse_rpsi performs unchecked unsigned arithmetic on attacker-controlled RTCP fields: (1) `rpsi_len = (pj_ntohs(hdr->length)-2)*4` wraps negative for hdr->length < 2, and the wrap also makes the guard `length < rpsi_len + 12` under-admit (2^W-8+12 wraps to 4), permitting direct out-of-bounds reads at `padlen = *p++`; (2) `rpsi->rpsi_bit_len = rpsi_len*8 - 16 - padlen` underflows whenever padlen exceeds the payload bits (padlen is a raw attacker byte, 0-255, never checked), producing a ~2^(W-3)-byte length passed to pj_strset — a massive out-of-bounds read primitive on any use of rpsi->rpsi.

evidence.reason: Unsigned underflow at the sink: padlen (attacker byte, 0-255, no clamp anywhere) is subtracted from rpsi_len*8-16 with no check that rpsi_len >= 2 and padlen <= rpsi_len*8-16. Trigger: hdr->length=3 (rpsi_len=4), padlen=255 → rpsi_bit_len = 32-16-255 = -239 → wraps to 2^W-239; (rpsi_bit_len+7)/8 ≈ 2^(W-3) is stored as the rpsi string length on a ~20-byte buffer, an out-of-bounds read of astronomically attacker-scalable length. With hdr->length=2 (rpsi_len=0) the same line yields 0-16-padlen underflow.

Taint origin of the second trigger: for attacker-set hdr->length = 0, (0-2)*4 = -8 converts to pj_size_t as 2^W-8; the guard `length < rpsi_len + 12` then computes (2^W-8)+12 = 4 (wrap) and `4 < 4` is false, so a 4-byte buffer passes, after which `padlen = *p++` reads 1-2 bytes out of bounds at offsets 4-5.

assumptions: pj_size_t is unsigned (PJSIP convention), so the negative results of (ntohs(length)-2)*4 and rpsi_len*8-16-padlen wrap to near-max values.

pj_strset(str, ptr, len) only assigns ptr/slen (standard PJLIB semantics); the out-of-bounds read materializes on any consumer of rpsi->rpsi, but storing an out-of-domain huge length is already the defect at line 26.
pjmedia_rtcp_common is 4 bytes (V/P/RC/X, PT, 16-bit length), so sizeof(*hdr)=4 offsets the reads in the hdr->length<2 trigger.
limitations: DoS/robustness variants that need a consumer of rpsi->rpsi not shown are not counted as separate findings; the verdict rests on the in-code OOB reads (lines 23-24 with length==4) and the wrapped lengths stored at lines 25-26.
The trust level of the calling process is unknown, so severity is capped at medium rather than rated for privilege-gain info disclosure.

verdict.summary: gen_assignment consumes attacker-supplied AST nodes but every arithmetic/stack sink is bounded by quoted guards: gen_values' return is clamped by 'if (n < 0) { n = 15; push(); }' and all subsequent increments are capped by 'if (n < 14)' / 'if (n < 15) { n++; if (n == 15) { pop_n(14); genop_2(s, OP_ARRAY, cursp(), 15); } }', whose pop counts match the pushes made on the same path; the lv_idx use is guarded by 'if (idx > 0)'. No attacker-instantiable memory-corruption, injection, or bypass trigger survives simulation.

assumptions: nint/nsym/lv_idx/gen_values/gen_hash/gen_move/genop_*/new_sym/attrsym/pop_n/push/dispatch behave per mruby codegen register-slot conventions; gen_values' limit argument caps its return and a negative return signals variable-length args (converted to n=15 by the quoted check).
codegen_error does not return (raises), so the NODE_NVAR/default error arms terminate generation.
limitations: Dereferences such as 'tree->cdr', 'tree->cdr->car', and 'tree->cdr->cdr->car' have no NULL checks in this code; a malformed AST from the not-shown parser would NULL-deref the same-privilege compiler process — a robustness issue (CWE-476-shaped crash), not instantiated as corruption here.

Push/pop slot balance for the NODE_CALL path ultimately relies on the unshown register semantics of gen_values, gen_hash, and gen_move; an imbalance there would misallocate VM stack slots but is not quotable from this code.

Unlike upstream mruby gen_assignment, this code contains no block-argument handling (tree->cdr->cdr->cdr / OP_SENDB path) for the NODE_CALL/NODE_SCALL arms; this is a functional omission with no security effect visible here.

Dismissed only because the harmful use is entirely in code not given and no in-domain contract is quotable.

verdict.summary: Top-level ISO box parser. All memory-sensitive sinks are guarded: the JP unknown-box deref is protected by the short-circuit (box->dataSize==4) check before c[0..3], the otyp list insert is protected by 'if (pos<0) pos=0;', and moov->mvhd is unconditionally validated before its later use. Remaining defects are same-privilege NULL-deref crashes on malformed files (trak without mdia/minf; moof without mfhd) and a dead seg_ssix/root_ssix cleanup typo whose trigger (root_ssix non-NULL) is never produced in this code — none instantiate a direct security impact per discipline 3.

assumptions: gf_isom_parse_root_box returns a non-NULL box on success (e>=0) and a negative error otherwise, per standard GPAC semantics; the 'if (e >= 0)' arm therefore receives a valid 'a'.
gf_isom_box_del and gf_list_del_item tolerate NULL arguments per standard GPAC semantics.
mov struct fields (e.g. root_ssix) are zero-initialized at file-open; this code contains no other assignment to root_ssix.
limitations: NULL-deref crash (CWE-476): 'if (trak->Media->information->sampleTable->sampleGroups)' dereferences Media/information/sampleTable with no NULL check; a moov containing a trak without an mdia (or mdia without minf) crashes the parser in non-debug mode. Impact is a same-privilege crash on attacker-supplied file content — robustness/DoS, excluded from the verdict per discipline 3.

NULL-deref crash (CWE-476): 'mov->NextMoofNumber = mov->moof->mfhd->sequence_number+1;' in GF_ISOM_OPEN_KEEP_FRAGMENTS mode dereferences mfhd without a NULL check; a moof box without mfhd crashes the parser. Same crash-only classification.

Latent UAF/double-free (CWE-416) not triggerable in this code: 'gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix); mov->root_ssix = NULL;' frees the seg_ssix box but clears root_ssix, leaving mov->seg_ssix dangling; a later SSIX box would double-free it at 'if (mov->seg_ssix) gf_isom_box_del(mov->seg_ssix);'. However, the guarding branch requires mov->root_ssix != NULL and no statement in this code ever assigns root_ssix — the trigger precondition (an external setter of root_ssix) could not be instantiated from the given code.
Unchecked 'gf_list_new()'/'gf_list_add(mov->emsgs, a)' returns would deref NULL only under allocation failure (OOM) — speculative resource condition.
When GPAC_DISABLE_ISOM_FRAGMENTS is defined, totSize is accumulated from an uninitialized value (CWE-457), but it is never consumed after initialization paths — no reachable impact.

verdict.summary: Every attacker-influenced write to the output tensor is guarded by the quoted bounds check `OP_REQUIRES(ctx, 0 <= loc && loc < output_elements, ...)` placed immediately before each of the four `output_t(loc)` assignments on all paths; the check uses the correct operators and the exact element-count unit matching the flat output buffer size, blocking out-of-range inner products (including negative and int64-wrapped values). No primary vulnerability survives the simulation.

assumptions: `ValidateShapes` is invoked via `OP_REQUIRES_OK` and aborts the op on invalid input structure (its body is not shown, so no security conclusion rests on its internal checks).
`output->flat<float>()` has exactly `output_shape.num_elements()` elements because the tensor was allocated from `output_shape` via `ctx->allocate_output("output", output_shape, &output)`.
limitations: Rank-edge cases could not be fully simulated: with a rank-0 truth shape, `std::vector<int64_t> group_dims(truth_st_shape.dims() - 1)` underflows to a huge size (allocation failure/abort), and with a rank-1 truth shape `output_strides[output_shape.dims() - 1] = 1` indexes an empty vector at -1. Both triggers require that the not-shown `ValidateShapes` accept rank<2 shape vectors; reachability rests on unshown code, so these are recorded as speculative crash/DoS paths, not confirmed defects.

A rank mismatch between hypothesis and truth (e.g., `hypothesis_st_shape.dim_size(d)` for d beyond the hypothesis rank in the AddDim loop) could similarly CHECK-fail if not rejected by the not-shown `ValidateShapes`; speculative.
`output_t(loc) /= truth_seq.size()` under `normalize_` is a floating-point division by a size_t converted to float; an empty sequence yields IEEE infinity, not an integer division-by-zero fault.

verdict.summary: gf_avc_parse_nalu dereferences avc->s_info.sps (and n_state.sps) at line 79 with no effective NULL guard: the only checks are a debug-only assert (line 77) and a NULL test (line 148) that executes after the first use. The SVC arm (line 29) explicitly discards svc_parse_slice's failure return and memcpy's a state with sps==NULL and nal_unit_type==GF_AVC_NALU_SVC_SLICE into avc->s_info; that type value defeats the AU gate at lines 57-60, so the next parsed non-IDR slice reaches the unchecked dereference, crashing the process parsing the attacker-supplied stream (denial of service).

evidence.reason: Root cause: avc->s_info.sps is dereferenced with only a debug assert as validation (no-op under NDEBUG); the later 'if (ret && avc->s_info.sps)' check at line 148 runs after this first use. Trigger: an SVC-slice NAL (type 20, ref_idc 0) that fails parsing leaves avc->s_info.sps NULL with nal_unit_type 20 (memcpy lines 37/40), the gate at lines 57-60 admits nal_unit_type==20, and a following valid non-IDR slice with frame_num=0, field_pic_flag=0, nal_ref_idc=0 reaches line 79 and dereferences the NULL sps.

Origin of the tainted state: the failure sentinel of svc_parse_slice is deliberately discarded, so a parse failure (e.g., slice referencing an undefined PPS in an attacker stream) leaves n_state.sps NULL; lines 37/40 then memcpy this state (nal_unit_type=20, sps=NULL) into avc->s_info, enabling the unchecked dereference at line 79.

assumptions: svc_parse_slice fails without setting n_state->sps on streams lacking the referenced PPS/SPS — its standard failure path, though the callee body is not shown.
Release builds compile with NDEBUG so assert(avc->s_info.sps) is inert; in debug builds the assert itself aborts on attacker input, which is still a crash.
limitations: Line 127 'avc->last_ps_idx = (s32) gf_bs_read_ue(bs);' stores an attacker-controlled exp-Golomb value with only a '< 0' test and no upper-bound check; a potential out-of-bounds index, but the array indexing that would consume last_ps_idx is not in this code, so the impact is not instantiated here.

Line 34 'avc_compute_poc(&n_state)' runs after the discarded svc_parse_slice return; if avc_compute_poc dereferences si->sps it would crash first, but its body is not shown — either path yields the same NULL-sps denial of service.

verdict.summary: afra_box_read validates entry_count against the remaining box size (line 14) but never validates global_entry_count before using it as the loop bound (line 37); an attacker-supplied u32 count drives a loop that heap-allocates a GF_GlobalAfraEntry and grows a list on every iteration, with the only brake (ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE) permitting one allocation per ~20 consumed bytes and firing only after the allocation, enabling attacker-scalable memory/CPU consumption while parsing a crafted MP4 file.

evidence.reason: global_entry_count is a full-domain attacker-controlled u32 read from the file and used directly as a loop bound with a per-iteration heap allocation and list insertion, with no count-vs-remaining-size check (the twin check 'if (ptr->size / ((ptr->long_offsets ? 16 : 12)) < ptr->entry_count) return GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE;' exists at line 14 for entry_count but has no counterpart here). Trigger: global_entries=1, global_entry_count=0xFFFFFFFF in a crafted afra box causes unvalidated count-driven allocation until data exhaustion, an attacker-scalable resource-consumption (DoS) primitive.

assumptions: ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE rejects (returns GF_ISOM_INVALID_FILE) when ptr->size < the requested byte count and subtracts it otherwise, matching standard GPAC semantics; under that semantics no out-of-bounds read or write is reachable, so the defect is resource consumption, not memory corruption.
The box lists (local_access_entries/global_access_entries) are pre-initialized by the GPAC box framework, so gf_list_insert is operating on valid containers.
limitations: Memory amplification is bounded to roughly a small constant factor of the box payload size as long as the caller enforces declared box size <= remaining file bytes; the unbounded 2^32-allocation scenario additionally relies on the caller tolerating boxes whose declared size exceeds the file (truncated-file handling not shown), which could not be verified from this code.
The return value of gf_list_insert is not checked (lines 31, 61); on allocation failure the freshly allocated entry leaks — a same-privilege robustness issue only, not a security verdict driver.

The entry_count validation at lines 13-15 was verified correct at both flag branches and both boundaries (divisor exactly matches per-entry consumption of 12/16 bytes); no operator or unit anomaly found there.

verdict.summary: The single element of the attacker-supplied x5c array (att_cert) is consumed via cbor_bytestring_handle/cbor_bytestring_length without any cbor_isa_bytestring type check; a remote WebAuthn registrant who places a CBOR integer (or float/array/map) inside x5c causes a type-confused union read, producing an attacker-chosen pointer and size that gnutls_x509_crt_import dereferences, crashing the authentication server (remote DoS) or reading out of bounds.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing type check on att_cert before the bytestring accessors. Trigger: attStmt = {"x5c": [<CBOR negative int 0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA>], "sig": h'00'} passes line 48 (array, size 1), and cbor_bytestring_handle type-confuses the union, yielding an attacker-controlled pointer/size passed to gnutls_x509_crt_import at line 55, which dereferences it. The analogous guard 'if (sig == NULL || !cbor_isa_bytestring(sig))' exists at line 93 for sig but is absent for att_cert.
Origin of the tainted value: the x5c value is taken directly from the attacker-controlled attStmt CBOR map with no validation of its element types at this point.

assumptions: cbor_bytestring_handle/cbor_bytestring_length on a non-bytestring item read the item's data union, which for integer/float items holds the numeric payload rather than a valid data pointer (libcbor accessor semantics; these accessors are only defined for bytestrings).
gnutls_x509_crt_import parses DER from cert_dat.data[0..cert_dat.size], dereferencing the supplied pointer.
limitations: o_strlen((char *)client_data) at line 87 assumes client_data is NUL-terminated; the producer is not shown, so an over-read there depends on an unexhibited caller and is not instantiated here.

A size_t wrap in the o_malloc length sum (line 98) would require attacker-controlled lengths near 2^64, which this code's producers (not shown) would have to supply; not instantiable from the given statements.
The lenient key comparison MIN(o_strlen("x5c"), cbor_string_length(key)) lets a key 'x5' match 'x5c', but both extracted values are still type/NULL-checked downstream, so no bypass was demonstrated.
Impact is a forged-pointer dereference (crash / out-of-bounds read) inside gnutls import; no direct memory write primitive was identified.

verdict.summary: The bounds checks `offsets[tile_idx] + sizeof(int)*5 > size` (tiled) and `offsets[y_idx] + sizeof(int)*2 > size` (scanline) perform 64-bit unsigned addition that wraps: an attacker-supplied chunk offset near 2^64 (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB) wraps the sum to a small value that passes the check, so `head + offsets[i]` yields a pointer BEFORE the input buffer and the subsequent memcpy reads out of bounds (heap underflow read, up to ~20 bytes before `head`, repeatable per tile/scanline block). The missing guard is an overflow-safe bound (e.g. `offsets[i] > size || size - offsets[i] < header_size`), which appears nowhere in the code.
