Origin of the leaked allocation: this kzalloc'd object has no matching kfree on any error exit in this function, so each failed probe orphans it.

assumptions: rsi_find_bulk_in_and_out_endpoints can return nonzero for attacker-controlled USB descriptors (missing bulk endpoints), making the error paths reachable by a hostile device; this is the standard contract of endpoint-enumeration helpers and matches the call's error handling here.
limitations: adapter->rsi_dev = rsi_dev (line 11) is stored before failure; if the caller frees adapter on error while this leaked rsi_dev still holds adapter->priv, any later dereference is undefined — but no such use is shown, so no UAF is instantiated here.
usb_set_intfdata(pfunction, adapter) (line 21) runs before the error exits, leaving stale intfdata if the caller tears down adapter; consequences would occur only in the not-shown disconnect handler.
Per-event leak size is one struct rsi_91x_usbdev, so exploitability is limited to slow memory exhaustion via repeated device replug; severity assessed low for this reason.

verdict.summary: No memory-safety vulnerability in this snippet: the memset at line 10 is provably in-bounds because dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) at line 6 allocates the exact same constant expression, and skb_pull is a no-op on a fresh skb (len=0) so it cannot move skb->data out of bounds. verdict.summary: Off-by-one loop bound in crun_command_exec: `for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)` copies one element too many, passing the C-guaranteed NULL sentinel argv[argc] to xstrdup (line 44), causing a NULL-pointer dereference; additionally args_len is set to argc (line 41), an overcount versus the argc-first_arg-1 real entries, leaving NULL members in the args array handed to libcrun_container_exec_with_options. Trigger is deterministic for any `crun exec <id> <cmd...>` invocation; the crash lands in a runtime process typically spawned by a privileged container manager with user-originated command lines, giving at least denial of service.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)
        process->args[i] = xstrdup (argv[first_arg + i + 1]);
evidence.reason: The loop bound `argc - first_arg` admits one iteration past the last real argument: at i = argc-first_arg-1 the source index is first_arg+i+1 = argc, so xstrdup receives argv[argc], which the C standard guarantees is NULL; strdup(NULL) dereferences NULL and crashes. The only nearby check, `crun_assert_n_args (argc - first_arg, ..., 2, -1)`, enforces a minimum count, not the loop bound; the allocation on line 42 is (argc+1) pointers and does not constrain the read. Missing guard: `i < argc - first_arg - 1`. Concrete trigger: `crun exec ct /bin/sh` → argc=4, first_arg=2, i=1 reads argv[4]==NULL.

args_len is recorded as the full argc although only argc-first_arg-1 argument strings are populated (remaining slots are xmalloc0-zeroed NULLs); the length overcount travels with exec_opts.process into libcrun_container_exec_with_options, so NULL members are presented within the declared array length. This is the origin statement of the same defect family as the line 43-44 sink.

assumptions: xstrdup is the crun helper wrapping strdup (no NULL-accepting overload quoted in this code); strdup(NULL) is undefined behavior that on glibc dereferences NULL and crashes. Even under a hypothetical NULL-returning implementation, a NULL member would remain inside the args_len-declared array.

argp_parse with ARGP_IN_ORDER leaves first_arg at the index of the first non-option argument (the container id), matching upstream crun semantics; the code itself relies on this via argv[first_arg] at line 19.
argv[argc] == NULL is a C-standard invariant, so the trigger value is always instantiable, not attacker-forged.
limitations: The concrete impact is a NULL-pointer dereference/crash (denial of the exec path) rather than memory corruption; there is no out-of-bounds write because the destination buffer is allocated with argc+1 pointers, larger than any index the loop writes.

The downstream effect of args_len = argc (line 41) depends on libcrun_container_exec_with_options, which is not shown; a consumer that iterates args_len entries would meet NULL members, but that use is outside this code.

crun_context.listen_fds is taken from getenv("LISTEN_FDS") via unvalidated strtoll (lines 28-31); negative or huge values flow into preserve_fds, but the variable is controlled only by the same local user who invoked crun and its consumption is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated here.

Severity is rated low: the crash is deterministic (every `crun exec` invocation without --process fails), and while OCI runtimes are typically spawned by privileged container managers with user-originated command lines, the crash is confined to the per-request runtime process.

verdict.summary: In the Orcad tool-change-stop-switch path, `tmps = get_line(fd++);` post-increments the gerb_file_t pointer past its heap allocation; the subsequent `fd->filename` argument to gerbv_stats_printf reads a filename pointer from out-of-bounds heap memory and prints it via %s, giving an attacker (who crafts a drill file containing "TCST") an out-of-bounds read that can crash the parser or disclose adjacent heap contents. The tool_num array indexing is correctly guarded.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the post-increment in `get_line(fd++)` advances fd by one whole struct; the error printf then dereferences `fd->filename` at fd+1, outside the gerb_file_t allocation. Trigger: any untrusted drill file containing the sequence 'T','C','S','T' (satisfying `(fd->ptr + 2) < fd->datalen`), reaching L26-L30 with fd mis-pointed; the OOB-read pointer is printed via %s.

assumptions: gerb_file_t objects are heap-allocated per-file by the caller (gerbv's gerb_fopen), so fd+1 reads past the end of the allocation; even if it landed in adjacent heap, reading and %s-printing a garbage pointer is an OOB read/info disclosure.
TOOL_MAX matches the image->aperture array capacity (gerbv convention TOOL_MAX == APERTURE_MAX), making the quoted `tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX` check a complete guard at both bounds.

The `if ('\n' == temp || '\r' == temp) gerb_ungetc(fd);` is dead code placed inside `if (EOF == temp)`, so newlines after tool definitions are consumed instead of restored — functional line-counting bug only.
`16 + 8 * tool_num` integer overflow would require TOOL_MAX > ~2.7e8; tool_num is rejected `>= TOOL_MAX` first, and no such macro value is shown, so this is not instantiated.

verdict.summary: string_scan_range guards the 4-byte r_read_le32 optimization read with `needle < to - 4`, which is computed in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic; when the attacker-controlled scan range ends at to < 4 (e.g. from=0, to=bf->size=3 for a 1-3 byte input), to-4 wraps to ~2^64, the guard passes, and r_read_le32 reads 4 bytes from a heap buffer of only to-from (1-3) bytes — a heap out-of-bounds read of up to 3 bytes.

evidence.snippet:
if (needle < to - 4) {
			ut32 n1 = r_read_le32 (buf + (needle - from));
evidence.reason: The bound `needle < to - 4` is the only guard on the 4-byte read, but `to - 4` underflows in ut64 when to < 4, so the guard passes and r_read_le32 reads buf[0..3] from a buffer sized calloc(to-from, 1) (1-3 bytes). Trigger: from=0, to=3 (scan of a 3-byte file: to = bf->size); len=3 passes the `len < 1 || len > ST32_MAX` check, the while condition passes, and 0 < 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF is true, yielding a 1-3 byte heap overread.

static int string_scan_range(RList *list, RBinFile *bf, int min,
			      const ut64 from, const ut64 to, int type, int raw, RBinSection *section) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: `from` and `to` are unchecked ut64 parameters of this exported, non-static API (instantiable from file size or scan-range arguments across the trust boundary); no statement in the function rejects to < 4 or enforces to-from >= 4 before the read at line 78.

assumptions: r_read_le32 reads exactly 4 bytes from the given pointer (standard semantics of the radare2 byte-reader helper).

from and to reach this function from callers such as bin string scanning where to is derived from the input file size or user-supplied range, making values with to < 4 instantiable; even without that, the parameters' full ut64 domain is the input surface per the width-domain rule.
limitations: `int outlen = len * 4` (line 47) can overflow signed int for len > 0x1FFFFFFF (~512MB range), producing a negative outlen passed to r_charset_encode_str; the effect depends on the not-shown callee's handling of a negative length, so no impact is instantiated here.

The charset re-encode path sets `len = res` (line 58) where res may be an error sentinel from r_charset_encode_str; the loop bound `needle < to` still uses the original range, but all reads remain inside the 4x over-allocated `out = calloc(len, 4)` (line 48), so no out-of-bounds access results.

The ascii_only re-scan path (`needle = str_start; continue`) could theoretically oscillate without progress for crafted data, an unbounded-consumption concern; the is_breaked callback and the unproven re-detection sequence make this speculative.
The overread value n1 is only tested for zero, so the practical impact is a small ASAN-detectable heap overread rather than a meaningful disclosure.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability is fully instantiated within this code. The loop bound `i < bin->ne_header->SegCount` caps indexing of bin->segment_entries, but the allocation that sizes segment_entries is not in this snippet, so an out-of-bounds read cannot be proven (nor excluded) here. Unchecked NULL dereferences of bin->ne_header, bin->segment_entries, and the r_list_newf result would only crash the same-privilege process parsing the attacker's own file and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: bin->ne_header, bin->segment_entries, and bin->alignment are populated by the NE file loader (not shown) and hold attacker-derived file content.
r_list_newf, R_NEW0, and r_str_newf follow their documented semantics (list/new/strdup-style allocation, returning NULL on failure).
limitations: Speculative: possible out-of-bounds read at `NE_image_segment_entry *se = &bin->segment_entries[i];` if bin->segment_entries was allocated with fewer than bin->ne_header->SegCount entries. The allocating statement is not in this code, so the precondition (undersized array) could not be instantiated; if the unshown loader sizes the array from a different field or truncates on read failure, this becomes CWE-125.

Robustness: `bin->ne_header` is dereferenced without a NULL check (`bin->ne_header->SegCount`); a NULL from the unshown header-parse path yields only a same-privilege crash (CWE-476 class, DoS at most).

Robustness: `segments = r_list_newf (free)` result is not NULL-checked before r_list_append; and bin->segment_entries NULL with SegCount > 0 would deref near NULL. Both are malloc-failure/crash-only paths in the same-privilege parser process.
Calling r_bin_ne_get_segments twice on the same bin overwrites bin->segments without freeing the previous list (memory leak, non-security).

verdict.summary: This is the mruby VM dispatch loop. Every memory-effecting use of bytecode-decoded operands (register indexing, upvar stack access, argument copying, jump targets, integer stores) is preceded, in execution order, by a verifiable runtime guard quoted in the code (mrb_stack_extend sized from the same irep that supplies register operands; MRB_ENV_LEN bounds checks at both boundaries; strict-arity checks with clamped copy lengths; mrb_int_*_overflow sentinel tests; INT32 range check on pool INT64 values; catch-handler range containment on OP_JMPUW). No trigger instantiable within this code reaches a sink unguarded.

assumptions: mrb_stack_extend, cipush, mrb_ary_new_from_values, stack_copy, value_move and mrb_int_*_overflow have standard semantics (allocate/copy exactly the requested count, report overflow) — these are characterizable standard-library functions of the same codebase.
The irep executed here is produced by the in-process mruby compiler/parser, not by a bytecode-deserialization statement present in this function.
limitations: If this VM were fed unverified .mrb bytecode (mrb_load_irep) from an attacker, operands such as register index a (uint8/uint32) exceeding irep->nregs would index regs[] out of bounds; this code is not the intake point for bytecode, so that producer contract could not be quoted or violated here — no such trigger was instantiated.

mrb_assert(a >= 0 && a < irep->ilen) in OP_JMPUW's restore path is compiled out under NDEBUG; the restored value originates from a break object this code itself created via THROW_TAGGED_BREAK, so no concrete out-of-range value could be produced inside this function, but a hostile caller of mrb_vm_exec planting state in mrb->exc could bypass it.

The FETCH_*/CASE macros and helper callees (ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE, uvenv, catch_handler_find, UNWIND_ENSURE) are defined outside this excerpt and were judged by their standard mruby semantics; a defect hidden inside those helpers would not be visible here.

verdict.summary: handle_PORT consumes the network peer's PORT argument without validating the sscanf match count (uninitialized a-f reach the inet_aton branch, log output, and the stored data port) and stores a fully attacker-chosen host:port for the outbound data connection without verifying it matches the control-connection peer, enabling an FTP-bounce/SSRF pivot to arbitrary internal targets.

evidence.reason: The sscanf return value (number of matched fields) is never checked; a-f (declared without initializers on line 3) stay uninitialized when the attacker sends e.g. 'PORT 1,2,3,4,5' or 'PORT x', and those uninitialized values then reach the inet_aton accept/reject branch (line 18), the stored data_port (line 25), and DBG/ERR output (lines 19, 27).

evidence.snippet:
strlcpy(ctrl->data_address, addr, sizeof(ctrl->data_address));
	ctrl->data_port = e * 256 + f;
evidence.reason: Outbound data-connection host and port are taken entirely from the attacker's command ('PORT 192,168,0,5,0,22' yields data_address=192.168.0.5, data_port=22); the only check (inet_aton, line 18) validates well-formedness, and no statement compares addr against the control-connection peer, so the server stores a target for a bounce/SSRF connection to any host:port.

assumptions: ctrl is a non-NULL internal handler context and str is the raw argument of the FTP PORT command from the network peer, per the handler naming and command string.
The stored data_address/data_port are later used to open the FTP data connection (standard PORT semantics), which is what makes the stored host:port an outbound-request target.
limitations: e*256+f can signed-overflow for out-of-range e (CWE-190), but the attacker already reaches any 16-bit port with in-range e,f, so no additional capability is granted; treated as robustness.

Uninitialized a-d produce a garbage dotted-quad that inet_aton usually rejects (500 reply); the practical impact of the uninit path is stack-derived values reaching the branch/log/stored port rather than attacker-learnable disclosure, since no reply echoes addr to the client.
No race condition or memory-safety violation found: snprintf and strlcpy are bounded by quoted sizeof guards.

verdict.summary: No primary vulnerability instantiated. The quoted guard at line 3 rejects NULL bin and a NULL segment-entry array (the calloc-failure sentinel), and every remaining candidate fails impact or instantiation: the unchecked bin->ne_header dereference (line 7) yields at most a same-privilege crash of the file-parsing process (robustness per CWE-476 discipline), the potential OOB read of segment_entries[i] requires the not-shown init code to allocate an array smaller than SegCount — a state no statement of this code produces — and the offset*alignment ut64 wrap only affects a display string built with a literal format.

assumptions: NE_image_segment_entry fields and NE header fields are small fixed-width unsigned integers (ut16), so the int loop counter i cannot overflow relative to SegCount.
r_list_newf/r_list_append tolerate the objects used here per radare2 API semantics (allocation failure of the list returns NULL and is propagated, not dereferenced).
limitations: Speculative: line 7 dereferences bin->ne_header without a NULL check (only bin and bin->segment_entries are tested at line 3). A NULL ne_header causes a same-privilege crash (CWE-476); the state ne_header==NULL with segment_entries!=NULL is never produced by any quoted statement (the entry array is sized from SegCount read via ne_header in the not-shown init), and per the impact model a mere crash with no corruption/disclosure/bypass is a robustness issue, not the verdict.

Speculative: indexing bin->segment_entries[i] for i < SegCount has no local guard tying the array length to SegCount; if the not-shown allocation sized the array smaller than SegCount, this would be a heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). No statement in this code instantiates a short array, and a calloc failure yields NULL, which the quoted line-3 check rejects; the precondition could not be instantiated here.

Cosmetic: bs->paddr = (ut64)se->offset * bin->alignment can wrap for attacker-chosen offset/alignment, but the wrapped value only feeds the r_str_newf name string and section metadata display; no memory primitive consumes it.
Minor: on R_NEW0 failure (line 9) the partially built list is returned and bin->segments is not set, leaking the list on the caller side; robustness only.

verdict.summary: The attacker-controlled serialized ensemble is consumed only behind a checked bool sentinel (`if (!result->InitFromSerialized(...))`), and the error path correctly pairs `result->Unref()` with `result.release()` before returning, preventing the double-free/UAF that the absence of that release would cause. The tolerated ALREADY_EXISTS status is documented intended resource semantics, not a fail-open security state; remaining issues are same-privilege CHECK aborts on mismatched input shapes and unshown-callee (InitFromSerialized/CreateResource) semantics.

assumptions: BoostedTreesEnsembleResource is a ref-counted resource whose fresh instance has refcount 1, so `result->Unref()` on the parse-failure path destroys it and `release()` correctly disarms the unique_ptr (matching the in-code comment).
CreateResource/HandleFromInput are TensorFlow-internal helpers with standard ownership-transfer semantics; their bodies are not shown.
limitations: Passing a non-scalar or wrong-dtype tensor triggers a CHECK-style abort inside `scalar<T>()()` — a crash of the same-privilege process, not a security impact per discipline 3.
`InitFromSerialized` internals are not shown; any validation gap inside that callee cannot be attributed to this code, whose own sentinel check is present.
If `CreateResource` fails with a status other than ALREADY_EXISTS and does not take ownership of the released pointer, the resource leaks; the helper body is not shown, so this remains speculative.

The ALREADY_EXISTS path returns OK without installing the requested ensemble; this is documented as intended ('Only create one, if one does not exist already.') and is a semantic, not a security, behavior.

verdict.summary: This is mruby's core VM interpreter (mrb_vm_exec). All memory accesses consume compiler-generated bytecode operands bounded by irep->nregs/plen/slen, with the VM stack extended to irep->nregs at every method-entry path (mrb_stack_extend) and upvar accesses guarded by exact checks (b < MRB_ENV_LEN(e), MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1). Integer arithmetic uses checked overflow primitives; array construction sizes capacity from the same expression as its copies. mruby's documented trust model treats irep bytecode as compiler-trusted and this code contains no bytecode decoding/intake path, so no attacker-controlled input reaches any sink with an absent guard.

assumptions: ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE and FETCH_* macros are not shown; ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE(a, &c, insn) is assumed to initialize the local `blk` before its read at `if (mrb_proc_p(blk))` and its pass to prepare_missing, matching upstream mruby where the macro performs that assignment; no in-code path bypasses the macro call.
mrb_div_int is assumed to handle division by zero (Ruby semantics), as in upstream mruby.
irep/pool/syms bytecode and register operands are compiler-generated and treated as trusted per mruby's security model; this function performs no bytecode loading or decoding.
limitations: If an application feeds raw attacker-controlled bytecode (e.g., via mrb_load_irep on untrusted data), the many unchecked index uses (regs[a], pool[b], syms[b], irep->reps[b], stack[m1+r+m2+kd]) would become out-of-bounds reads/writes (CWE-125/787); that defect would live in the bytecode loader, which is not part of this code.

OP_JMPUW's restore path bounds the reloaded jump target with mrb_assert only (disabled in release builds); the value is written by THROW_TAGGED_BREAK from an in-range `a` within this same handler, so no wrap/escape trigger could be instantiated from the shown statements.

Local variable `blk` in L_SENDB_SYM is initialized inside the unshown ARGUMENT_NORMALIZE macro; if that macro left it unassigned on some opcode variant, a CWE-457 uninitialized read would exist at `if (mrb_proc_p(blk))`, but this could not be confirmed without the macro definition.

verdict.summary: This is the guarded variant of ImageMagick's GetEXIFProperty: every attacker-controlled index, offset, component count, and stack level passes through an exact-bound guard before use (directory <= exif+length-2 for the entry-count read, q <= exif+length-12 for the 12-byte IFD entry, dir_offset+number_bytes <= length for value data, the length clamp in EXIFMultipleValues/EXIFMultipleFractions, and level < MaxDirectoryStack-2 for directory_stack pushes). Boundary arithmetic at both ends of every check confirms no under-admitting value; no primary candidate survives the mention sweep and trigger simulation.

assumptions: AcquireString allocates strlen(source)+MagickPathExtent (standard ImageMagick semantics), so FormatLocaleString(key,MaxTextExtent,...) after key=AcquireString(property) cannot overflow the key buffer.
ReadPropertyByte(&exif,&length) advances the pointer and decrements length only while length > 0 (standard semantics), so the 'Exif\0\0' scan loop cannot read past the profile.

FormatLocaleString NUL-terminates within its size argument and returns the formatted length; even a negative or oversized return is neutralized by the size_t clamp 'if (length >= (MaxTextExtent-1)) length=MaxTextExtent-1;' executed in the same iteration.
limitations: The duplicate-IFD check 'directory_stack[i].directory == (exif+tag_offset1)' compares stored IFD pointers against the profile base and is ineffective at detecting duplicates; this is functional only, since the splay-tree entry dedup (GetValueFromSplayTree(exif_resources,q) == q) and the MaxDirectoryStack level cap bound both revisits and depth, so no infinite loop or stack overflow is instantiable.

EXIF_FMT_SINGLE/EXIF_DOUBLE format values through ReadPropertySignedLong, producing wrong numeric output for float/double tags; this is a functional accuracy issue with no memory-safety or security consequence.

Components are capped at 2^31-1; on a hypothetical platform with 16-bit size_t the product-overflow guard analysis would need re-verification, but all mainstream 32/64-bit widths were checked and every wrap case is caught by 'number_bytes < components'.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect in this code: the only local memory write, memset(skb->data, 0, MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE), is bounded by the allocation dev_alloc_skb(MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE) which is sized from the same expression and NULL-checked before use, and skb_pull cannot overpull or shrink tailroom because skb->len is 0 and skb_pull returns NULL without mutation when the pull length exceeds skb->len. The remaining anomalies (64-byte mask used for dword alignment; the alignment pull being a silent no-op) are functional robustness issues whose consequences would occur inside the not-shown rsi_prepare_beacon.

assumptions: Standard Linux skb allocator semantics: dev_alloc_skb(n) guarantees tailroom >= SKB_DATA_ALIGN(n) >= n and leaves skb->len == 0.
Standard skb_pull semantics: it returns NULL and performs no mutation when the requested length exceeds skb->len (skb->len is 0 at the call site here, pull amount is 1..63).
rsi_prepare_beacon, skb_queue_tail, rsi_set_event, and rsi_dbg are not shown; the call passes an in-domain fresh skb with full tailroom, and the callee return is sentinel-checked.
limitations: Candidate dismissed (tailroom-loss overflow): if skb_pull(skb, 64 - dword_align_bytes) had advanced skb->data by up to 63 bytes, tailroom would shrink below MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE and a subsequent MAX_MGMT_PKT_SIZE write in rsi_prepare_beacon could overflow. Dismissed because skb_pull is a verified no-op here (skb->len == 0) and because the putative write occurs inside a callee not shown.

Candidate dismissed (functional bug, not a security impact): the mask 0x3f with (64 - dword_align_bytes) computes 64-byte alignment while the variable is named dword (4-byte) alignment; since the pull is inert, skb->data may stay non-dword-aligned, a robustness/functional defect whose only consequence would manifest inside the not-shown rsi_prepare_beacon (e.g., unaligned descriptor construction).
Cannot analyze rsi_prepare_beacon or the tx thread consuming common->tx_queue[MGMT_BEACON_Q]; any defect there is out of scope of the given code.

verdict.summary: adts_decode_extradata consumes the return value of ff_copy_pce_data() without a sentinel check: '(ff_copy_pce_data(&pb, &gb) + 3) / 8' feeds a possible negative failure return into adts->pce_size and then sets write_adts=1 and returns 0, presenting success on an error path with an out-of-domain negative copy length derived from attacker-crafted AAC extradata (chan_config=0 with oversized/invalid PCE). The sibling parse return 'off' IS checked (if (off < 0) return off;), proving the missing 'ret < 0' guard is the defect.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unchecked failure-sentinel return of ff_copy_pce_data consumed in arithmetic; a negative parse/copy-failure return (in-domain per standard sentinel semantics) yields negative adts->pce_size, then line 45/47 store write_adts=1 and return 0 (fail-open). Attacker trigger: crafted extradata with chan_config=0 and a PCE that fails in ff_copy_pce_data; no ret<0 check exists anywhere in the function, unlike the 'if (off < 0)' check for the sibling callee.

assumptions: ff_copy_pce_data can return a negative failure sentinel for an attacker-supplied PCE (parse/copy failure shape per discipline 4(ii)); the function is a parse of attacker data, so its failure sentinel is in-domain.
adts->pce_size is later consumed as a copy length by the ADTS header writer (standard muxer semantics), which the out-of-domain negative value would corrupt.
limitations: ff_copy_pce_data's body is not shown, so the precise failure mode (bounded-reject vs unbounded write inside the callee) cannot be quoted; the heap-overflow variant of this defect lives inside that callee.

The final memory-corruption crash site (ff_adts_write_frame_header consuming pce_size) is outside this snippet; the quoted impact here is the fail-open success return plus storage of an out-of-domain negative size at lines 41-47.
size*8 overflow at line 8 requires size >= 2^28 and standard init_get_bits semantics degrade the context to empty rather than corrupt memory.
Truncated extradata leaving gb exhausted makes get_bits return 0, passing the flag checks — a robustness/fail-open-on-content issue, not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: When the attacker-controlled 'tree_ensemble_serialized' input fails proto parsing, Compute calls result->Unref() (which frees the BoostedTreesEnsembleResource via its refcount of 1) and then returns via OP_REQUIRES(context, false, ...); the still-owning std::unique_ptr then deletes the already-freed object, causing a double free / use-after-free with heap corruption.

evidence.reason: On the parse-failure path, result->Unref() deletes the object (refcount starts at 1), and OP_REQUIRES with literal false returns from Compute while the unique_ptr still owns the pointer; its destructor then deletes the already-freed object — double free. The missing guard is an ownership release (result.release()) before the return; no such statement exists before the return.

Trigger origin: the attacker fully controls the serialized-proto tensor content; any non-parseable payload makes InitFromSerialized return false (standard failure sentinel), instantiating the double-free path.

assumptions: BoostedTreesEnsembleResource derives from ResourceBase/core::RefCounted, so Unref() on the freshly-constructed object (refcount 1) performs 'delete this' (standard TensorFlow resource semantics).
OP_REQUIRES is the standard TF macro containing a 'return;' from Compute on the failing condition (literal false here always fails).
std::unique_ptr's default deleter calls delete on the pointer at scope exit.
limitations: stamp_token_t->scalar<int64>()() (line 5) and tree_ensemble_serialized_t->scalar<tstring>()() (line 14) lack any dtype/shape validation of the attacker-supplied tensors; a wrong-dtype or non-scalar input triggers a CHECK-failure abort — a crash-only denial of service of the same-privilege process, not the verdict driver.
The tolerated tensorflow::error::ALREADY_EXISTS from CreateResource is intentional idempotent-create behavior, not a fail-open authorization gap.

verdict.summary: The PCX RLE encoder is memory-safe for all in-domain inputs. Every pointer dereference (*from) is covered in execution order by a quoted guard: the outer 'while (from < end)', the short-circuit 'from >= end || data != *from', and the inner '(from < end) && (*from == data)'. The emitted run-count bytes are provably bounded at 0xc1-0xcf because after the max_run loop 'from - start < 15*step' and the difference is always a multiple of step. The only defects (division by zero and infinite loop at step==0, backwards OOB walk for negative step, signed overflow of step*15 for |step|>143M) all require the unshown caller to pass an out-of-domain stride, which no statement of this code instantiates.

assumptions: This function is an internal encoder invoked by the same module's row writer with a positive bytes-per-pixel stride; it parses no untrusted input itself, so its attacker-controlled surface is only the image byte values, which never index or size memory here.
end >= from on entry, per the row-writer contract; the outer loop condition 'while (from < end)' makes an inverted range a no-op rather than a memory error.
limitations: step == 0 would cause an infinite loop in the inner run scan and a 0/0 division at '(from - start) / step'; no quoted guard on step exists, but the triggering value cannot be produced by any statement in this code and rests on an unshown caller.
step < 0 would walk 'from' backwards below the buffer (out-of-bounds read whose bytes would be written to the output file); same unshown-caller precondition, not instantiable here.

int max_run = step * MAX_RUN_COUNT can overflow for |step| > 143,165,575, making max_run negative and the 'while (from - start >= max_run)' loop unbounded; requires an absurd stride no shown code produces.
If a row length is not a multiple of step, up to step-1 trailing bytes are skipped (image truncation), a functional issue with no listed security impact.

verdict.summary: In ex_retab() (FEAT_VARTABS), after set_string_option_direct("vts", new_ts_str, OPT_FREE|OPT_LOCAL, 0) applies the new 'vartabstop' — releasing and rebuilding the buffer's existing vartabstop array — the code unconditionally executes vim_free(old_vts_ary) on the saved pointer curbuf->b_p_vts_array, freeing already-released heap memory (double free / use-after-free). Trigger: ':retab 4,8' (or any argument) when 'vartabstop' is in use or the argument has multiple tabstops. Matches CVE-2022-4292; upstream fix removed these two statements.

evidence.reason: Sink: vim_free(old_vts_ary) frees curbuf->b_p_vts_array a second time after set_string_option_direct(..., OPT_FREE, ...) already released/rebuilt that array while applying the new 'vartabstop'; no ownership or sentinel guard exists between the call and the free. Instantiated trigger: user-supplied ':retab 4,8' with 'vartabstop' in use (tabstop_count(old_vts_ary) > 0), causing heap double-free/corruption (CVE-2022-4292).

Origin: the dangling pointer is captured here before the option-apply call at lines 203-204 releases the array it references; the pointer is then passed to vim_free at line 206 without any revalidation.

assumptions: The release of the old b_p_vts_array inside set_string_option_direct is not quoted in this file; it is characterized from the OPT_FREE delegation and confirmed by the upstream fix for CVE-2022-4292, which deleted 'curbuf->b_p_vts_array = new_vts_array;' and 'vim_free(old_vts_ary);'.
limitations: alloc/memmove block (lines 128-139) verified exact-fit: writes total start_col + len + (old_len - col + 1) == allocation size, and col <= old_len because the scan loop breaks at ptr[col] == NUL; no overflow found.
Non-VARTABS division by new_ts is guarded by the quoted range checks on lines 55-61; a hypothetical b_p_ts == 0 from 'tabstop' could not be instantiated from this code.
Impact requires the command argument to reach ex_retab (ex-command execution); the memmove path itself is memory-safe for all representable buffer contents.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one loop bound in crun_command_exec: `for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)` allows one iteration past the valid argument range, passing the C-guaranteed NULL sentinel argv[argc] to xstrdup/strdup (NULL dereference), crashing the (typically root-run) container runtime exec helper on every `crun exec <container> <cmd>` without --process. The required bound `argc - first_arg - 1` appears nowhere in the code.

evidence.snippet:
for (i = 0; i < argc - first_arg; i++)
        process->args[i] = xstrdup (argv[first_arg + i + 1]);
evidence.reason: Off-by-one: the loop should iterate argc - first_arg - 1 times (container id at argv[first_arg], real args at argv[first_arg+1..argc-1]); with the given bound the final iteration i = argc - first_arg - 1 reads argv[first_arg + i + 1] = argv[argc], the standard NULL sentinel, and passes it to xstrdup (strdup semantics: NULL input dereferences and faults). Trigger: any invocation `crun exec myctr /bin/true` gives argc=4, first_arg=2, i=1 reads argv[4]=NULL. The only nearby check, crun_assert_n_args(argc - first_arg, ..., 2, -1) at line 17, enforces only a minimum arity and does not cap the index; no statement bounds first_arg + i + 1 <= argc - 1.

assumptions: xstrdup follows standard strdup semantics for NULL input (undefined behavior, crash under glibc); its implementation is not shown, so the crash-vs-harmless outcome of the sentinel pass is inferred from standard-function behavior.

crun_assert_n_args is assumed to error-exit when argc - first_arg is below its minimum (standard crun helper); it therefore guarantees argc - first_arg >= 2 in the else branch but imposes no upper bound on the loop index.
argv[argc] is a NULL pointer per the C standard, so the extra read is within the argv allocation; the defect is the sentinel reaching a string function, not an out-of-allocation read.
limitations: process->args_len is set to argc while only argc - first_arg - 1 strings are stored (remaining slots are xmalloc0-zeroed NULLs); any downstream misuse would be inside libcrun_container_exec_with_options, which is not shown.

LISTEN_FDS is parsed with strtoll and added to preserve_fds without range validation (possible negative/huge value, wrap on unsigned addition); its consumption occurs in container setup code not shown, and the variable is supplied by the invoking user's own environment.

The crash impact is a denial of the exec attempt only (no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass observed); when crun exec is invoked directly by the same user the crash is same-privilege robustness rather than a security boundary crossing.

verdict.summary: This is SELinux's PTRACE_TRACEME hook. The authorization decision is correctly ordered: task_sid_subj(parent) supplies the tracer's (parent's) SID as the subject and task_sid_obj(current) supplies the tracee's SID as the object for the PROCESS__PTRACE permission, matching the hook contract (check that the parent may safely trace the current process), the sibling selinux_ptrace_access_check direction, and the equivalent AppArmor/Smack hooks. An unauthorized parent (no 'allow parent_t current_t:process ptrace' rule) receives avc_has_perm's -EACCES, which is returned verbatim; there is no fail-open path, no argument swap, no memory/format/injection sink, and the NULL audit-data argument only suppresses the AVC audit message, not the denial.

assumptions: avc_has_perm enforces the MAC decision for its (subject, object, class, permission) arguments and returns 0 on grant / negative error on denial, which is standard, characterizable semantics for the SELinux AVC API.
task_sid_subj/task_sid_obj return the task's current cred SID for the subject and object roles respectively, per their upstream definitions.
limitations: The NULL audit-data argument means a denied PTRACE_TRACEME produces no SELinux audit record (unlike ptrace_access_check, which passes audit data); this reduces audit visibility of denied traceme attempts but does not weaken the enforcement, so it is a functional/logging note, not a vulnerability.
The analysis covers only the shown function; the composite LSM decision (Yama/other hooks, ptrace.c logic) is outside this code and was not judged.

verdict.summary: Ragel-generated HTTP parser: every dereference of attacker-controlled request bytes is preceded by a quoted boundary check (`if ( p == pe ) goto _test_eof;` / `if ( ++p == pe ) goto _test_eofN;`) that provably keeps p within [buffer, pe); all callback slices (PTR_TO/LEN, header_done) end at p <= pe and have non-negative lengths; the only external precondition (off <= len) is asserted in the code. No primary candidate survives.

assumptions: asserts are active in the build of this code as given (no #ifdef NDEBUG appears in the code); the quoted `assert(off <= len ...)` therefore enforces the off precondition
the parser is resumed across execute() calls only with the same buffer within one request, the standard contract of this Ragel resume design (mark/field_start are stored as offsets into buffer)
puma_parser_has_error and the callbacks are not shown; they receive in-bounds (pointer,length) slices
limitations: off > len would cause an out-of-bounds read at the first `(*p)` only if the build defines NDEBUG (removing `assert(off <= len && "offset past end of buffer")`) AND a caller violates that quoted precondition; under NDEBUG the second assert is also vacuous because `(size_t)(pe - p)` and `len - off` wrap identically — speculative, not instantiated by this code

a stale `parser->mark`/`field_start` from a prior call resumed with a different, shorter buffer could pass an out-of-range slice to callbacks; only the debug asserts `parser->mark < len` would catch it — requires an unshown caller behavior
on a parse error (cs = 0) `parser->cs` is not updated (`if (!puma_parser_has_error(parser)) parser->cs = cs;`); impact depends on the not-shown has_error/puma caller and could not be instantiated
bytes 0x80-0xFF are accepted into URI/fragment fields (signed-char comparison asymmetry) — functional parsing behavior, no memory-safety or injection impact within this code

verdict.summary: SVDF Prepare indexes attacker-controlled tensor dimension arrays (dims->data[0]/[1]) and quantization scale arrays (scale->data[0]) from a parsed .tflite model without validating the array length. A crafted model whose input/weights_feature/weights_time/bias tensors have fewer dimensions than the index used (e.g. rank-0 or rank-1 tensors) causes heap out-of-bounds reads whose garbage values flow into num_filters/num_units and subsequent tensor resizing. The only rank guard in the function, TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2), covers the state tensor only and runs after the unguarded reads.

evidence.snippet:
const int batch_size = input->dims->data[0];
  const int num_filters = weights_feature->dims->data[0];
evidence.reason: Root cause: dims->data[] of model-supplied tensors is indexed with no NumDimensions/rank check. Instantiated trigger: a crafted model gives weights_feature (or input) a rank-0 tensor, so dims is a heap TfLiteIntArray with size==0 and data[0] reads past the allocation (heap OOB read); the garbage value becomes num_filters and drives subsequent size checks and ResizeTensor calls.

Same missing rank guard: weights_time->dims->data[1], input->dims->data[1] and weights_feature->dims->data[1] all require the respective tensor to have at least 2 dimensions, but no dimension-count check exists for these tensors; the only check in the function, TF_LITE_ENSURE_EQ(context, NumDimensions(state), 2) at line 47, covers state and executes after these reads. A rank-1 weights_time or input yields a heap OOB read.

Quantization scale arrays from the model are indexed at data[0] with only quantization.type != kTfLiteNoQuantization checked (lines 184-198) — the wrong property. A model whose quantization has an empty scale list yields a size-0 TfLiteFloatArray, so scale->data[0] reads out of bounds (secondary instance of the same unchecked-length class).

assumptions: Tensor dims, rank, and quantization metadata originate from an attacker-supplied .tflite model loaded across a trust boundary; this Prepare function is the validation intake point.
TfLiteIntArray and TfLiteFloatArray are heap allocations whose data[] capacity equals their size field, so indexing data[i] with i >= size is a heap out-of-bounds read.
GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe/GetTemporarySafe bound-check the tensor index against the node's input/output/temporary lists, not the tensor's dimension count.
limitations: memory_size * num_filters (lines 49-50) can overflow int32, allowing an inconsistent state tensor to pass the size check (e.g. memory_size = num_filters = 65536 wraps to 0); the resulting harm materializes in Eval, which is not shown, so this CWE-190 candidate is not counted in the verdict.
TfLiteIntArrayCreate results (output_size_array, scratch_size_array, etc.) are not NULL-checked before data[] writes; on allocation failure this is only a same-privilege crash (robustness).
Negative params->rank passes the 'rank != 0' check and can yield negative num_units/dim values, but these are rejected downstream by ResizeTensor; functional robustness only.

The scale->data[0] trigger assumes the model populator preserves an empty scale list as a size-0 TfLiteFloatArray (producer not shown); the in-function absence of any scale->size check is the quoted defect.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans writes coverage bytes into the mask buffer (base = pixman_image_get_data(r->mask)) using lengths derived directly from attacker-controlled span coordinates without any bounds check. len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x is never validated against the mask buffer width, so *m++ = spans[0].coverage; memset(m, coverage, --len); m += len performs a heap out-of-bounds write of up to ~2GB (int domain of spans[].x). The only guards present (num_spans == 0, coverage comparisons, len > 1, x != x0) do not bound m or len.

evidence.reason: Unbounded heap write: len comes from spans[1].x - spans[0].x (attacker-controlled int domain) and no statement in the function bounds it (or m - base) to the mask buffer size; e.g. spans[0].x=0 (coverage 0x80), spans[1].x=0x40000000 makes memset write 0x3FFFFFFF bytes past the mask buffer.

Origin of the tainted length: raw subtraction of two attacker-controlled span x coordinates with no range validation; additionally, with num_spans == 1 the do-while body still executes once and reads spans[1] out of bounds.

assumptions: spans and num_spans originate from scan-converter output over a trust boundary (rendered/path data) and are treated as attacker-data with the full declared width domain since no producer-side narrowing is quoted in this code.
pixman_image_get_data returns a buffer whose width is the compositor's clip extent; its size is never quoted in this function, so it cannot serve as a guard.
limitations: The upstream cairo pipeline normally clips spans to the clip extents before this callback; that contract is not quoted in this code, so the defect is judged here as the last line of defense (this is the known CVE-2020-35492 class heap overflow, fixed upstream by adding explicit span/width validation in this function).
The OOB read of spans[1] when num_spans == 1 is recorded as part of the same write chain rather than a separate finding, since the read value feeds the same unbounded memset.
NULL from pixman_image_get_data (r->mask == NULL) was not instantiated because no statement here can produce or quote that state.

verdict.summary: parallels_open validates every attacker-controlled field it consumes: catalog_size is bounded by the quoted check `if (s->catalog_size > INT_MAX / 4)` (max admitted 536870911; *4 = 2147483644, no wrap, fits the int read length), allocation and pread use the identical `s->catalog_size * 4` expression so sizes cannot diverge, the le32_to_cpus loop bound matches the allocation exactly (4 bytes per element), zero tracks are rejected, and both bdrv_pread calls have error arms that exit before any use. No reachable sink lacks a verified guard.

assumptions: BDRVParallelsState fields catalog_size/tracks are 32-bit unsigned (le32_to_cpu producers), matching the guard's arithmetic.
bs->opaque is zero-allocated by the block layer, so the fail path's g_free on a possibly-never-assigned catalog_bitmap is safe.
bdrv_pread either fills the requested byte count or returns a negative sentinel, so `ph` and catalog_bitmap are fully initialized on the success path.
limitations: A transient g_malloc of up to ~2GB (catalog_size = 536870911) is permitted before bdrv_pread validates the file actually contains that much data; the quoted check bounds it to 2GB and the allocation is freed on the read-failure path, so this is bounded resource amplification rather than unbounded consumption.
ph.nb_sectors is stored to bs->total_sectors without local validation; its consumer (generic block-layer request clamping) is not in this code, so no impact is instantiated here.

The eventual consumer of s->catalog_bitmap/s->tracks (parallels read path mapping sector offsets through the catalog) is not shown; catalog-index bounds in that not-given code could not be audited and is the natural place a sibling of this defect would live.
catalog_size = 0 yields g_malloc(0) → NULL with an empty in-loop; no dereference occurs in this function.

verdict.summary: _inplace_src_spans writes span data into r->_buf via *m++ and memset(m, coverage, --len) with no bound on the cumulative bytes or on len against the buffer extent; attacker-controlled span coordinates (from a rendered document/path) produce len values that drive m far past the end of the destination row buffer, a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-chosen coverage bytes (Cairo CVE-2020-35492 pattern).

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded write sink. len = spans[1].x - spans[0].x (attacker-controlled span coordinates, e.g. 0x2000000) passes the only nearby test (len > 1, a lower bound) and memset writes len bytes past r->_buf, whose extent is never compared against m or len on any path; coverage branches (==0xff, ==0x0) only bypass the sink for two coverage values, leaving every other coverage value with the full attacker-scale write.

Taint origin: span x coordinates arrive unvalidated at this handler (parameter spans of a *_spans render callback); the unchecked difference becomes the memset length at line 85 with no clamp to the destination/buffer width anywhere in the function.

assumptions: r->_buf is an allocation of finite extent (row-buffer sized to the destination width) established outside this function; its exact size is not shown, but no finite buffer can contain the arbitrarily large len values accepted at line 85.

Span arrays are produced by cairo's coverage tessellator from rendered path data (e.g., PDF/SVG content), placing spans across a trust boundary; per discipline 4 the full domain of cairo_half_open_span_t .x (int) is instantiable.
limitations: Reading spans[1].x at line 15 when num_spans == 1 (do-while executes once) is a potential one-past read, but it presumes the caller supplies an array with exactly one span and no terminator element — a caller contract not quotable from this code, so it stays speculative.
The pixman_image_composite32 calls receive attacker-derived x/width values; any OOB inside pixman is not characterizable from this excerpt and was not counted as a separate defect.
h and y are passed unvalidated to pixman composites; misuse would occur inside the not-shown callee.

verdict.summary: Array.prototype.splice caches the object's length (line 16) and then converts attacker-controlled start/delete arguments (lines 21/37), whose valueOf/toString can execute attacker JavaScript that mutates the array (e.g. a.length=0). The fast-array path then sizes capacity via njs_array_expand from the mutated live array->length (line 98) while the memcpy at lines 116-117 is bounded by the stale cached length (start+items), producing a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker JS values past array->start.

evidence.reason: Sink: memcpy writes items elements at array->start[start] with start and items derived from the length cached at line 16, while the capacity was expanded at line 98 against the live array->length shrunk by a valueOf side effect on the delete argument (line 37). Trigger: a=[1,2,3,4,5]; a.splice(1, {valueOf(){a.length=0; return 2;}}, v1..v97) gives length=5, start=1, items=97, delta=95, capacity≈95, memcpy writes indices 1..97 → 48-byte heap overflow.

Origin of the desynchronized bound: length is cached here, before the user-code-executing conversions at lines 21 and 37 can shrink array->length; no later statement re-validates array->length against length (see also the negative count computed at line 105 under the same desync).

assumptions: njs_value_to_integer on an object argument invokes valueOf/toString (standard JS ToPrimitive semantics), allowing attacker JS to run between the length cache at line 16 and the raw-memory uses.
njs_array_expand(vm, array, 0, delta) sizes capacity against the array's live length/size, which is the only state it can observe.
Setting a fast array's length to a smaller value updates array->length while preserving the fast_array flag and not shrinking the allocated buffer.
limitations: The behavior of njs_array_copy_within with the negative count produced at line 105 (array->length-(start+delete)) is not shown; under the same trigger it is a no-op for a signed count, so it does not independently drive the verdict.
The stale-slot reads at lines 61-63 (n up to the cached length after user code shrank array->length) stay within the original allocation and leak no data the same script could not already read.
Exploitability beyond the 48-byte controlled overflow (heap layout, adjacent object control) is not shown and does not affect the verdict.

verdict.summary: ReshapeSparseTensor never validates that the column count of input_indices_in matches the rank of input_shape (built from the independent attacker-controlled vector input_shape_in). It passes both into ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor, which must read one index per input dimension, so a mismatched pair (e.g. indices [1,2] matrix with input shape [2,2,2]) causes an out-of-bounds heap read whose value flows into the output tensor. The single missing guard is an OP_REQUIRES equating input_indices_in.shape().dim_size(1) with input_shape.dims().

evidence.snippet:
OP_REQUIRES_OK(context, functor::ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor<Device>()(
                                context, input_shape, output_shape,
                                input_indices_in.matrix<int64>(),
                                result_indices->matrix<int64>()));
evidence.reason: Unvalidated use: input_shape (rank 3, from input_shape_in=[2,2,2]) is passed together with input_indices_in.matrix<int64>() of shape [1,2]; the reshape computation reads one index column per input dimension, so column index 2 is read out of bounds of the 2-column matrix. No statement equates dim_size(1) with input_shape.dims(); trigger: indices=[[0,0]], input_shape_in=[2,2,2], target_shape_in=[8] passes every quoted check (IsMatrix, num_elements equality 8==8, dense_size>0 && product>0).

Origin of the mismatch: input_shape's rank (length of the attacker-supplied input_shape_in vector) and input_indices_in's column count are two independent attacker-controlled values; this is the first place both are consumed and no consistency check is ever performed, enabling the out-of-bounds read at the functor call (and the shape-inconsistent passthrough on the line 74 shortcut).

assumptions: ReshapeSparseTensorFunctor iterates j over input_shape.dims() reading input_indices(i, j) without re-validating that the matrix's column count matches (standard TensorFlow reshape semantics; its body is not shown in this code).
Eigen/TF matrix accessors do not bounds-check in release builds.
limitations: product *= size (line 44) can signed-overflow with attacker sizes (e.g. [2^63-1, 2^63-1] wraps to 1), but every downstream use is guarded (product>0 at lines 50/96, product*missing==dense_size at line 56, num_elements equality at line 66); no memory-safety consequence inside this code, so it does not decide the verdict.

TensorShape construction (line 20), AddDim (line 45), and set_dim (line 62) with huge or negative attacker values may CHECK-fail inside the not-shown TensorFlow callee (potential denial of service); behavior not quotable here.
The line 74-75 shortcut forwards an indices matrix whose column count may not equal output_rank to downstream consumers; downstream misuse is not shown and is subsumed by the same missing rank guard.

verdict.summary: stl_remove_degenerate writes to stl->neighbors_start[neighbor1].neighbor[(vnot1 + 1) % 3] using values read directly from parsed STL neighbor data. The only guard is an equality test against -1; neighbor and which_vertex_not values are never range-checked, so any parsed neighbor index (e.g. 1000000) or negative vnot (e.g. -2, giving index -1) causes an out-of-bounds heap write.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: neighbor1 is read unvalidated from parsed data (line 45) and only tested for != -1; an attacker-supplied neighbor value such as 1000000 (or a negative value other than -1) passes this check and indexes far outside neighbors_start. Additionally (vnot1 + 1) % 3 with vnot1 = -2 yields -1, so the sub-array index itself can be negative. Mirrored sinks exist at lines 65-66 and 73.

Taint origin: neighbor1/neighbor2 are read from the neighbors_start array populated from the parsed STL file with no local range validation; their full int domain flows unchecked into the indexing writes at lines 61-66.

assumptions: stl->facet_start and stl->neighbors_start contents (neighbor, which_vertex_not fields) originate from an attacker-supplied STL file processed by the loader; per the width-domain rule their full int domain is instantiable since no in-code narrowing is quoted.

C's % operator yields -1 for (-2 + 1) % 3 on two's-complement implementations, which is universal for the targets this code builds on (implementation-defined but consistently negative for negative operands).
limitations: The `facet` parameter itself is never bounds-checked in this function (unbounded index into facet_start at lines 14-17 and 45-58); if a caller can pass an out-of-range facet, this is an additional OOB read/write, but the caller is not shown, so it is folded as the same missing-validation family rather than a separate confirmed trigger.

stl_update_connects_remove_1 and stl_remove_facet are not shown; raw unvalidated neighbor indices are passed to them at lines 49, 52, 72, and any harm inside those callees is not separately enumerated.
Exact heap layout and exploitability (control of written value neighbor2/neighbor1) depend on allocation details outside this snippet.

verdict.summary: The function is a loop-and-dispatch wrapper over a packet batch. It performs no memory operations, arithmetic, parsing, or output construction itself: every attacker-influenced value (packet contents, dl_type, zone, hash_basis) is passed unmodified into callees, and the sole callee return that gates behavior is checked before use. Lock/unlock pairs are symmetric on all paths, and both refill calls pass only the iteration's own batch, packet, and index. No guard is absent at any sink because no sink exists in this code.

assumptions: dp_packet_batch_refill, the DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH macro, ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, and ipf_handle_frag behave as their names/signatures indicate; their implementations are not shown.
pb (the packet batch) is caller-owned and not concurrently accessed by other threads, so refilling it under ipf->ipf_lock on one path and outside it on the other introduces no race.
limitations: The actual fragment-header parsing and reassembly logic (ipf_handle_frag, ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag) is not included; if a memory-safety defect exists there (e.g., mishandling of attacker-controlled fragment offsets/lengths), it is outside this snippet and could not be evaluated.

dl_type, zone, and hash_basis are attacker-adjacent parameters with no local validation, but they are only forwarded to callees as in-domain typed values; any misuse would occur inside code not shown.

verdict.summary: In find_pattern_in_path(), the include-file stack is grown only when ALLOC_MULT() succeeds; on allocation failure the code still executes files[depth + 1].fp = mch_fopen(...). When depth + 1 == old_files == max_path_depth (reachable with a 50-deep attacker-crafted include chain and no prior stack pops), this writes one full struct past the 50-entry heap array (heap out-of-bounds write of a FILE* and, if fopen succeeds, of the attacker-influenced filename pointer, lnum, and matched fields). The subsequent 'forget one file' branch then reads files[old_files].name out of bounds and frees the uninitialized adjacent-heap value (arbitrary free). No statement bounds depth + 1 < max_path_depth or checks bigger == NULL before the push.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: with depth=49, old_files=max_path_depth=50 and a 50-entry array from lalloc_clear(max_path_depth * sizeof(SearchedFile)), the attacker-driven include chain reaches depth + 1 == old_files, ALLOC_MULT returns NULL (standard in-domain failure sentinel), the growth block is skipped, and this statement writes one full struct at index 50 past the array, followed by further OOB writes of files[50].name/lnum/matched if fopen succeeds.

Origin of the defect: the only NULL check on bigger gates just the growth copy; when it fails, control falls through to the unconditional push at line 268 with no bound of depth + 1 < max_path_depth anywhere on the path.

Executed after the OOB write when ++depth == old_files == max_path_depth: reads files[50].name out of bounds from the 50-entry array and frees the uninitialized adjacent-heap value (arbitrary free / use-after-free primitive), then increments old_files past max_path_depth, propagating further OOB accesses in the pop and cleanup loops.

assumptions: ALLOC_MULT(SearchedFile, 100) returning NULL is treated as an always-in-domain standard failure sentinel per the analysis rules; the surrounding code itself documents this path ('lalloc() for \'bigger\' must have failed above'), confirming it is an expected state.

The include-chain depth and new_fname values are attacker-influenced via the parsed buffer contents matched by the 'include' regexp, which this function itself decodes (it is the intake point, so missing validation cannot be deferred to a caller).
sizeof(SearchedFile) >= sizeof members used (.fp, .name, .lnum, .matched), so index 50 is past the end regardless of struct layout.
limitations: Practical triggering requires the modest growth allocation (~100 structs) to fail, i.e., a memory-pressure condition; an attacker can deepen the include stack and consume resources but cannot directly force the allocation failure on a healthy system.

Marginal upstream-acknowledged assumptions left unfixed here: 'IObuff[i-2]' can read one byte before IObuff when i==1 and IObuff[0]==' ' (only the comment 'thus i >= 2' supports safety, no quoted check), and 'STRNCPY(IObuff, aux, i)' relies on the comment 'IOSIZE > compl_length' rather than a quoted bound; both were judged too contrived/speculative to instantiate as primary candidates.

Callers of find_pattern_in_path and the semantics of vim_strncpy/ALLOC_MULT internals are taken from standard function behavior (copy exactly n, allocation returns NULL on failure); no other unshown component is relied upon for the primary finding.

verdict.summary: In the FTPWHO branch, when the attacker-controlled upload path length sl is >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename, the else arm copies the full array width of bytes into shm_data_cur->filename with no NUL-terminating write (the only terminator, filename[sl] = 0, is on the untaken sl < sizeof branch), and the source offset sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U underflows to (size_t)-1 when sl == sizeof, making memcpy read one byte before the name buffer. The shared-memory filename field is left as an unterminated, fully attacker-filled array.

evidence.reason: Else arm taken when strlen(name) >= sizeof shm_data_cur->filename (the code's own line-149 branch instantiates this state). It copies sizeof filename bytes — filling the entire array with no NUL terminator anywhere in this arm — and the source index sl - sizeof shm_data_cur->filename - 1U evaluates to (size_t)-1 when sl == sizeof filename, so memcpy reads from name[-1] (out-of-bounds read). Trigger: FTP client STORs a path whose strlen is >= the shm filename array width; the resulting unterminated shm_data_cur->filename is later consumed as a string, overrunning the field.
Origin of the tainted length: sl is the length of the attacker-supplied upload path name and is the variable consumed unguarded by the else-arm memcpy at lines 153-155.

assumptions: FTPWHO support is compiled in and shm_data_cur is non-NULL on the upload path; shm_data_cur->filename is a fixed-size char array (the code compares sl against its sizeof, implying an array).
Consumers of shm_data_cur->filename (e.g. the ftpwho/pure-ftpwho shared-memory readers) treat it as a C string, so the missing terminator yields an out-of-bounds read there.
limitations: When strlen(name) == sizeof shm_data_cur->filename exactly, the impact also includes a one-byte out-of-bounds read of the byte preceding the name buffer (CWE-125) copied into shared memory; for longer names the copy source is in bounds and only the missing termination applies.

ulhandler.total_uploaded is read after a failed ul_init (line 165-171) without a sentinel-clearing write in this code; if ul_init fails before initializing the struct this would be an uninitialized read (CWE-908), but ul_init's failure behavior is not shown, so this stays speculative.

Under SHOW_REAL_DISK_SPACE, FSTATFS(f, &statfsbuf) is called after close(f); using the closed descriptor is a robustness issue (typically EBADF) in the same-privileged process, not a confirmed security impact.

verdict.summary: In string_scan_range, the fast-path guard `if (needle + 4 < to)` uses wrappable ut64 addition: when needle is within 4 bytes of the top of the 64-bit address space (needle+4 wraps to a small value < to), the guard passes and `r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from)` reads 4 bytes at an offset that can be len-1, crossing the end of the heap buffer allocated as calloc(len,1) — up to 3 bytes out of bounds. The wrap-safe form `to - needle > 4` appears nowhere on the path.

evidence.snippet:
if (needle + 4 < to) {
			ut32 n1 = r_read_le32 (buf + needle - from);
evidence.reason: Root cause: the bound `needle + 4 < to` is computed with wrappable ut64 addition, so for needle in {2^64-3, 2^64-2, 2^64-1} the sum wraps to 0..3 and passes the check; the subsequent 4-byte read at buf+(needle-from) then indexes up to len+2 in a calloc(len,1) heap buffer. Instantiated trigger: from = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF0, to = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF gives len = 15 and buf = calloc(15); scanning advances needle to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFC, where needle+4 wraps to 0 < to and r_read_le32 reads buf[15] one byte past the buffer (up to 3 bytes OOB at needle = to-1). No other statement constrains needle before this sink.

evidence.snippet:
static int string_scan_range(RList *list, RBinFile *bf, int min,
		      const ut64 from, const ut64 to, int type, int raw, RBinSection *section) {
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted values: `from` and `to` are ut64 parameters of an exported string-scanning API whose ranges derive from parsed binary metadata (e.g. section addresses in attacker-supplied files); per the width-domain rule their full ut64 domain is instantiable, including ranges adjacent to 2^64-1 that trigger the wrap in the line-77 guard.

assumptions: from/to are reachable with values near the top of the ut64 domain because the function is an exported API whose range parameters are derived from attacker-controlled binary metadata (no quoted statement in this code restricts them).
Standard radare2 decoder callees (r_utf8_decode, r_utf16le_decode, r_utf32le_decode) respect the ptrlen argument passed as `to - needle`; their internals are not shown, so no finding rests on them.
limitations: `int outlen = len * 4` (line 47) can overflow signed int when len > 0x1FFFFFFF, but exploiting it requires the operator-controlled RABIN2_CHARSET environment variable, a successful ~2GB calloc, and the unshown r_charset_encode_str to mishandle a negative outlen — the impact chain is not characterizable from this code, so it remains speculative.
`r_buf_read_at (bf->buf, from, buf, len)` at line 42 ignores its return value; on failure buf stays zeroed (calloc), so this is robustness only, not uninitialized-read (no CWE-908).
The OOB-read value n1 only influences control flow (skip vs decode); no direct disclosure of the out-of-bounds bytes was found, hence severity low.

verdict.summary: This function is a dispatch/filter wrapper over a packet batch. It performs no parsing, copying, sizing, or indexing on attacker-controlled data; it only compares dl_type against two constants (total branch with a safe pass-through else-arm), forwards packet pointers and typed scalars to not-shown callees, and tests the only callee return it consumes (if (!ipf_handle_frag(...))). The mutex lock/unlock pair is balanced on every path with no early return between them. No primary candidate survives simulation.

assumptions: dp_packet_batch_size and DP_PACKET_BATCH_REFILL_FOR_EACH maintain the standard batch-iterator invariant that pb_idx stays in [0, pb_cnt) and dp_packet_batch_refill consumes that same index.
ipf points to valid caller-owned state; this module's own lock field is dereferenced, which is internal-trusted state.
limitations: All fragment parsing and reassembly logic (ipf_is_valid_v4_frag, ipf_is_valid_v6_frag, ipf_handle_frag) is not shown; any vulnerability in parsing attacker packet bytes would live there, and this analysis cannot confirm or exclude it.

The pass-through behavior for packets whose dl_type matches but whose is_valid_*_frag check fails (line 24) forwards malformed traffic to normal per-packet processing; this is the extraction filter's intended semantic and asserts no security state, so it was not treated as fail-open.

hash_basis, zone, and now are forwarded unmodified to ipf_handle_frag; any unsafe use of these values would be a defect of that callee, not of this call site, which passes them within their declared types.

verdict.summary: pcx_write_rle dereferences `*from` at line 14 after `from += step` without first checking that `from` is still in bounds: the `from == end` test is ordered after the `data != *from` deref, so on the final iteration of every call whose scan length is a multiple of `step`, `*from` reads one byte past the end of the buffer (and up to step-1 bytes past when the length is unaligned). This is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) on attacker-supplied image data; the inner run-extension loop at line 20 uses the correct bounds-first ordering, proving the missing guard is the deref-before-bounds ordering at line 14.

evidence.reason: Root cause: after `from += step` (L13), `from` can equal or exceed `end`, yet L14 evaluates `data != *from` before the `from == end` operand, dereferencing one-past-end. Instantiated trigger: with step=1 and buffer b[n] (from=b, end=b+n), the final loop iteration sets from=end=b+n and reads *(b+n), one byte past the allocation — occurs on every call with (end-from)%step==0; no statement between L13 and the deref bounds `from` (the loop guard at L10 covers only the pre-increment position, and L20's bounds-first pattern does not apply here).

Origin of the tainted pointer state: the loop guard `from < end` is checked only at loop entry, before `from` is advanced by `from += step`; the subsequent increment at L13 invalidates the invariant that `from` is dereferenceable at the L14 read.

assumptions: `from`/`end` delimit the caller's buffer with `end` at the allocation boundary (no slack/padding byte beyond `end`); if the caller always over-allocates by `step` bytes the read stays mapped but is still out-of-bounds relative to the logical row.
`gp_fputc` has standard write semantics; its ignored return value affects only error handling.
limitations: Degenerate `step` values (step ≤ 0, or step near INT_MAX causing signed overflow in `step * MAX_RUN_COUNT` at line 8) would produce backward/overshooting reads, an always-true chunk loop, or infinite loops (CWE-190/400); dismissed as speculative because `step` is a non-data-carrying configuration parameter (bytes-per-pixel) with no attacker-controlled producer shown, and no caller is visible.

The OOB-read value cannot alter the emitted PCX encoding (simulation shows both branches of the `if` at L14 produce identical output for the boundary byte), so no confidentiality leak channel was instantiated; the impact is the out-of-bounds memory access itself (potential crash on unmapped memory).
Unchecked `gp_fputc` return values (write errors) are a robustness issue only.

verdict.summary: In the axis_ == -1 path, input_min/input_max tensors are only checked for dims() == 0 or 1; the size checks (dim_size(0) == depth) are scoped inside 'if (axis_ != -1)'. A 0-element 1-D min tensor passes validation, the backprop outputs are allocated with that [0] shape, and the functor is handed scalar<T>() maps over empty buffers, producing an out-of-bounds write (and OOB read) of one element — heap memory corruption triggered by any attacker-supplied tensor shapes.

evidence.snippet:
input.template flat<T>(), input_min_tensor.scalar<T>(),
        input_max_tensor.scalar<T>(), input_backprop->template flat<T>(),
        input_min_backprop->template scalar<T>(),
        input_max_backprop->template scalar<T>());
evidence.reason: Sink: on the axis_ == -1 path, scalar<T>() is called on input_min/input_max and on backprop outputs whose shape is copied from input_min_tensor.shape() (line 42) without any element-count validation. With input_min of shape [0] (dims()==1, passes the line 20-24 check), the maps cover element 0 of zero-element buffers; the functor writes one T past the 0-byte output allocation — out-of-bounds write (CWE-787), plus an OOB scalar read of the empty input.

Origin of the defect: the only size validation of input_min_tensor (dim_size(0) == depth) is executed only when axis_ != -1, so when axis_ == -1 (the op default) the attacker-controlled min/max tensor size is never checked against the single element that scalar<T>() and the scalar backprop writes require.

assumptions: Tensor::scalar<T>() maps the tensor's base data pointer as a rank-0 Eigen TensorMap without an element-count CHECK (standard TensorFlow Tensor semantics), and a [0]-shaped output allocation yields a writable non-null 0-byte heap region via the standard TF CPU allocator; if the allocator returned NULL instead, the write degrades to a NULL-deref crash.
The QuantizeAndDequantizeOneScaleGradientFunctor writes one scalar to each of the passed-in min/max backprop maps (the outputs are allocated but otherwise unwritten).
limitations: Secondary issue sharing the same missing guard: with input_min of shape [N], N>1, outputs 1 and 2 are allocated with shape [N] but only element 0 is written by scalar<T>(), returning N-1 uninitialized heap elements to the caller (CWE-908 information disclosure).

Under axis_ != -1, input_min_tensor.dims() == 0 is permitted and input_min_tensor.dim_size(0) then reads a non-existent dimension index inside the check itself; in release builds without the bounds CHECK this is an out-of-range read of the shape representation, though the resulting comparison almost always fails the OP_REQUIRES.

flat_inner_outer_dims<T,3>(axis_ - 1) with axis_ == 0 passes start_index = -1; this is dismissed as the designed 'no leading dimensions' value, consistent with the quoted guard axis_ < input.shape().dims() and with depth = input.dim_size(axis_).

verdict.summary: uECC_sign_with_k passes the caller-supplied unsigned hash_size directly to bits2int(tmp, message_hash, hash_size, curve) with no length/range check anywhere in the function; hash_size originates from the exported signing API (full 32-bit domain instantiable), and bits2int consumes it as the byte extent used to index/convert message_hash, so an out-of-domain value (e.g. smaller than BITS_TO_BYTES(curve->num_n_bits) or larger than the actual hash buffer) drives an out-of-bounds read — the missing local validation at the call site is the defect.

evidence.reason: Attacker-derived hash_size (unsigned, origin line 3, no producer shown, full 0..0xFFFFFFFF domain) is used as the consumed byte extent for message_hash in bits2int with no bounds/range/length check anywhere in the function (mention sweep: hash_size appears only at its declaration and here); an out-of-domain value (e.g. 16 for a 256-bit curve, or 0xFFFFFFFF) drives bits2int's extent/wrap arithmetic off the message_hash buffer, an out-of-bounds read whose contents then influence the emitted signature.

Origin of the tainted value: hash_size is a parameter of the signing path (exported via uECC_sign/uECC_sign_deterministic) whose producer is not shown in this code; its full unsigned 32-bit domain is instantiable and no statement in this function constrains it before the sink at line 61.

assumptions: curve (and its fields num_words, num_n_bits, num_bytes) is treated as library-selected trusted constant data; if a hostile curve struct were instantiable, many loops/copies would be unbounded, but no attacker-reachable path to forge one is shown in this code.
The size of the signature output buffer is assumed to be 2*curve->num_bytes per the standard uECC API contract (unquotable in this code).
bits2int consumes hash_size as the byte extent used to read/convert message_hash, per its role as the hash-to-integer converter in this signing routine.
limitations: The concrete out-of-bounds read occurs inside bits2int, which is not shown; the exact read extent/wrap arithmetic cannot be quoted here, so the finding is anchored on the unchecked call site per the input-validation call-site rule.
message_hash == NULL would only crash the same-privilege process (robustness issue, not a verdict driver).
The blinding fallback tmp[0]=1 when no RNG is set weakens side-channel resistance by design; not a memory-safety defect in this code.
Potential side-channel leakage of k/private key via timing is out of scope for this analysis.

verdict.summary: drill_parse_T_code() parses the attacker-supplied tool number from an untrusted Excellon drill file into tool_num (full int domain, negative values admitted via '+'/'-' check). The bounds check `if (tool_num < TOOL_MIN || tool_num >= TOOL_MAX)` only emits an error message and does not return, so out-of-range values (e.g. T99999 or T-5) fall through to `state->current_tool = tool_num`, the out-of-bounds read `apert = image->aperture[tool_num]`, and the out-of-bounds pointer writes `image->aperture[tool_num] = g_new0(gerbv_aperture_t, 1)`, corrupting memory at an attacker-controlled index.

evidence.reason: Fail-open bounds check: it correctly detects tool_num outside [TOOL_MIN, TOOL_MAX) but only logs an error; with no return/break, execution continues with the attacker-controlled out-of-range index. Simulated trigger: 'T99999C0.010' → tool_num=99999 enters this arm and still reaches the indexing sinks.
Out-of-bounds read of the aperture pointer array using the unvalidated tool_num; the garbage pointer may also be dereferenced at `apert->parameter[0] != size` (line 114) if non-NULL.

Out-of-bounds write: stores a heap pointer at image->aperture[tool_num] with attacker-controlled tool_num (e.g. 99999 or -5), corrupting memory beyond the array; the identical write recurs at line 184 for undefined tools.
Taint origin: tool_num is parsed directly from the untrusted drill file with full int domain (negative values admitted by the '+'/'-' acceptance at line 40) and no range validation before use.

assumptions: TOOL_MIN/TOOL_MAX define the valid index range of image->aperture (the bounds check at line 63 is the code's own statement of that domain); TOOL_MAX and the array extent are not shown, so any tool_num outside the checked range is treated as out-of-bounds per the width-domain rule.
gerb_fgetint parses arbitrarily long digit strings and leading '-', so the full int domain of tool_num is instantiable from file content.
limitations: Line 26 `tmps = get_line(fd++);` post-increments the fd parameter, so the subsequent `fd->filename` at line 30 reads through a pointer one struct past the object (out-of-bounds read passed as %s); noted as a secondary anomaly, not the verdict driver.
state->current_tool is set to the unvalidated tool_num (line 71); any out-of-range indexing by consumers of that field occurs in code not shown.
The `if ('\n' == temp || '\r' == temp) gerb_ungetc(fd);` inside the EOF branch (lines 174-175) is dead code, a logic flaw with no direct security impact.

verdict.summary: In mrb_vm_exec, the environment-length guards for OP_BLKPUSH and OP_ARGARY ('MRB_ENV_LEN(e) <= m1+r+m2+1') omit the kd slot that the subsequent access reads ('stack[m1+r+m2+kd]' / 'stack[m1+r+m2+1]' with stack = e->stack+1). With the kd bit set and MRB_ENV_LEN(e) == m1+r+m2+2, the VM reads e->stack[LEN], one mrb_value past the environment's stack allocation, and promotes that out-of-bounds/stale value to a live Ruby object (the yielded block), an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: OP_BLKPUSH guard: the only length check before the sink 'if (mrb_nil_p(stack[m1+r+m2+kd]))' / 'regs[a] = stack[m1+r+m2+kd];' (lines 1180, 1184), where stack = e->stack+1 so the read hits e->stack[m1+r+m2+kd+1].
