assumptions: priv is allocated and populated by the driver's registration path (not shown); its pointer value is treated as driver-internal state rather than attacker-crafted data.
nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort, nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit, nci_unregister_device, and nci_free_device follow their standard kernel semantics (no double-free/UAF reachable from this call sequence).
limitations: priv (and the priv->ndev->nfc_dev chain) is dereferenced without a NULL check on line 2/4; a NULL priv would crash the kernel cleanup path. The trigger requires an unshown caller passing NULL and the consequence is crash-only with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass, so it is a robustness issue, not a verdict-driving vulnerability.

The fw_download_in_progress check and the subsequent abort/deinit calls are not atomic; a concurrent firmware-download completion between the check and the teardown could race, but no concurrent attacker-reachable path is exhibited in this code.
The bodies of nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort() and nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_deinit() are not shown; any defect inside those callees (e.g., double free, work-queue UAF) could not be verified from this code alone.
If this function were invoked twice on the same priv (e.g., a buggy disconnect path), kfree(priv) would double-free; no such second invocation exists in the given code.

verdict.summary: No attacker-value produces a fully instantiated security impact inside this code: the axis tensor is gated by a quoted rank-0 WithRank, a nullptr check, WithRankAtLeast, and checked-status Subshape calls; the remaining defect candidates (min_rank overflow/truncation for |concat_dim| >= 2^31, unchecked dtype in the else arm, trusted index parameters) each require unshown callee or caller behavior to cause harm, so none can be confirmed from this code alone.

assumptions: The contents of concat_dim_t (the tf.concat axis tensor) are attacker-data with the full signed int32/int64 domain; start_value_index/end_value_index/dim_index are treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule since no in-code check constrains them.

InferenceContext::Subshape/WithRank/WithRankAtLeast are treated as validation-returning callees because every call site propagates their Status via TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR; their internal bounds checks are not quotable here.
The flat<T>()(0) access is treated as in-bounds because the quoted 'TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(dim_index), 0, &unused));' forces a scalar (1-element) tensor.
limitations: 'const int min_rank = concat_dim < 0 ? -concat_dim : concat_dim + 1;' overflows at concat_dim = INT64_MAX (concat_dim + 1 wraps) and is UB at INT64_MIN (-concat_dim), and the int64-to-int truncation lets |concat_dim| >= 2^31 produce min_rank = INT32_MIN/0, so the quoted WithRankAtLeast guard under-enforces; the out-of-bounds consequence would occur only inside the unshown InferenceContext::Subshape/Dim implementations, whose validation cannot be quoted — impact not instantiated.

The 'else' arm 'concat_dim = concat_dim_t->flat<int64>()(0);' assumes DT_INT64; a non-int32/int64 dtype would CHECK-fail inside the callee (same-privilege crash/DoS only), and reaching it requires bypassing the not-shown op-def dtype validation at graph construction.

'ShapeHandle input = c->input(end_value_index - 1);' indexes the input list with a caller-supplied parameter; end_value_index <= start_value_index would read out of bounds, but no caller is shown and no in-code guard exists — trigger precondition could not be instantiated in this code.

The huge-rank path (dims.reserve(rank) with attacker-chosen input rank) offers roughly 1:1 resource amplification versus the attacker's own shape-construction cost, so it is not a scalable CWE-400 candidate.

verdict.summary: In mobi_parse_index_entry, the raw pointer control_bytes (initialized to the entry start at line 41 and incremented once per TAGX entry with control_byte == 1 at line 62) is never bounded against the buffer end, so a crafted TAGX header with a large tags_count drives control_bytes far past the heap buffer and line 66 reads control_bytes[0] out of bounds — an attacker-scalable heap over-read (crash/DoS, read bytes flow into parsed tag values).

evidence.reason: Root cause: control_bytes (set at line 41 to buf->data + buf->offset) is advanced once per tag with control_byte == 1 with no bound against buf->data + buf->maxlen or cap at tagx->control_byte_count; the loop only bounds i, not the pointer. Trigger: crafted index record with tags_count = 0x10000, all but the last tag control_byte == 1 → control_bytes[0] at line 66 reads ~64 KB past the heap buffer; the OOB byte is ANDed into value and flows into value_count/value_bytes stored in parsed tags.

assumptions: tagx->tags_count, tagx->control_byte_count, tagx->tags[].control_byte/bitmask and idxt.offsets are parsed from the attacker-supplied MOBI file (their producers are not shown), so per the width-domain rule their full declared domains are instantiable.
mobi_buffer_get8/mobi_buffer_seek/mobi_buffer_get_varlen are bounds-checked against buf->maxlen (standard buffer-helper semantics); the raw control_bytes pointer deliberately bypasses them.
limitations: line 7 entry_length = idxt.offsets[n+1] - idxt.offsets[n] can wrap to a huge value and bypass the line 16 check via wraparound of buf->offset + entry_length, but line 20 then sets buf->maxlen below the original size, so all mobi_buffer_* accesses fail closed — no memory-safety impact demonstrated here.

label_length is reassigned by the unshown callees mobi_getstring_ordt / mobi_indx_get_label before strncpy at line 38; a return exceeding the stack buffer text[INDX_LABEL_SIZEMAX] could over-read the stack, but the callees are not shown, so this stays speculative.

curr_number indexes idxt.offsets[curr_number] and [curr_number + 1] at lines 7-8 before any local bound against the offsets array size; the caller is not shown, so an out-of-range curr_number could not be instantiated within this code.
The error paths that return after allocating indx->entries[entry_number].label leak memory; robustness issue only, no security impact established.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot is not vulnerable: the only value reaching memory-access sinks is the loop index i, provably bounded by the quoted loop guard 'for(i = 0; i < MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS; i++)' at both boundaries and in execution order; the only pointer write is guarded by 'if(handle)'; the MemorySet length is a fixed sizeof matching its destination. No attacker-data crosses a trust boundary into this function.

assumptions: MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS and TRANSIENT_FIRST are compile-time constants with MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS small enough that i + TRANSIENT_FIRST cannot wrap TPMI_DH_OBJECT (both are constants in the enclosing TPM code, not runtime inputs).
MemorySet is a void fixed-size memset wrapper with no failure sentinel to check.
limitations: Potential race on the global s_objects array (two concurrent calls could return the same unoccupied slot) cannot be evaluated: no locking or concurrency model is shown in the given code; treated as speculative.
The function does not itself mark the returned slot occupied; whether the caller does so before another lookup is a contract not shown here.

verdict.summary: FindEmptyObjectSlot scans a fixed-size internal array with a correctly bounded loop, checks the optional out-pointer before writing, and zero-initializes the returned object; no attacker-data input reaches any unguarded sink.

assumptions: MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS matches the declared size of s_objects, as this is the same constant used for both per standard TPM reference code.
TRANSIENT_FIRST + MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS - 1 fits in TPMI_DH_OBJECT (UINT32), which holds for the standard TPM2 transient-handle range and small MAX_LOADED_OBJECTS values.
limitations: If a caller of this function fails to set attributes.occupied after receiving the zeroed object, the slot remains CLEAR; that defect would live in the not-shown caller and is speculative here.

The zeroing MemorySet clears attributes AFTER the occupied check was read from the same element; this is correct ordering here since the same element is being claimed, and no guard or invariant is violated.

verdict.summary: reg_match_visual contains all of the upstream guards: the lnum bounds check (`lnum < top.lnum || lnum > bot.lnum`) runs before any use, the Ctrl_V path re-fetches rex.line/rex.input after getvvcol flushes them, and the MAXCOL arm (`end = MAXCOL`) bounds the only overflow-shaped expression. The remaining arithmetic edges (`bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')` with bot.col==MAXCOL, `end - 1` with end==0) wrap into the reject direction, causing at worst a failed \%V match (over-rejection), never an out-of-domain accept, memory error, or bypass.

assumptions: colnr_T is a signed 32-bit int and MAXCOL is 0x7fffffff, matching the Vim headers this code is drawn from.
rex.input/rex.line point inside the currently matched buffer line (regexp engine invariant), so col = rex.input - rex.line is within [0, line_len].
reg_getline(rex.lnum) returns the line currently being matched; the quoted lnum guard proves it is a valid buffer line, so a NULL return is not instantiable.
limitations: `bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')` overflows if bot.col == MAXCOL in charwise mode; the wrapped value makes the test always-true → returns FALSE (functional over-rejection, no security impact); upstream Vim has the same shape.
`cols > end - (*p_sel == 'e')` evaluates to `cols > -1` when end == 0 and 'selection' is "exclusive", over-rejecting the match; functional only.

A NULL from reg_getline would deref NULL at `rex.input = rex.line + col`, but the quoted lnum guard and the engine invariant that the line is being matched make that state unreachable in this code alone.

verdict.summary: SProcXkbSelectEvents validates the variable-length tail of the client request before byte-swapping it: dataLeft is computed from the (already minimum-size-checked) wire length, each event's required byte count is checked via 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength' before the swaps() / swapl() writes, unknown affectWhich bits are rejected by the switch default, and leftover data is rejected after the loop. dataLeft is always non-negative and a multiple of 4 (length*4 minus the 16-byte fixed header, all consumption in 4/8-byte units), so the size==1 path's '>= 2' test still covers its 4-byte consumption and cannot underflow. No unguarded sink remains.

assumptions: SIZEOF(xkbSelectEventsReq) is 16 (a multiple of 4), and X protocol request lengths are in 4-byte units, so dataLeft = stuff->length*4 - 16 is always a non-negative multiple of 4; this is what makes the 'dataLeft < (size * 2)' check (which tests 2 for size==1 while 4 bytes are consumed) sufficient at both boundaries (0 rejected, 2/3 unreachable, >=4 covered).

The X server request dispatcher delivers a buffer of at least stuff->length*4 bytes, so dataLeft accurately bounds the bytes reachable via from.c8; REQUEST_AT_LEAST_SIZE(xkbSelectEventsReq) is quoted and runs before dataLeft is computed, preventing initial underflow.
limitations: The known vulnerable twin of this function (pre-fix upstream X.Org code) performs the swaps() / swapl() calls without the 'if (dataLeft < (size * 2)) return BadLength;' check, allowing a client to set affectWhich bits on a short request and cause out-of-bounds writes past the request buffer; in the code as given, that check is present and verified at both bounds.

ProcXkbSelectEvents (the callee handling the swapped request) is not shown; its own handling of the trailing data cannot be assessed here, but the swapper's memory accesses are fully bounded by the quoted dataLeft guard.

For size==1 events the guard requires dataLeft >= 2 while 4 bytes are skipped; this is only safe because of the 4-byte granularity of dataLeft — a hypothetical request encoding with non-4-byte-granular length would break this reasoning, but X protocol lengths do not allow that.

verdict.summary: All buffer reads (the attribute count and the four per-entry ut16 reads) are guarded by 'if (buf_offset + offset + 8 > sz)', which is checked before the first use of each iteration, uses the correct operator and absolute-byte unit, and provably keeps every R_BIN_JAVA_USHORT(buffer, offset) index in bounds. Remaining issues are robustness-only: a possibly-NULL obj is passed to a callee whose NULL handling is not shown, and error paths leak attr/icattr->name allocations.

assumptions: buffer, sz and buf_offset are supplied by the class-file attribute reader such that buffer[0] sits at absolute offset buf_offset in a buffer of size sz; the quoted guards are written in exactly this unit and are internally consistent.
r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list tolerates a NULL obj argument (callee not shown; at worst a same-privilege parser crash).
limitations: obj may be NULL when passed to r_bin_java_get_item_name_from_bin_cp_list because the NULL case only eprintfs and continues; if that callee dereferences obj it would be a NULL-deref crash while parsing an untrusted class file (robustness/DoS at same privilege, not memory corruption).

Memory leaks on attacker-triggerable error paths: early 'return NULL' leaks attr, and the final 'free (icattr); break;' after 'icattr->name = r_str_dup (NULL, "NULL")' leaks name and flags_str and drops the parsed entry (functional/leak, bounded per attribute).
buf_offset + offset + 8 could wrap ut64 only if the unshown caller supplies a buf_offset near 2^64; no statement in this code can produce such a value, so this is speculative.

verdict.summary: In st21nfca_connectivity_event_received, an attacker-controlled HCI EVT_TRANSACTION frame with a short skb->len causes the params_len bound check 'transaction->params_len > ((skb->len - 2) - sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction))' to wrap unsigned (skb->len - 2 < sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction)), so the check fails open and memcpy writes up to 255 attacker-controlled bytes into a devm_kzalloc(skb->len - 2) allocation that can be as small as a few bytes — a heap out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Defective guard: with skb->len=7, skb->len-2=5 minus sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) (>=18, since aid alone is 16 bytes) wraps in unsigned size_t arithmetic to ~2^64-19, so '255 > huge' is false and any params_len passes; the check fails open for every frame shorter than sizeof(struct)+2.

Sink: with skb->len=7 the devm_kzalloc at line 26 allocates 5 bytes, but params_len=255 (from skb->data[3]) is admitted by the wrapped check and memcpy writes 255 attacker-controlled bytes at offset sizeof(struct) (~24) — heap out-of-bounds write of ~274 bytes past the allocation.

Origin of the undersized destination: the allocation is sized solely from skb->len - 2, which the attacker sets as low as 5 (or lower, since the line-22 '&&' check also lets shorter tagged frames through), while the params copy at lines 50-51 is bounded only by the wrapping check on line 47.

assumptions: struct nfc_evt_transaction (not shown) contains at least the two length fields and a u8 aid[16] array, so sizeof(struct nfc_evt_transaction) >= 18 > skb->len - 2 for any frame of len <= 19; the trigger uses len=7, so the wrap holds for any plausible layout of that struct.
skb->len is unsigned (struct sk_buff) and sizeof yields size_t, so '(skb->len - 2) - sizeof(...)' is evaluated in unsigned arithmetic and wraps negative results.
limitations: Secondary out-of-bounds READS in the same path: the '&&' at lines 22-23 should be '||', so a frame with len=3 and data[0]==0x81 passes validation, and skb->data[aid_len+2], skb->data[aid_len+3], and the aid memcpy source at lines 36-37 read past skb->len (consequence of the same unvalidated frame; not counted as an independent CWE).
skb->len < 2 makes 'skb->len - 2' wrap to ~4GB, but devm_kzalloc then fails and the NULL check at lines 27-28 returns -ENOMEM — no overflow.
Error returns (-EPROTO, -EINVAL) skip kfree_skb, leaking the skb — a resource leak, not a security impact.
Exact reachability from a physical NFC peer vs. a local HCI injection point is a deployment property; per the width-domain rule the handler's skb parameters are attacker-data regardless.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability. The attacker-controlled namespace URI length (len) is guarded at every sink: allocation is sized from the same expression as the subsequent memcpy (len + EXPAND_SPARE), the reuse path skips realloc only when len <= b->uriAlloc (so capacity is always >= len), both allocation branches precheck len > INT_MAX - EXPAND_SPARE to prevent size wrap, REALLOC/MALLOC results are NULL-checked, and the b->uri[len - 1] write is covered because the same m_namespaceSeparator condition that enables it has already executed len++ earlier in execution order. Prefix-name indexing (name[1..5]) is protected by short-circuit comparisons that cannot run past the NUL terminator. This is the fixed variant of expat's addBinding (the CVE-2022-22822 overflow checks are present and verified at both boundaries).

assumptions: uri is a non-NULL, NUL-terminated string supplied by expat's internal parser/pool (the intake point for termination is the tokenizer, not this function); no candidate trigger depends on this contract being violated.
parser->m_freeBindingList entries have b->uriAlloc consistent with a prior allocation of the same expression; this is internal state, not attacker-data.
EXPAND_SPARE is a positive constant so that len + EXPAND_SPARE and the separator write remain in range; its value is not shown.
limitations: The counting loop `for (len = 0; uri[len]; len++)` has no internal cap, so a namespace URI of >= 2^31 characters would wrap the int len (signed overflow) before any guard runs, potentially enabling a negative-length memcpy. This requires an attacker to push a >2 GiB single attribute value through the parse into the pool; that scale cannot be instantiated or bounded by any quoted statement in this snippet, so it is recorded as theoretical (CWE-190-shaped) rather than confirmed.

If uri were not NUL-terminated, the counting loop would read out of bounds; termination is guaranteed by the (not shown) parser pool that produces uri, and this function is not the intake point for it.

A NULL uri or NULL prefix would dereference at the first statement; neither is instantiable from XML content — these come only from internal call sites within expat and are contract-level, not attacker-data.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable defect. The position-consuming sinks (getvvcol) are bounded by the quoted guards 'rex.reg_buf != curbuf' and 'if (lnum < top.lnum || lnum > bot.lnum) return FALSE', all column comparisons fail closed (return FALSE), and the MAXCOL+1 signed wrap in 'bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')' produces a fail-closed negative, not a bypass. The only theoretical gap (stale curbuf->b_visual after user deletes lines, making bot.lnum exceed the buffer in getvvcol) is not attacker-instantiable — it requires user editing actions, not data across a trust boundary.

assumptions: rex.lnum/rex.reg_firstlnum/rex.input/rex.line are produced by the regex engine's own iteration over the searched buffer and are therefore always valid in-buffer positions; no statement here re-derives them from attacker data.
getvvcol/getvcol/win_linetabsize consume valid position arguments per their standard semantics; no copy or allocation is sized from attacker data in this function.
VIsual, VIsual_mode, wp->w_cursor, wp->w_curswant and curbuf->b_visual are editor session state set by user interaction, not by parsed file content.
limitations: Speculative: if the user makes a blockwise Visual selection and later deletes lines so curbuf->b_visual.vi_end.lnum exceeds ml_line_count, 'getvvcol(wp, &bot, ...)' (line 55) could read out of bounds inside getvcol/ml_get_buf (CWE-125); the precondition (user line deletion) is not attacker-instantiable and is not guarded here (only 'lnum > bot.lnum' bounds lnum, not bot against the line count).

Signed integer overflow in 'bot.col + (*p_sel != 'e')' when bot.col == MAXCOL (CWE-190, UB) wraps to a negative value, but the resulting comparison 'col >= negative' is TRUE, so the function returns FALSE — fail-closed, no security impact.
The 'V' (linewise) mode returns TRUE after only the lnum check; this is intended semantics (whole-line selection), not a fail-open gap.

verdict.summary: In the octet-counting framing parser (eInOctetCnt digit branch), every received digit is appended to the session message buffer via *(pThis->pMsg + pThis->iMsg++) = c; with no check that pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine. The only bound in that branch (if(pThis->iOctetsRemain <= 200000000)) caps the accumulated counter VALUE, not the number of digit bytes written; a frame consisting of more than iMaxLine '0' digits keeps iOctetsRemain at 0 (0*10+0=0), so the cap never fires and each digit writes one attacker-chosen byte past the end of the iMaxLine-sized pMsg buffer (capacity proven by the twin guard if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) guarding the identical write in the octet-stuffing branch), yielding an unbounded heap out-of-bounds write driven by untrusted TCP input.

evidence.reason: Unbounded out-of-bounds write: in the digit branch of the octet-counting state, iMsg is incremented per digit with no capacity check. The nearby check if(pThis->iOctetsRemain <= 200000000) bounds the counter value, not iMsg; a trigger frame of N > iMaxLine '0' digits keeps the value at 0 and writes N attacker-chosen bytes into pMsg, whose capacity is iMaxLine per the sibling guard if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine) present only in the octet-stuffing branch. Root cause: missing iMsg < iMaxLine bound at this sink.

assumptions: pMsg is allocated with capacity iMaxLine; this is quoted indirectly by the identical write in the stuffing branch being guarded by if(pThis->iMsg < iMaxLine), which is only meaningful if iMaxLine is the buffer capacity.

buffLen is a non-negative receive length from the caller; the memcpy clamps (buffLen < octatesToCopy and octatesToCopy + pThis->iMsg > iMaxLine) then bound the copy to min(buffLen, iMaxLine - iMsg), which holds only for buffLen >= 0.
limitations: A negative buffLen would flow into memcpy as a huge size_t (int -> size_t conversion) and cause an OOB access, but instantiating it requires the unseen caller passing a negative length, which no quoted statement in this code produces; treated as speculative.
doSubmitMsg is assumed to reset iMsg and finalize the message; its internals are not shown.

On the emergency-flush path (iMsg >= iMaxLine, stuffing framing), iMsg is not explicitly reset in this function; if doSubmitMsg does not reset it, subsequent handling relies on the iMsg < iMaxLine write guard, which still blocks the stuffing write — no separate overflow on that path.

verdict.summary: nft_flow_rule_create checks every failure sentinel (NULL from nft_flow_rule_alloc and kzalloc, negative return from expr->ops->offload) before first use, sets err on every goto path, and never passes an attacker-derived raw size, index, or offset into any memory or copy operation. The two structurally suspicious candidates — a num_actions undercount versus entries appended by offload callbacks, and a use-after-free if a callback invalidated expr — both have their entire impact chain inside not-shown callee code and are therefore speculative under this code alone.

assumptions: expr->ops points to kernel-registered nft_expr_ops with compile-time ops->size; rule->dlen equals the sum of the sizes of the expressions actually present, so the nft_expr_next/nft_expr_more iteration terminates exactly at nft_expr_last(rule).

The offload callbacks invoked via expr->ops->offload are assumed (not provable from this code) to append at most one flow-action entry per expression carrying NFT_OFFLOAD_F_ACTION and to not free or replace the expression; these assumptions could not be quoted.
limitations: If any registered expression's offload callback appends a flow-action entry without NFT_OFFLOAD_F_ACTION, or appends more than one entry, the kcalloc'd action array sized by num_actions would overflow inside that callback (not shown); the defect would then live at the callback, and this function's count loop would be the root cause. Not instantiated here.

expr = nft_expr_next(expr) reads expr->ops after expr has been handed to an arbitrary callback; a use-after-free requires a callback that frees or rewrites the expression — no in-tree evidence was available to instantiate this, so it remains speculative.
num_actions integer overflow would require a rule with more than 2^31 expressions, which rule-size limits preclude.

verdict.summary: tipc_crypto_key_rcv() parses a network-supplied key-distribution message but consumes the attacker-controlled key length before validating it: skey->keylen is read from the message payload (line 23) and used as the memcpy length (lines 25-26) into an allocation sized from a different, unvalidated message field (size, line 16), while the only size sanity check (line 29) executes after the copy. A peer sending a small message with a large 32-bit length field causes a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-controlled bytes in the kernel (CWE-787, CVE-2021-43267).

evidence.reason: Root cause: skey->keylen is taken from attacker-controlled message data (line 23) with no bound against the allocation size, then used as the memcpy length at lines 25-26 into the heap object allocated with kmalloc(size) (line 16). Trigger: msg with size=36 and length field 0xFFFFFFFF at offset 32 → memcpy of up to 65535 bytes into a 36-byte heap allocation, a network-triggered kernel heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled content.

This is the only size validation, but it executes after the memcpy at lines 25-26, so it cannot prevent the out-of-bounds write; the intended guard is present but placed after first use (guard-after-use).

assumptions: msg_data_sz/msg_data return the length/payload of a network-received TIPC message, so size and data contents are attacker-controlled across a trust boundary.
struct tipc_aead_key::keylen is at most 16 bits wide, capping the overflow length at 65535 bytes, which is still far larger than the kmalloc(size) allocation for small size values.
limitations: A secondary out-of-bounds read exists when size < TIPC_AEAD_ALG_NAME + sizeof(__be32): lines 23-24 read past the message payload (CWE-125); it is subsumed by the primary OOB-write candidate and does not change the CWE.
The unaligned 4-byte read at line 23 and the kmalloc(0) case when size == 0 are robustness/hardening notes; the primary heap overflow dominates.

verdict.summary: cgroup1_parse_param validates every attacker-supplied field before use: 'name' size is bounded to MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN-1 (verified at both bounds: size 63 fits exactly with NUL in the 64-byte buffer, size 64 rejected), empty names rejected, content restricted to [\w.-] by an explicit whitelist loop that also bounds the param->string[i] index read, and all negative fs_parse sentinels (-ENOPARAM and opt < 0) are checked before the switch. No sink consumes attacker data without a quoted, execution-order-verified guard.

assumptions: param->size is set by the in-kernel fs parameter parser to the strlen of param->string, and param->string/param->key are NUL-terminated — framework contract, not quotable in this snippet, but no in-code statement can produce a negative or size>strlen value either.
MAX_CGROUP_ROOT_NAMELEN is 64 (kernel definition, not shown).
limitations: A negative param->size would skip the whitelist loop and the bound (negative fails both '!' and '>63'), but no producer in this code can instantiate it; if a caller ever passed a negative size the name would be accepted unvalidated — depends on code not shown.

Opt_release_agent stores param->string (an arbitrary path later executed via call_usermodehelper on cgroup release) with no local validation; the execution site is outside this code and the mount path requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, so no impact is instantiated here (cf. CVE-2022-0492 hardening done elsewhere in the kernel).
Kernel _ctype table is assumed to be signed-char-safe (spans -128..255), preventing an OOB read in isalnum on high-bit bytes; such bytes are rejected by the whitelist anyway.

verdict.summary: The guest-controlled nargs value used to compute args.rets is bounded by the quoted check 'if (be32_to_cpu(args.nargs) >= ARRAY_SIZE(args.args)) ... goto fail', which executes before the indexed use on the only path, rejecting exactly-at-limit and all larger 32-bit values; kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest return values are checked and args_phys is masked with KVM_PAM. No primary candidate survives.

assumptions: kvm_read_guest/kvm_write_guest validate the guest-physical address range and return nonzero on failure, per standard KVM semantics; their return codes are checked here.
d->handler->handler pointers come from host-registered RTAS token definitions, not guest data.
limitations: The RTAS handlers invoked via d->handler->handler(vcpu, &args) are not shown; the comment states each handler must validate nargs/nret and may write at most rets[0], which this code guarantees to be in-bounds (args.args[nargs] with nargs <= ARRAY_SIZE(args.args)-1). If a not-shown handler writes more rets than fit past args.args[nargs], that would be a defect in that handler, not in this function.
A guest supplying a bogus args pointer or overflowing nargs only fails the hcall out to host userspace, which is the documented intended behavior for that trust boundary.

verdict.summary: No exploitable defect in this code: buf is only consumed as string data against literal format strings, the qh_find_handler return is NULL-checked before use, qh->description is NULL-guarded, and the unused len parameter never reaches any memory operation. The only theoretical concern — buf not being NUL-terminated — depends entirely on the unshown caller that produced buf, not on any statement here.

assumptions: buf is a NUL-terminated C string as produced by the (not shown) input dispatcher; no in-code statement establishes or checks this, but no length-consuming memory operation here can be under-bounded without it.
qhandlers is a NULL-terminated linked list, as implied by the traversal 'for (qh = qhandlers; qh != NULL; qh = qh->next_qh)'.
limitations: Speculative (caller-dependent): if the caller of qh_help can pass a buffer that is not NUL-terminated within its allocation, strcmp(buf,...) and the %s printfs would read out of bounds (CWE-125/170). The trigger is a caller-state precondition not instantiable from any value in buf's own domain, and this code performs no length-based copy that could corrupt memory, so it is not confirmed as a primary finding.

The unused len parameter suggests a caller-side bound exists; no validation of len against strlen(buf) is performed here, but since len is never used in any sink, this is a code-hygiene note with no security consequence in this function.
Attacker-controlled buf is echoed back on the same socket to the same peer (nsock_printf_nul with '%s'); no log, HTML, or header sink is constructed here, so no CWE-117/79/113 applies in this code.

verdict.summary: In suggest_trie_walk() STATE_REP, a REP replacement from the spell file is applied with STRMOVE(p + tl, p + fl) and mch_memmove(p, ftp->ft_to, tl) after only a source-pattern match (STRNCMP of ft_from); no statement bounds the resulting fword length. An attacker-supplied spell file with ft_to longer than ft_from, applied to a long bad word, writes past the end of the caller's fixed-size fword buffer (out-of-bounds write).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: ftp->ft_to/ft_from lengths come from the attacker-controlled spell-file REP table (gap->ga_data); the only preceding check is the source match 'if (STRNCMP(ftp->ft_from, p, STRLEN(ftp->ft_from)) == 0'. With ft_from="a" (fl=1) and a 30-byte ft_to (tl=30) applied at ts_fidx=0 to a ~230-byte bad word, STRMOVE(p+30, p+1) shifts the 230-byte tail to offsets 30..259, past the 254-byte fword buffer; the overflow scales with tl-fl and no guard on any path bounds p + tl + tail.

Taint origin: ftp (REP item from spell file, across the trust boundary) is fetched from the attacker-influenced garray; the STRNCMP verifies only that the source pattern matches fword content and constrains neither tl nor the resulting destination extent, so the replacement proceeds unbounded into the STRMOVE sink at lines 1364-1369.

assumptions: fword is the caller's fixed-size buffer (in Vim, char_u fword[MAXWLEN], MAXWLEN=254 in suggest_try_change); its extent is the bound the STRMOVE violates.

REP items (ft_from/ft_to) originate from a spell file that an attacker can supply (e.g., via a downloaded .spl/.aff loaded with 'set spell'); their lengths are not bounded by any statement in this code.
limitations: Writes to tword[]/stack[] via go_deeper/TRY_DEEPER and the compflags[ts_complen+1]=NUL one-past candidate depend on the depth bound inside the unshown TRY_DEEPER macro; if that macro includes 'depth < MAXWLEN - 1' (as in upstream Vim), those candidates are bounded and were not triggerable here.
preword[MAXWLEN*3] append arithmetic (split + skipped-char copies) is marginally sized but no concrete overflow value could be instantiated within this code alone.
STATE_REP_UNDO mirrors the vulnerable STRMOVE in the restore direction; it is the same defect, not counted as a second CWE.

verdict.summary: No attacker-controlled data crosses into this GLib client callback; every callee return (connect_finish error, proxy lookup, protocol resolution) is sentinel-checked at or before first use, ownership transfers use g_steal_pointer before unrefs, and no memory primitive, injection, or authorization sink exists.

assumptions: The current 'attempt' is not an element of data->connection_attempts by the time the cancel loop runs; this is governed by connection_attempt_new/connection_attempt_remove, which are not shown.
GLib async callback parameters (source, result, user_data) are produced by GLib's own machinery and are not attacker-instantiable across a trust boundary.
limitations: Potential double-unref of 'attempt' (loop unrefs list entries, then connection_attempt_unref(attempt) at line ~50) is speculative: whether 'attempt' is still in data->connection_attempts depends on connection_attempt_new/connection_attempt_remove, not shown; no quoted statement places it in the list.

The non-TCP arm calls g_set_error_literal without g_clear_error, which would trip GLib's 'error already set' assertion if data->last_error were set; the arm requires a non-TCP GSocketConnection from a TCP-oriented client path, which no quoted statement can produce (code itself calls it a GLib bug).

Reentrancy of g_cancellable_cancel inside the attempt-cancellation loop potentially mutating data->connection_attempts mid-iteration is a callee-internal behavior not shown here; no quoted chain links it to a use-after-free in this code.
A NULL 'protocol' from g_proxy_address_get_protocol flows only through NULL-tolerant lookups and a printf '%s' (prints '(null)'); cosmetic at worst.

verdict.summary: Constant-time 256-bit modular reduction; all attacker-influenced data is confined to 64-bit limb arithmetic with explicit carries, and no input value reaches an index, length, or pointer. All memory accesses are safe for the only calling context (p->size == 4).

assumptions: p points to the library's static ecc_modulo for the 256-bit curve with p->size == 4 and p->m of at least 3 limbs, as this hardcoded reduction (2^96-1 low-limb structure) is only correct for that curve; this is internal trusted library state, not attacker data.
rp is a caller buffer of 2*p->size limbs, per the ecc_modp calling convention.
limitations: The function performs no runtime check that p->size == 4; if it were ever registered for a smaller curve, indices like rp + n - 4 (with n >= p->size >= 2) and the hardcoded stores rp[2]/rp[3] could go out of bounds. Not attacker-triggerable from this code, so speculative.
assert (q2 < 2) is compiled out with NDEBUG; it guards arithmetic correctness (which holds by the carry chain), not memory safety.

verdict.summary: write_entry consumes the return of make_key() without any sentinel/bounds check: keylen is an int assigned from a bounded-copy helper (line 26) whose full domain includes a negative failure sentinel produced when the attacker-controlled mboxname/uid/entry/userid key cannot fit in key[MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1]. keylen is then passed unchecked as the key length to read_old_value (line 29), cyrusdb_delete (line 68), and cyrusdb_store (line 93); a negative value widens to a huge size_t, driving out-of-bounds reads past the stack buffer.

evidence.snippet: keylen = make_key(mboxname, uid, entry, userid, key, sizeof(key));
evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: the int keylen is assigned from make_key(), a callee that enforces the sizeof(key) bound and signals overflow via its return value, but no statement in the function tests keylen (no 'keylen < 0', no 'keylen >= sizeof(key)', no clamp) before its first use on line 29.

evidence.snippet: r = cyrusdb_store(d->db, key, keylen, data.s, data.len, tid(d));
evidence.reason: Sink: cyrusdb_store receives key (a MAX_MAILBOX_PATH+1-byte stack buffer) with keylen as its length. Trigger: attacker sets an annotation with an entry name long enough that make_key returns -1; keylen = -1 widens to (size_t)-1, so the DB layer reads key far out of bounds (first unchecked use is read_old_value on line 29, same defect).

assumptions: make_key's keysize parameter exists to bound the copy into key and it returns a negative failure sentinel when the composed key overflows, matching the standard bounded-copy semantics the declared int return admits; its exact body is not shown.

Attacker reachability: this is the Cyrus annotation write path; entry, userid, uid, and value are IMAP client-supplied (SETANNOTATION), so overlong entry names are instantiable per the width-domain rule.
limitations: If make_key silently truncates and returns a non-negative length instead of a sentinel, the OOB read does not materialize; make_key's body is not in the given code.
The quota arithmetic at line 44 (value->len - (quota_t)oldval.len) is a potential integer-overflow candidate but cannot be instantiated at any value a quoted statement admits here.
The DEBUG syslog uses of keylen (lines 64, 89) are inside #if DEBUG and not compiled; key_as_string with a negative keylen would be an additional format/sentinel issue only in debug builds.

oldval.s NULL inside the line-33 memcmp is not instantiable because reaching it requires oldval.len == value->len > 0, which implies read_old_value populated the buffer; no quoted path yields len > 0 with s == NULL.

verdict.summary: qh_help consumes attacker-supplied buf only through NULL-checked string comparisons and literal-format printf calls; every use is guarded and no memory, length, or output-construction sink consumes unvalidated attacker data. The unused len parameter never reaches a bound.

assumptions: buf is a NUL-terminated string per its char* contract with the (not shown) query dispatcher; all uses (strcmp, qh_find_handler, %s printing) are string-typed.
qh_find_handler and the nsock_printf helpers behave per standard semantics: string-key lookup with a NULL miss sentinel, and printf-style output with no memory writes back into buf.
limitations: If the unseen caller could pass a non-NUL-terminated buf, strcmp/qh_find_handler would over-read; no such caller is shown and this code passes buf only as the string it is declared to be, so the defect would reside entirely in unshown code.
A registered query_handler with a NULL handler function pointer would crash at qh->handler(sd, "help", 4); the registry population code is not shown, so this is not instantiable here.
The 'len' parameter is declared but never used; it is dead in this function and cannot contribute to any overflow.
The '> 200' return-value threshold is a functional heuristic on the handler's exit code, not a security decision; its failure mode is a cosmetic message.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks are guarded: every strlcat bound (MTAB_OPTIONS_LEN) exactly matches the calloc allocation size and is additionally wrapped by a NULL check (`if (mountent.mnt_opts)`), every sentinel return (setmntent, fileno, fstat, sigprocmask, lock_mtab, toggle_dac_capability, addmntent, my_endmntent) is tested before the value it protects is used, and all format strings are literals. The unvalidated attacker-derived devname/mountpoint/fstype strings are appended verbatim to /etc/mtab via addmntent (record forging), but the harmful impact requires a consumer of /etc/mtab that is not shown and the writer has already legitimately completed the mount; the calloc-failure path passes a NULL mnt_opts to addmntent but is instantiable only via memory exhaustion and at worst crashes the same-privilege process; the atexit(unlock_mtab) plus explicit unlock_mtab() permits a double unlink of the lock file only inside an unexhibited race window. These are recorded as limitations, not verdict-flipping findings.

assumptions: glibc/standard libc semantics: addmntent appends a formatted record and fprintf("%s") tolerates NULL; strlcat appends at most size-1 bytes and NUL-terminates; calloc returns NULL on failure.
MOUNTED is /etc/mtab and addmntent performs no whitespace/newline escaping (consistent with libc behavior; libmount does its own escaping precisely for this reason).
getusername returns a NUL-terminated heap string or NULL; its NULL case is handled by `if (mount_user)`.
limitations: Unvalidated attacker-derived strings (devname, mountpoint, fstype) are written into /etc/mtab via addmntent with no canonical-form/escaping check anywhere in the function; a mountpoint containing spaces or a newline can forge or corrupt mtab entries. Dismissed as a verdict driver because the security impact requires an mtab consumer not shown in this code (an mtab entry is not one of the enumerated output-construction classes) and because the writer must already have successfully completed the mount being recorded.

If calloc fails, mountent.mnt_opts remains NULL and is passed to addmntent; on glibc this prints a '(null)' field (corrupted mtab entry), and on a less tolerant libc it is a NULL dereference. Trigger is memory exhaustion, not attacker-controlled data, and the crash is same-privilege → robustness issue.

atexit(unlock_mtab) is registered before lock_mtab(); on all paths where unlock_mtab() is also called explicitly, the process exit path calls unlock_mtab a second time, which can unlink a lock file re-created by another process in that window — an unexhibited race.
The `fd < 0` error path calls unlock_mtab() but never endmntent(pmntfile), leaking the FILE*; mount_user is never freed (memory leak).

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled inputs are validated before use: resource is bounds-checked against RLIM_NLIMITS before array indexing, the user rlimit copy is EFAULT-checked, rlim_cur is checked against rlim_max, raising rlim_max requires CAP_SYS_RESOURCE, RLIMIT_NOFILE max is capped at NR_OPEN, and the LSM hook result is tested before the write. No memory-corruption, authorization-bypass, injection, or fail-open path is reachable.

assumptions: rlim_t and cputime_t width/signedness follow the standard kernel definitions (unsigned), so the cur>max and infinity comparisons have no signedness confusion.
RLIM_NLIMITS equals the element count of signal->rlim, as in the kernel definition.
limitations: Setting RLIMIT_CPU to RLIM_INFINITY skips resetting a previously armed CPU timer, so a process may receive SIGXCPU/SIGKILL earlier than its new infinite limit: fail-closed, self-inflicted, same-privilege robustness issue, not a security vulnerability.
The kernel intentionally does not report an error when rejecting an RLIMIT_CPU value (documented in the code's own comment); no unvalidated value is applied on that path.

A very large finite RLIMIT_CPU value may overflow the cputime conversion and arm a shorter timer, but this only harms the caller's own process (fail-closed) and causes no corruption, disclosure, or bypass.

verdict.summary: win_redr_status appends flag markers to the global NameBuff[MAXPATHL] without any bounds check on len. With a buffer name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes and a set flag (help/preview/changed/read-only), the statement *(p + len++) = ' ' clobbers the buffer's only NUL terminator, leaving len == MAXPATHL; vim_snprintf is then called with size MAXPATHL - len == 0 (writes nothing) and len += STRLEN(p + len) reads past the end of the 1024-byte global array (out-of-bounds read). The garbage len further flows into MAXPATHL - len (negative int → huge size_t → out-of-bounds write via vim_snprintf when a second flag is set) and into the p += len - (this_ru_col - 1); *p = '<' truncation write, giving a memory-corruption chain from an attacker-controlled file path.

evidence.reason: Origin: the ' ' is appended with no check that len < MAXPATHL - 1. With an attacker-supplied buffer name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes (attacker-controlled file path) and b_p_ro/bt_help/bufIsChanged/w_p_pvw true, this writes at NameBuff[MAXPATHL-1], destroying the only NUL terminator and setting len = MAXPATHL.

evidence.snippet:
vim_snprintf((char *)p + len, MAXPATHL - len, "%s", _("[RO]"));
	    len += (int)STRLEN(p + len);
evidence.reason: Sink: with len == MAXPATHL, MAXPATHL - len == 0 so vim_snprintf writes nothing and NameBuff stays unterminated; STRLEN(p + len) then reads NameBuff[1024...], past the end of the char_u NameBuff[MAXPATHL] global array (out-of-bounds read), and the resulting unbounded len feeds MAXPATHL - len (negative → huge size_t → out-of-bounds write in a subsequent vim_snprintf) and the p += len - (this_ru_col - 1); *p = '<' write. No statement anywhere in the function compares len against MAXPATHL.

assumptions: NameBuff is the global char_u NameBuff[MAXPATHL] with MAXPATHL = 1024, per Vim's standard declaration.

get_trans_bufname fills NameBuff with the buffer name (file path); the best case for the code (a name of exactly MAXPATHL-1 bytes, NUL-terminated in-bounds) still triggers the defect, so no assumption about the unshown callee is needed.
vim_snprintf with size 0 writes nothing (standard snprintf semantics); if an implementation wrote a terminator anyway, the defect would be an immediate one-byte OOB write instead.
limitations: The out-of-bounds read length (bytes until an adjacent-memory NUL) and thus the concrete value of len after STRLEN(p + MAXPATHL) depend on adjacent global layout; the escalation to an out-of-bounds write additionally needs a second flag (help/preview/changed) set or a garbage len exceeding this_ru_col - 1 + MAXPATHL.
Whether get_trans_bufname itself truncates names longer than MAXPATHL-1 (which would be a separate overflow in the unshown callee) is not determinable from this code.

The column arithmetic on this_ru_col fed to screen_puts/screen_fill could address off-screen columns for extreme 'ruler' settings, but clamping inside the unshown screen functions could not be verified — speculative.
The static busy flag is not thread-safe, but no security impact was instantiated.

parse_errors: no valid JSON verdict found in output

verdict.summary: In inflate()'s gzip EXTRA handling, `len = state->head->extra_len - state->length;` dereferences state->head BEFORE the `state->head != Z_NULL` guard on the next line. A gzip stream with the FEXTRA flag (flags = 0x0408, passing the method/e000 checks) and a nonzero XLEN plus at least one extra byte reaches this line with state->head == Z_NULL (the default when inflateSetHeader is not called, a value the code itself anticipates with six other NULL tests), causing a NULL-pointer read and crash — a denial of service against any process inflating attacker-supplied data.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `state->head->extra_len` is read at line 144 before the `state->head != Z_NULL` check at line 145, so the guard is bypassed in execution order. Trigger: attacker-supplied gzip stream with flags = 0x0408 (FEXTRA) and XLEN >= 1 with at least one available input byte, while state->head is Z_NULL (no inflateSetHeader call) — line 144 dereferences NULL and the process crashes before the NULL test can run.

assumptions: GUNZIP is defined, as the gzip FLAGS/EXLEN/EXTRA code paths are compiled in the given source.
state->head == Z_NULL is the library default when inflateSetHeader is not called; the code itself treats NULL as in-domain via `if (state->head != Z_NULL)` at lines 52, 98, 107, 116, 129, and 135.
limitations: The NULL dereference is a read at a small offset from NULL; no memory-corruption or disclosure primitive was identified beyond the crash/DoS.

The `len + copy > state->head->extra_max` zmemcpy cap could theoretically wrap if a caller supplied extra_max near UINT_MAX alongside a multi-gigabyte buffer; no quoted statement instantiates that caller state, so it is not counted as a defect.

If the decompressing process were the same party that supplied the compressed data, this would reduce to a same-privilege robustness crash; the DoS classification rests on the standard trust boundary between a stream originator and the inflating process.

verdict.summary: In check_termcode(), the sentinel write `tp[len] = NUL;` writes at index *buflen of the caller-supplied buffer. The only local bounds check, `if (offset >= *buflen) break;`, bounds the loop variable offset, not the write index; no statement anywhere compares *buflen against bufsize. A caller-supplied completely full buffer (*buflen == bufsize, an in-domain parameter value) produces a one-byte NUL out-of-bounds write past the end of the allocation (CWE-787).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write: with buf != NULL, tp = buf + offset and len = *buflen - offset, so this statement writes buf[*buflen]. No check of *buflen against bufsize exists anywhere in the function; when the caller passes a full buffer (*buflen == bufsize, within the declared parameter domain), a NUL byte is written one past the end of the allocation. The trigger is fully instantiated at this line.

This is the only local check touching buflen, and it bounds the loop variable offset (wrong variable and unit) rather than the write index *buflen used by tp[len] = NUL at line 85; the missing guard is a check of *buflen against bufsize, which appears nowhere on any path.

assumptions: bufsize is the size of buf's allocation per the exported function's signature; an allocation larger than bufsize would require an unquoted caller contract.
get_bytes_from_buf/get_long_from_buf stop at NUL and return -1 (standard sentinel-checking semantics); the tp[len] = NUL sentinel written at line 85 bounds the scrollbar-loop reads to index len.
GUI-encoded values are bounded by the quoted check_menu_pointer validation for KS_MENU.
limitations: The buf != NULL path's real-world callers are not shown; if every caller guarantees a spare byte beyond bufsize (an unquoted contract), the overflow would not trigger in practice, which lowers confidence.
The buf == NULL path writes at typebuf.tb_buf[tb_off + tb_len]; typebuf allocation invariants are not shown, so no finding is claimed there.
Bugs inside handle_csi/handle_osc/handle_dcs/check_termcode_mouse/put_string_in_typebuf are out of scope (callees not shown).

verdict.summary: Every dereference of pols[i] for every index admitted by the loop bound is covered in execution order by quoted guards: pols[0] is checked for NULL and ERR_PTR before *num_xfrms = pols[0]->xfrm_nr, and *num_pols is incremented to 2 only inside if (pols[1]) after the IS_ERR(pols[1]) arm returns, so pols[1] is provably valid when the loop reads pols[1]->action. Remaining defects require caller states or callee behavior not shown (entry num_pols >= 2 with NULL later entries, xfrm_nr not bounded by this code, and the -1 num_xfrms sentinel consumed by an unshown caller), so no trigger is instantiated inside this code.

assumptions: The sole caller (not shown) invokes this helper with *num_pols == 1 and a validated pols[0], as the guards' structure implies; *num_xfrms = -1 is a sentinel the unshown caller interprets.
xfrm_nr and pols[] fields originate from netlink-configured XFRM policies; their producers (policy creation validation) are outside this code.
limitations: Candidate (a): if a caller ever passed *num_pols >= 2 with pols[1] == NULL, the loop 'if (pols[i]->action != XFRM_POLICY_ALLOW)' would NULL-deref; not instantiable from this code and only a same-context crash per discipline 3.

Candidate (b): entry *num_pols == 2 plus a sub-policy-typed pols[0] would overwrite pols[1] (reference leak) and increment num_pols to 3, causing the loop to read pols[2] beyond the caller's pols[] array (out-of-bounds read); the entry state and the array bound are both unshown, so this remains speculative.
Candidate (c): *num_xfrms can sum two xfrm_nr values (up to 510) exceeding XFRM_MAX_DEPTH; this code only stores the value, and any downstream overuse in the unshown caller could not be verified.

Candidate (d): a blocked (non-ALLOW) policy sets *num_xfrms = -1 while the function returns 0; whether the caller treats -1 as drop is not shown, so no policy-bypass/fail-open impact could be instantiated.
Candidate (e): entry *num_pols == 0 with a non-NULL pols[0] would leak that policy reference; entry state not producible here and a refcount leak is not a security impact.

verdict.summary: gopherToHTML parses attacker-controlled gopher-server data into fixed TEMP_BUF_SIZE stack buffers. The overflow guard (len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE) permits llen to reach TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, and line[llen + 1] = '\0' then writes one byte past the end of LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) — a remotely triggerable off-by-one out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787). Independently, the host field of a gopher menu line is inserted raw into an HTML HREF attribute (snprintf with plain %s, no html_quote/rfc1738 escaping, unlike name and selector), enabling attribute breakout and markup injection into the page rendered to the browsing client (CWE-79).

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write: llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (either unclamped when gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 passes the line-77 check, or after the line-79 clamp plus line-93 accumulation), so index llen+1 == TEMP_BUF_SIZE writes '\0' one byte past LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE). Trigger: a gopher server sends one line of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 bytes ending in '\n'.

This is the only bound on llen, and its operator admits the boundary value: with gopherState->len == 0 and llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 the >= test is false (no clamp), and when it clamps it sets llen = TEMP_BUF_SIZE - len - 1, which after line 93 becomes TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 — exactly the value that makes line[llen + 1] write out of bounds. The clamp needed to be TEMP_BUF_SIZE - len - 2 (or the terminator moved to line[llen]).

evidence.snippet: snprintf(tmpbuf, TEMP_BUF_SIZE, " %s\n", icon_url, host, gtype, escaped_selector, html_quote(name));
evidence.reason: Markup injection: host originates from the attacker-supplied gopher line (line 124, delimited only by TAB and chopped only at TAB/CR/LF, so '"', '<', '>' are all representable) and is substituted raw into the HREF attribute while name is html_quote'd and selector is rfc1738-escaped; a host like h\"> breaks out of the attribute and injects markup into the page rendered to the client.

assumptions: LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) is a stack array of exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes; TEMP_BUF_SIZE >= 2.
gopherState->buf is at least TEMP_BUF_SIZE bytes so the line-85 memcpy with the clamped llen stays in bounds (its declaration is not shown).
gopherState->len starts at 0; not needed for the no-clamp trigger path (len==0, llen==TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1).
limitations: Null dereference at lines 225/228: port = strchr(host, TAB) (line 129) can return NULL when the menu line has only two TABs; the 'if (port)' guard at line 131 covers only the chop block, and '*port ? ...' at line 225 dereferences NULL for a telnet/3270 gopher line ('7name<TAB>sel<TAB>host\n'), crashing the proxy (remote DoS, CWE-476). Crash-only impact, recorded here per discipline 3 rather than driving the verdict.
Integer overflow of gopherState->len + llen (line 77) requires a single call with len near 2^30 (a >1GB inbuf); the caller's buffer sizing is not shown, so this wrap trigger is speculative.
After a parsed non-'.' line, 'line' is not re-memset, so a stale byte can survive at line[llen] from a previous longer line; same-server, same-connection data only — not a cross-boundary disclosure.
snprintf into tmpbuf truncates oversized gopher fields instead of overflowing (mitigation, not a defect).

verdict.summary: In the KS_DEC_MOUSE branch of check_termcode(), (void)getdigits(&nr) scans attacker-supplied terminal input digits without any length bound; the only bound check, 'if (nr >= tp + len)', executes after the scan. A remote terminal peer that fills the typebuf with 'ESC [' followed by digit bytes to the end of the allocation makes getdigits read one or more bytes past the heap buffer (heap out-of-bounds read, crash/DoS); stale attacker-planted digit bytes beyond tb_len extend the scan further.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the digit scan getdigits(&nr) consumes attacker-controlled terminal bytes with no bound on how far nr may advance; the sole length check 'nr >= tp + len' is a sentinel that runs after the first use, so the bytes between tp+len and the first non-digit (including one past the heap allocation) are read out of bounds. Trigger: typebuf filled with ESC [ 111... so the scan runs off the end of the allocation.

evidence.snippet:
tp = typebuf.tb_buf + typebuf.tb_off + offset;
		    len = typebuf.tb_len - offset;	// length of the input
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted data: tp points into typebuf.tb_buf, whose content and length are raw terminal input from the remote peer; nothing in this code NUL-terminates the buffer at tp+len, so an unbounded scan past len is an out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: getdigits advances a pointer over digit bytes with no length parameter and no bound other than the first non-digit byte (characterizable standard parse semantics); its definition is not shown here.

The trigger assumes the terminal advertised DEC mouse support so a termcodes[] entry with name KS_DEC_MOUSE and code "ESC [" is registered, and that vim is in Normal mode or 'ek' is set (line 82 does not skip ESC).

Reading beyond tb_len but within the typebuf allocation reads stale attacker-planted input; the past-allocation read requires the allocation to be digit-filled up to its end, which the attacker controls by sending maximal digit input.
limitations: The KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR loops read tp[j], tp[j+1], tp[j+2] with no 'j < len' bound and get_*_from_buf has no length knowledge, but key_name[0] can only become KS_VER_SCROLLBAR/KS_HOR_SCROLLBAR/KS_MENU when the GUI registered those termcodes (gui.in_use), whose event producers are the local GUI toolkit, not data across a shown trust boundary; recorded as a functional overread risk, not a confirmed remote trigger.
check_termcode_mouse() is called with tp but without len; any overread inside it occurs entirely in a callee not shown, and tp itself is in-domain at the call.

modifiers2keycode's maximum return value and the mb_char2bytes write into string[MAX_KEY_CODE_LEN + 1] are bounded only by an unquoted callee contract; potential overflow of 'string' not instantiated.

'argp = tp + 2' is computed even when len == 1, producing a pointer past the buffer end, but every dereference is gated by quoted 'len >= 3' / 'len >= 2' checks in short-circuit order, so no out-of-bounds read occurs.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled inputs are bounded by verified guards: resource is rejected at both bounds by 'if (resource >= RLIM_NLIMITS) return -EINVAL;' before any array indexing or write; rlim_cur<=rlim_max, the CAP_SYS_RESOURCE and NR_OPEN checks all fail closed with return-before-state-write ordering; copy length is the fixed sizeof(*rlim). The only remaining anomaly (potential secs_to_cputime overflow for huge RLIMIT_CPU values) is self-inflicted on the calling process with no cross-boundary impact.

assumptions: cputime_t width/config (secs_to_cputime semantics) is not shown; treated as a standard kernel conversion, not a security primitive.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled nargs is copied from guest memory and used unvalidated to compute args.rets = &args.args[be32_to_cpu(args.nargs)], indexing past the fixed args.args[] array of the stack-allocated rtas_args struct; the RTAS handler then writes return values through this out-of-bounds pointer, giving a guest VM an out-of-bounds write into the host kernel stack at an attacker-chosen offset.

limitations: If a future/other handler never writes through args->rets, the impact degrades to computing an out-of-bounds pointer without dereference; in the RTAS framework every token handler stores return codes via rets.
kvm_write_guest write-back is safe because args.rets is restored to orig_rets (line 41) before the copy-out; no secondary finding there.
args.nargs values that also make nargs + number-of-return-values exceed 16 are an additional latent overflow even with a naive nargs < 16 check; a complete fix should bound nargs plus the rets count.

verdict.summary: Curve-specific modular reduction (nettle ecc_256_modp). Whether nci_unregister_device/nci_close_device can race with an in-flight firmware-download worker (nfcmrvl_fw_dnld_abort/deinit internals not shown) cannot be judged from the given statements; no concrete race window is exhibited here.

verdict.summary: The allocation size `elem_size * smap->map.max_entries` is computed in u64 without any overflow check; with attacker-chosen u32 map attributes (value_size near 2^32 and max_entries near 2^32) the product wraps past 2^64 to an allocatable ~4 GiB value, the undersized allocation passes the non-NULL check, and pcpu_freelist_populate then writes ~2^32 buckets at ~2^32-byte strides out of bounds of that buffer — kernel out-of-bounds write.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the allocation size expression `elem_size * smap->map.max_entries` (u64 x u32 -> u64) wraps at 2^64. With value_size = 0xFFFFFFFF and max_entries = 4294967266, elem_size = sizeof(bucket)+2^32-1 and the product is 2^64 + 2^32 - 930, wrapping to ~4 GiB, so a far-too-small buffer is allocated; the NULL check on line 9 cannot detect it and pcpu_freelist_populate on line 16 then writes max_entries buckets of elem_size bytes out of bounds.

Taint origin: smap->map.value_size is a u32 map attribute of the full domain [0, 2^32-1] set from user-supplied map-creation data (producer not shown in this code, so the whole width is instantiable); values above 2^32 - sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) make elem_size exceed 2^32, which is the precondition for the wrapping multiplication on line 7.

assumptions: smap->map.value_size and smap->map.max_entries are u32 fields populated from user-supplied bpf_attr at map creation (the producer is outside this snippet, so per the width-domain rule any u32 value is instantiable).
sizeof(struct stack_map_bucket) is small (16-32 bytes); the exact value only shifts the constants in the trigger, not its existence.
pcpu_freelist_populate writes one freelist node per entry at elems + i*elem_size for i in [0, max_entries), per its role in populating the preallocated per-element freelist.
limitations: Impact requires the wrapped allocation size (~4 GiB, the minimum reachable wrapped value) to actually be allocated (kvmalloc/vmalloc) on the target host; on memory-constrained hosts bpf_map_area_alloc returns NULL and the function safely returns -ENOMEM.

The in-tree caller stack_map_alloc (not shown) may impose its own bounds on value_size/max_entries; no such check is quotable from the given code, so it cannot dismiss the candidate, but it would gate real-world reachability.
The wrapped size cannot be made arbitrarily small: the minimum reachable wrapped allocation is approximately 2^32 - sizeof(bucket)^2 bytes, so exploitation needs a multi-GiB-capable host.

In this code the guard is present and verified at both bounds, so that candidate does not survive.
The post-loop 'if (dataLeft > 2)' check at line 69 is a protocol-strictness check, not a memory-safety guard; it runs after the (in-bounds) swaps and only rejects leftover padding.

verdict.summary: The sparse map size is read from the archive as a decimal string, bounded only by TYPE_MAXIMUM(size_t) (the full size_t domain), and used directly as the xcalloc element count for sparse_map. sparse_add_map (not shown) appends entries while sparse_map_avail < sparse_map_size; the loop bound at line 56 equals the allocated count from line 53, so no out-of-bounds write occurs there.

verdict.summary: gst_flxdec_chain parses attacker-supplied FLIC chunk headers; the only size check (line 105, `if (avail < flxfh.size)`) tests adapter availability against the chunk size but never enforces flxfh.size >= FlxFrameChunkSize, so any flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize (e.g. 0) passes and the expression `flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize` at lines 111-112 wraps to ~4G guint32, handing an out-of-domain size to gst_adapter_take (massive OOB read/failed 4GB alloc); if take returns NULL, line 113 dereferences it unchecked, and sizes in [FlxFrameChunkSize, FlxFrameChunkSize+FlxFrameTypeSize) yield an undersized chunk buffer that FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS reads/writes out of bounds. Root cause is an unsigned integer underflow of attacker-controlled flxfh.size.

evidence.reason: Sink: attacker-controlled guint32 flxfh.size is not bounded below against FlxFrameChunkSize, so flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize underflows (e.g. size=0 -> 0xFFFFFFFA) and the wrapped ~4G size is passed into the adapter copy operation; with size just above FlxFrameChunkSize the returned buffer is smaller than FlxFrameTypeSize, causing the out-of-bounds struct access at line 113.

The only guard on flxfh.size: it tests availability (avail) against size but not size against FlxFrameChunkSize; with size=0 and avail>=FlxFrameChunkSize the comparison `avail < 0` is false and the underflow path is reached — the decisive missing lower-bound check.
Origin: flxfh.size is copied verbatim from the attacker-supplied FLIC stream into the chunk header; full guint32 domain is instantiable with no downstream narrowing.

assumptions: FlxHeaderSize, FlxFrameChunkSize and FlxFrameTypeSize are positive constants (flxdec headers define them as sizeof-based/6/4-class values); the underflow trigger only requires FlxFrameChunkSize > 0.

gst_adapter_take either copies nbytes from the adapter (characterizable copy semantics, causing a ~4G out-of-bounds read with an empty adapter) or returns a NULL failure sentinel, which line 113 consumes without any check before first use; under either behavior the wrapped size at lines 111-112 is out-of-domain.
FlxFrameType fields span FlxFrameTypeSize bytes, and FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS at line 113 reads/writes those fields of the take-returned buffer without a length check.
limitations: Secondary candidate (CWE-190): `out = gst_buffer_new_and_alloc (flxdec->size * 4)` at line 124 wraps when width*height >= 2^30 (e.g. width=height=32768, valid guint16 header values), allocating a 0-byte output buffer while flx_colorspace_convert (created with the raw width/height at lines 68-69) writes width*height*4 bytes; the overflowing write occurs inside the unshown callee, so it does not drive the verdict or CWE here.

flx_decode_chunks is handed `chunk + FlxFrameTypeSize` and a chunk count with no remaining-length parameter, so a truncated chunk stream can drive out-of-bounds reads/writes inside the unshown callee; not independently confirmed.

If gst_adapter_take returns NULL for the underflowed size, the locally visible consequence at line 113 is a near-NULL dereference (crash of the same-privilege process); the memory-corruption reading rests on the take/copy semantics assumed above.
framerate denominator computed as `(gint) flxdec->frame_time / 1000` can be 0 (e.g. FLI with speed=0), a potential downstream divide-by-zero in consumers not shown.

verdict.summary: rpa_read_buffer's entry check `if (p > end)` under-admits p == end; the subsequent `len = *p++` then reads one byte past the end of the attacker-supplied message buffer (out-of-bounds read). The correct guard is `p >= end`.

The later check `if (p + len > end)` executes after the dereference and cannot protect this read.

The impact of the confirmed off-by-one read is limited: the byte read at p == end becomes `len`, and since p is then end+1, the `p + len > end` check always rejects, so the value never reaches memcpy or the return path; worst realistic outcomes are a crash at an unmapped boundary or silent UB.
The caller that sets *data == end is not shown; reachability rests on the parameter's full pointer domain and on line 17 (`*data += 1 + len`) being able to land exactly on end.

verdict.summary: No memory-corruption, injection, bypass, or resource-consumption defect is instantiated in this code. All allocation returns (Item_temptable_rowid, create_tmp_table) are NULL-checked before use, the func_count subtraction cannot underflow because temp_fields provably contains at least one element (the do-while body always executes once), and the remaining unchecked uses (fields->head() deref, fix_fields return, cnt/tablenr indexing) are bounded either by debug-only asserts or by producer contracts established in resolver code not shown, yielding at worst a same-privilege NULL-dereference crash.

assumptions: List::head() on an empty list returns NULL and List::elements is a count, per standard MariaDB container semantics.
Item_temptable_rowid::fix_fields returns bool and sets the THD error state on failure; downstream consumers of an unfixed item are outside this function.
tbl->alias.c_ptr() returns a NUL-terminated string per MariaDB String semantics, making the strlen call safe.
limitations: The only guard for the ((Item_field *) fields->head())->field->table deref is DBUG_ASSERT(fields->elements), which is compiled out in release builds; an empty SET list is syntactically impossible via the SQL parser (unquoted contract), and the worst case would be a same-privilege NULL-dereference crash (CWE-476), not memory corruption.

The return value of item->fix_fields(thd, 0) is not checked and the item is pushed to temp_fields regardless; any misuse of an unfixed item occurs inside create_tmp_table/calc_group_buffer, whose handling of unfixed items is not shown, so no concrete impact could be simulated.

Indexing of tmp_table_param+cnt, fields_for_table[cnt], tmp_tables[cnt] and join->map2table[...tablenr] has no local bounds check; the invariants bounding cnt (table_ref->shared) and tablenr are established in the update-planning and resolver code, which is not included, so an out-of-range trigger could not be instantiated from this code alone.

List_iterator_fast is reused across the accumulated unupdated_check_opt_tables list on each outer iteration, which re-emits rowid items for previously collected tables; this is at most a functional/efficiency concern since tmp_param->field_count is recomputed from the final list size after appends.

verdict.summary: In qtm_decompress, the match-copy branch taken when match_offset > window_posn copies match_length bytes into window[window_posn] without any clamp of the destination against qtm->window_size, unlike the sibling else-branch which clamps i to (qtm->window_size - window_posn). An attacker-crafted compressed stream can position window_posn near the window end and select a large match_length, writing attacker-decompressed data past the end of the heap-allocated window buffer (heap out-of-bounds write).

evidence.reason: Sink: unbounded destination copy in the wrap branch. rundest = &window[window_posn] (L92) and i = match_length (L93) are attacker-derived; no statement on this path bounds window_posn + match_length to qtm->window_size. Trigger: window_size=32768, window_posn=32767, match_length=50, match_offset=32768 → j=1 passes the L98 source check, then L108 writes window[32768..32816], 49 bytes past the heap buffer. The twin clamp at L112-113 exists only in the else branch.

Taint origin: match_length is decoded directly from the attacker-supplied compressed bitstream (QTM_GET_SYMBOL/QTM_READ_BITS) with no range validation before it becomes the copy length at L93 and drives the out-of-bounds write at L105/L108.

assumptions: QTM_GET_SYMBOL/QTM_READ_BITS macros deliver values from the compressed input as in libmspack-style Quantum decoders (tables indexed by sym with bounded extra_bits); this is consistent with the surrounding table-driven code.
qtm->window is a heap buffer of exactly qtm->window_size bytes as allocated at stream-init time (internal-trusted state).
limitations: The else-branch copy (L110-115) was verified safe: its clamp 'if(i > (int) (qtm->window_size - window_posn)) i = qtm->window_size - window_posn;' bounds both write extent and read source.

The source-side reads in the wrap branch are bounded by the quoted L98 check (j <= window_size keeps runsrc = &window[qtm->window_size - j] in-buffer) and by the j<i two-run structure; only the destination is unbounded.

Potential input-exhaustion behavior of the QTM_READ_BITS macro and the 'do { QTM_READ_BITS(i, 8); } while (i != 0xFF);' re-alignment loop depends on macro definitions not shown; any defect there would be speculative.
The 'overshot frame alignment' check and the window-wrap reset execute only after the overflowing copy has already occurred, so they cannot mitigate the primary finding.

verdict.summary: gst_flxdec_chain reads a FLX_FRAME_TYPE chunk header with attacker-controlled guint flxfh.size. The only check, `if (avail < flxfh.size)`, bounds adapter availability, not flxfh.size itself, so any flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize passes; `flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize` underflows to ~4GB, gst_adapter_take returns NULL, and FLX_FRAME_TYPE_FIX_ENDIANNESS / the `chunks` dereference operate on NULL (crash/DoS). Values just above FlxFrameChunkSize make take return a buffer smaller than FlxFrameTypeSize, causing a heap out-of-bounds read at the `((FlxFrameType *) chunk)->chunks` use. Trigger fully instantiated from untrusted file data; no lower-bound or NULL check exists anywhere on the path.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unsigned integer underflow. flxfh.size is a guint read verbatim from the attacker-supplied FLX stream (memcpy at line 98); with flxfh.size = 0 (representable in the declared width), flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize = 0xFFFFFFFA, gst_adapter_take returns NULL (nbytes > available), and line 113/114 dereference the NULL chunk without any sentinel test — instant crash of the decoding process via a malformed file. With flxfh.size = FlxFrameChunkSize + 2, take(2) returns a 2-byte buffer and the FlxFrameType field reads at 113-114 go past the allocation (heap out-of-bounds read). No lower bound on flxfh.size and no NULL/size check on chunk exists on any path.

The only guard on flxfh.size before the underflowing subtraction. It bounds the wrong variable and unit: it checks adapter availability against flxfh.size, not flxfh.size against FlxFrameChunkSize. Simulated with flxfh.size = 0 and avail = 1024: 1024 < 0 is false, so the guard passes the attack value through; it never rejects any flxfh.size below FlxFrameChunkSize, allowing the underflow at line 112. The missing guard is `if (flxfh.size < FlxFrameChunkSize) goto need_more_data;` (or a NULL/bounds check on chunk).

assumptions: flxfh.size is a guint (32-bit) field per FLX_FRAME_CHUNK_FIX_ENDIANNESS semantics; gst_adapter_take returns NULL when the requested nbytes exceed available data (standard GstAdapter semantics); FlxFrameChunkSize is a small constant (6), making flxfh.size - FlxFrameChunkSize wrap for any size < FlxFrameChunkSize.
limitations: The wrong_type error path (line 171) executes `gst_object_unref (flxdec)` on the borrowed `parent` object — an unbalanced unref (potential refcount underflow/UAF, CWE-416). The trigger (flxh->type not one of the three magics) is fully quotable, but whether the refcount reaches zero depends on external references not shown in this code, so the UAF consequence is not instantiated here.

flx_decode_chunks (lines 127-129) is passed attacker-controlled `chunks` count and a `chunk + FlxFrameTypeSize` pointer that may point past a buffer smaller than the chunk data implies; an out-of-bounds read/write inside that callee is plausible but the callee is not shown, so it was not counted as a primary defect.

The NULL-deref variant (flxfh.size = 0) crashes a same-privilege process (DoS); the confirmed out-of-bounds read at lines 113-114 for small positive take-sizes is the memory-safety impact retained in the verdict.

verdict.summary: SafeToRemoveIdentity aborts the whole process via CHECK when an Identity node's first input names a node absent from the node map. evidence.reason: Root cause: GetNode() is a lookup over the attacker-supplied GraphDef and returns nullptr when node.input(0) names a node not present in the graph (always in-domain for a missed lookup). The result is guarded only by a CHECK, which aborts the process instead of returning false. Trigger: untrusted model containing an Identity node with input(0)="missing_node"; simulation reaches line 20 with input==nullptr and aborts — denial of service of the process optimizing the untrusted graph. No early-return sentinel test exists anywhere on any path.
Origin of the tainted value: the attacker-controlled node name (node.input(0), full proto-domain string) is passed into the map lookup whose nullptr miss reaches the aborting CHECK.

assumptions: node_map_ is built from the same GraphDef being optimized, so node.input(0) can name any string, including a node absent from the graph or a control-dependency reference, making the nullptr return of GetNode reachable from untrusted model content.
The GraphDef being optimized originates across a trust boundary (untrusted model file), the standard Grappler threat model under which this CHECK-failure was fixed upstream.
limitations: Optimizer logic candidates (the node.input_size() > 1 && (IsRetval/IsMerge) condition and the IsSwitch control-dependency scan) could at worst cause incorrect node removal and graph-semantic changes; the consumer performing the removal is not shown, so no security impact is instantiated here.

IsRetval(*consumer) / consumer->input() dereference consumer pointers from node_map_->GetOutputs() without a NULL test; whether GetOutputs can yield NULL elements is not characterizable from the given code (NodeMap implementation not shown), so this stays speculative.
Impact is limited to denial of service via process abort; no memory corruption, disclosure, or bypass primitive was found in this function.

verdict.summary: pps_id is read as an unsigned Exp-Golomb value into a signed s32 and only upper-bound checked (`pps_id > 255`); a value >= 0x80000000 wraps to a negative s32 that passes the check and is used directly as an array index (`&avc->pps[pps_id]`) followed by a write (`si->pps->id = pps_id`), giving an out-of-bounds write before the pps array with attacker-chosen offset.

assumptions: gf_bs_read_ue_log reads an unsigned Exp-Golomb code whose value range is up to 2^32-1 (standard semantics); the bitstream `bs` carries attacker-supplied media data.
