limitations: CHECK(!conn.oneRttWriteCipher.get()) and CHECK(conn.oneRttWriteCipher) abort the process if the handshake layer ever re-derives or withholds a 1-RTT cipher inconsistently; no statement in this code can produce that state, so the crash is a speculative robustness issue (CWE-754), not a confirmed defect.

Validation of the client transport parameter CONTENT occurs inside processClientInitialParams, which is not shown; this function only verifies presence. If the callee misvalidates, that defect is outside this code.

Clearing conn.writableBytesLimit depends on the fizz-layer contract that a 1-RTT read cipher is exported only after CFIN is verified; a violating handshake layer would enable an amplification bypass, but no such path is shown here.

verdict.summary: DecodePngV2 validates all attacker-supplied dimensions before any allocation or copy: width/height are round-trip-checked against truncation (width != (int64_t)decode.width), bounded to [1, 2^27), and their product is bounded below 2^29, with the check executed before every sink. Given the PNG color model (channels <= 4, enforced by the not-shown CommonInitDecode/libpng), all downstream arithmetic fits: the stride decode.channels * width * sizeof(uint16) <= 2^30, and the float-path buffer height*width*channels <= 4*(2^29-1) = 2^31-4 fits int exactly as the code comments claim; allocation, stride, and copy sizes are exactly matched. No candidate's trigger and impact chain is fully instantiated in the quoted code.

assumptions: png::CommonInitDecode (not shown) sets decode.width/decode.height from the PNG IHDR and only succeeds on well-formed PNGs, and decode.channels is in [1,4] per the PNG color model; this bound is not quotable in the given listing.
new uint16[n] throws std::bad_alloc on failure rather than returning NULL; OP_REQUIRES_OK propagates allocate_output failure before output is used.
limitations: If the not-shown decoder could emit decode.channels >= 8, the int products decode.channels * width and height * width * decode.channels (DT_FLOAT branch) would overflow (e.g. channels=32, width=2^27-1 gives stride -32 and a negative allocation length -> bad_alloc abort; a heap overflow would additionally depend on unshown CommonFinishDecode semantics). The channels bound could not be quoted, so this stays speculative rather than primary.

If a kernel registered op_type_ == "DecodeGif" with data_type_ == DT_FLOAT, output->tensor<float,3>() would CHECK-fail on the 4-D tensor allocated for DecodeGif (crash only); op_type_ and data_type_ are registration attributes, not attacker-controlled inputs, and the combination is not instantiable by a PNG submitter.

std::bad_alloc from the float-path new[] is not caught in this function (robustness, same-privilege crash); a guard-bounded ~4GB allocation is the documented size policy, not attacker-scalable beyond the explicit limit.

verdict.summary: parse_query advances p by the callee-computed name_part_len without any local containment check; the only bound, `if (p + 4 > max)`, tests the upper direction only, so a negative or wrap-producing name_part_len yields p < start and the subsequent pj_memcpy calls read before the packet buffer (out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: p is derived from the unvalidated callee return name_part_len (full int domain, no local clamp) and only upper-bounded by `p + 4 > max`; a negative name_part_len makes p < start, the check passes, and pj_memcpy(&q->type, p, 2) reads out of bounds before the packet.

Origin of the tainted offset name_part_len; consumed at line 23 with no range check (and name_len is likewise used unvalidated in pj_pool_alloc(pool, name_len+4), an overflow candidate) — the absent local validation is the defect.

assumptions: get_name_len/get_name are not shown; their outputs name_part_len and name_len are treated per the width-domain rule as full-domain int values instantiable by attacker-crafted DNS packets.
max is the one-past-the-end pointer of the packet buffer, so reads at addresses >= max or < pkt/start are out of bounds.
limitations: The negative-name_part_len trigger depends on the unshown get_name_len returning a negative length with PJ_SUCCESS; no quoted statement in this code excludes it, but reachability was not provable from this snippet.

name_len+4 signed overflow in pj_pool_alloc (line 13) is a second candidate (CWE-190) with the same root cause — no local range check on callee-computed length — but its trigger also depends on the unshown callee; it was not counted as an independent primary.
If get_name_len is in fact guaranteed to return a non-negative, in-range length on success, both candidates collapse to non-issues; that contract is not quotable here.

verdict.summary: Off-by-one out-of-bounds stack write in gopherToHTML: the overflow guard `gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE` admits a total merged line length of TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1, but the terminator is written at `line[llen + 1]`, so a gopher-server line of exactly the residual-limit length makes the code write a NUL byte one past the end of the TEMP_BUF_SIZE `line` buffer.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one out-of-bounds write: after the merge at lines 92-95 (`llen += gopherState->len`), llen can equal TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 — the exact value the guard at line 77 permits since it only rejects `gopherState->len + llen >= TEMP_BUF_SIZE` — so this statement writes line[TEMP_BUF_SIZE], one byte past the LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE) stack buffer. Trigger: a first chunk with no newline leaving gopherState->len = T-2, then a 2-byte line 'X\n' (or a single T-1-byte line), fully attacker-controllable by the gopher server.

Insufficient guard: this is the only statement bounding the copy length, but it permits gopherState->len + llen == TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1 (operator >= fires one unit too late for a sink that writes index llen+1), and the clamp at line 79 also produces exactly TEMP_BUF_SIZE-1; no statement anywhere bounds llen+1 < TEMP_BUF_SIZE. This is the missing guard whose absence is the defect.

assumptions: TEMP_BUF_SIZE is the fixed size of both the `line` LOCAL_ARRAY and gopherState->buf, per `LOCAL_ARRAY(char, line, TEMP_BUF_SIZE)` and the shared check at line 77.
gopherState->len persists across gopherToHTML invocations for the same transaction, per the 'something left from last tx' comment and the line 86-87 accumulation.
The gopher server is an untrusted network peer: inbuf/len contents and chunk boundaries are attacker-chosen (discipline 4).
limitations: atoi(s_code)/atoi(s_recno) in the CSO branch consume strtok returns without NULL checks (a line of just '-\n' yields NULL); worst case is a same-privilege crash of the proxy process with no corruption, so it is a robustness issue, not the verdict.

`host` is interpolated unescaped into href attributes (e.g. "http://%s/"), allowing the gopher server to inject markup into the rendered HTML page; this is a secondary output-construction weakness and does not drive the single CWE under STEP 7's one-defect rule.

The byte at line[llen] is never explicitly NUL-terminated (only line[llen+1] is set), so a stale byte can follow the line content; treated as improper termination with no demonstrated security impact here.
snprintf calls are size-bounded by TEMP_BUF_SIZE, so their worst case is truncation, not overflow.

verdict.summary: Both attacker-controlled scalars (epsilon float, num_streams int64) are validated at their sinks: `epsilon > 0` rejects NaN, zero, -0.0 and negatives; `num_streams >= 0` rejects negatives. The admitted values are domain-valid and flow only as constructor arguments to an unshown callee, with no memory, copy, or indexing primitive in this code. Status sentinels from context->input and CreateResource are checked (OP_REQUIRES_OK, ALREADY_EXISTS handling re-raises other errors), so no fail-open path exists.

assumptions: context->input and CreateResource follow standard TF semantics: OP_REQUIRES_OK guarantees the output tensor pointer is non-NULL on OK status, and CreateResource unrefs the newly created resource on ALREADY_EXISTS as the comment states.
max_elements_ is an op attribute treated as internal-trusted; the constructor of QuantileStreamResource is not shown.
limitations: Speculative CWE-400/resource-exhaustion: num_streams = INT64_MAX passes `num_streams >= 0` and reaches `new QuantileStreamResource(epsilon, max_elements_, num_streams)`; if the unshown constructor allocates per-stream state or multiplies num_streams, this is attacker-scalable consumption — but that impact occurs entirely inside the not-shown callee and is not instantiable from this code.
Speculative numeric defect: epsilon = +inf or a tiny denormal passes `epsilon > 0`; any misbehavior of the quantile algorithm with such values occurs in the unshown constructor/resource.

Non-scalar or wrong-dtype inputs for epsilon or num_streams cause scalar<T>() to CHECK-fail, aborting the same-privilege TF process — a robustness/DoS issue, not a security impact per the same-privilege crash rule.

There is no upper-bound (e.g. `num_streams < K`) or finiteness check (`std::isfinite(epsilon)`) in this code; if the constructor turns out to be unsafe with extreme values, the missing clamp would be the defect, but no such unsafe use is visible here.

verdict.summary: The kernel reads an attacker-controlled int64 tensor scalar `num_streams` and passes it unvalidated as a count/size argument to `new QuantileStreamResource(epsilon, max_elements_, num_streams)`. Unlike `epsilon`, which is range-checked (`epsilon > 0`), `num_streams` has no check anywhere in the code, so any representable int64 value (0, negative, up to 2^63-1) reaches the resource constructor, enabling out-of-domain counts and attacker-scalable allocation/resource consumption.

evidence.reason: Root cause: `num_streams` is an attacker-supplied int64 tensor scalar with no validation of any kind (mention sweep of the variable yields only the fetch at line 14, the scalar read at line 15, and the use at line 18; no range/positivity/upper-bound check exists, in contrast to the epsilon check at lines 9-11). Trigger: an attacker supplies a num_streams tensor with value -1, 0, or 2^62, which is fully in-domain for int64 and passes both OP_REQUIRES_OK calls, then reaches `new QuantileStreamResource(..., num_streams)` as a raw size/count argument, giving out-of-domain counts and attacker-scalable resource consumption.

assumptions: The op's input tensors (kEpsilonName, kNumStreamsName) are supplied across a trust boundary by the graph/session caller, per the TensorFlow op-kernel execution model.

QuantileStreamResource uses num_streams to size or iterate per-stream state; the constructor body is not shown, so the precise downstream memory primitive is characterized rather than quoted — hence the root-cause CWE-20 rather than a memory primitive.
limitations: The internal use of num_streams inside QuantileStreamResource is not shown; the concrete downstream effect (CHECK-failure crash, wrap in vector sizing, or OOM) could not be simulated line-by-line, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.

A tiny positive epsilon (e.g. a denormal) passes the `epsilon > 0` guard and per the code comment degrades performance; this is treated as a functional/performance concern, not a security defect, since no security sink for epsilon is shown.
`max_elements_` is a constructor-registered member not set in this code; its domain could not be assessed and it was not treated as a per-call attacker input.

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line converts a parsed file line into the fixed 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv with an output index j that is never bounded: in the non-UTF8 (win-CP) path each input byte emits two output bytes, so a line of >1024 high-bit non-UTF8 bytes drives j past 2048, causing an attacker-controlled out-of-bounds stack write (and a subsequent OOB via strcpy of the overlong szLineConv).

evidence.reason: Unbounded out-of-bounds write: j is incremented up to twice per input byte (win-CP branch lines 18-19 fall through to this write) with no comparison of j against sizeof(szLineConv)=2048 anywhere in the function; the only loop bound 'i<len' (line 14) caps the input index, not the output index. Trigger: unicode_type=0, lineSize>=2048, file line of 1500 0xC1 bytes → j reaches 2048 at i=1024 and continues to 3000, writing attacker-influenced bytes past szLineConv[2048] on the stack.

Taint origin: attacker-controlled content of the parsed text file (up to lineSize-1 bytes) is loaded into szLine and drives len=strlen(szLine) (line 13) and the conversion loop that overflows the fixed 2048-byte stack buffer szLineConv (line 5).

assumptions: gf_fgets behaves like fgets: reads at most lineSize-1 bytes, NUL-terminates, stops at newline; the file referenced by txt_in is attacker-controlled content (parsed subtitle/text file).
The (szLine, lineSize) pair is the standard buffer/size API contract; lineSize is treated as the actual buffer size (also used by memset at line 8).
limitations: Candidate (secondary, not primary): 'i = (u32) gf_utf8_wcstombs(szLineConv, 2048, &sptr); szLineConv[i] = 0;' consumes the callee return without a sentinel check; a (size_t)-1 error return becomes i=0xFFFFFFFF (wild write / crash) and a return of exactly 2048 gives a 1-byte OOB NUL write at szLineConv[2048]. Not made primary because the callee's exact return semantics for these cases are not shown.
Minor OOB read: in the UTF-16 byte-swap while(1) loop, szLine[i+1] can be read one byte past the buffer when gf_fgets fills szLine to lineSize-1 with an odd trailing index.

memset(szLine,0,lineSize) and strcpy(szLine,szLineConv) trust the caller-supplied lineSize as the true buffer size; a caller passing a mismatched size would overflow szLine independently of the szLineConv defect (unverifiable caller contract).

verdict.summary: gf_text_get_utf8_line converts an attacker-supplied line (read via gf_fgets, length up to lineSize-1) into the fixed 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv, advancing the output index j twice per non-UTF8 high-bit input byte with no bound on j against sizeof(szLineConv). A line of >512 crafted bytes overflows the stack buffer with attacker-influenced data (out-of-bounds write).

evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional write into the 1024-byte stack buffer szLineConv at index j, with no check that j < 1024 anywhere in the function; j grows by 2 per crafted input byte, so a 513-byte line of 0xA0 0x41 pairs makes j exceed 1023 and writes attacker bytes past the buffer.

First out-of-bounds write for the attack value: this branch emits 2 output bytes per input byte (here plus the fall-through write at line 53), doubling the output length relative to len = strlen(szLine) which is bounded only by the caller-supplied lineSize, not by the 1024-byte output buffer.
Origin of taint: attacker-controlled text-file content and line length (up to lineSize-1 bytes) enter szLine here, supplying both the bytes and the length that drive j past 1024.

assumptions: unicode_type==0 (non-UTF8 single-byte path) is reachable, i.e. callers pass it for non-UTF8 subtitle/text files; this is the function's documented purpose.
gf_fgets behaves like fgets: NUL-terminates and reads at most lineSize-1 bytes, so len <= lineSize-1 and szLine[i+1] at i=len-1 reads the terminator in bounds.
limitations: Line 79 'szLineConv[i] = 0' consumes gf_utf8_wcstombs's return without a sentinel check; if it can return 1024 (off-by-one write at index 1024) or a negative error cast to u32 (wild write), that is a second OOB write, but the callee is not shown so its return domain is unverified.

Line 70 'if (!szLine[i] && !szLine[i+1]) break;' can read szLine[lineSize] (one past the memset-zeroed region) if a UTF-16 line fills the whole buffer with no double-NUL; depends on unshown gf_fgets UTF-16 termination behavior.
memset at line 8 trusts that the caller's lineSize matches the actual szLine buffer size; an inconsistent pair corrupts memory, but that contract is outside this code.

strcpy at lines 57/80 assumes szLineConv is NUL-terminated; if the conversion fills all 1024 bytes without a terminator the strcpy reads out of bounds — same missing-bound root cause as the primary finding.

verdict.summary: In the 352 (RPL_WHOREPLY) handler, arg_start may be set to 9 while argc is exactly 9 (when argv[8] is "*"), and argv[9] is then dereferenced without any argc > arg_start bound check, reading the NULL terminator slot of the split array and crashing the client. A malicious IRC server (or MITM) can trigger this remote denial of service with a single crafted 352 message.

evidence.reason: arg_start is set to 9 based solely on attacker-controlled argv[8] content, with no check that argc > 9; line 21 then dereferences argv[9], which is the NULL terminator of the split argv array when argc == 9 (reachable since line 18 only requires argc > 8). The needed bound `(argc > arg_start)` is used at line 24 but only after the first use, so it does not protect this sink. Trigger: server sends a 352 numeric with exactly 9 tokens whose 8th token is "*" → argv[9] == NULL → NULL pointer dereference and client crash (remote DoS).

assumptions: argv is produced by the IRC message splitter and, per standard split semantics, has exactly argc string entries plus a NULL terminator at argv[argc]; if this assumption does not hold, the same access becomes an out-of-bounds read at index argc, so the defect stands either way.
argc >= 9 is enforced by IRC_PROTOCOL_MIN_ARGS(5) plus the quoted `if (argc < 8) return WEECHAT_RC_OK;` and `if (argc > 8)`.
limitations: length = strlen(argv[4]) + strlen(argv[5]) + 2 (line 42) could overflow int only for strings totaling over ~2GB in one IRC message; no quoted bound makes that trigger instantiable here, and malloc/snprintf handling remains size-consistent, so it is not promoted.

The `+ 1` on argv[arg_start+1] (line 30) and argv[arg_start] (line 24) assumes a leading ':' token; a non-':' token merely drops one character of displayed hopcount (cosmetic, no memory-safety effect).

verdict.summary: FractionalMaxPool Compute never validates that pooling_ratio_[0] (and pooling_ratio_[3]) equals 1; the only guard (input_size[i] >= pooling_ratio_[i]) permits any ratio <= input dim, so with pooling_ratio_[0]=2 the output tensor is allocated with half the batch columns while the pooling loop iterates b over input_size[0] batches, driving out_offset beyond out_mat's column count and writing max-pooled attacker-controlled values past the end of the heap-allocated output tensor (out-of-bounds write).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: out_mat has output_size[2]*output_size[1]*output_size[0] columns (line 68), but out_offset=(b*output_size[1]+hs)*output_size[2]+ws with b up to input_size[0]-1 reaches up to input_size[0]*output_size[1]*output_size[2]-1. With pooling_ratio_[0]=2.0 and input shape [4,16,16,3]: out_mat cols=128, b=2,hs=7,ws=7 gives out_offset=191 -> heap OOB write of attacker-influenced pooled values.

Origin of the mismatch: the batch loop is bounded by the INPUT batch count while the output buffer is sized from output_size[0] = floor(input_size[0]/pooling_ratio_[0]); whenever pooling_ratio_[0] > 1 the loop overruns the output allocation. No statement ties b to output_size[0].

The only validation of pooling_ratio_ in this code: it merely lower-bounds the ratio by the input dim size and never enforces pooling_ratio_[0]==1 / pooling_ratio_[3]==1 (nor ratio>=1). For the attack value pooling_ratio_[0]=2.0 with input_size[0]=4 the check passes (4>=2), so it does not block the trigger; DCHECK_GT(output_size[i],0) at line 31 is debug-only and compiles out in release.

assumptions: height_cum_seq/width_cum_seq have output_size[1]+1 / output_size[2]+1 elements per the standard GeneratePoolingSequence contract, so hs and ws stay within output height/width; this only underpins the safe twin, not the primary finding.
Eigen::Map::col(k) is raw pointer arithmetic on the underlying buffer with no release-mode bounds check (standard Eigen semantics).
limitations: Secondary effects of the same missing check: if pooling_ratio_[3] != 1, in_mat (rows=input_size[3]) and out_mat (rows=output_size[3]) have mismatched row counts in the cwiseMax expression, a potential OOB read; folded into the same root cause.

pooling_ratio_[i] <= 0 or in (0,1) makes output_size[i] negative or larger than input, with the impact unfolding inside GeneratePoolingSequence, which is not shown; also height_cum_seq.size()-1 (size_t) would wrap if the sequence were empty — these paths are speculative because callee semantics are not quotable here.
Possible constructor/shape-function validation of pooling_ratio_ in core/ops/nn_ops.cc is not part of the given code and therefore cannot serve as a guard (judged as last line of defense).
int64 overflow of out_offset/in_offset requires tensor sizes that cannot be allocated; dismissed.

verdict.summary: No direct security vulnerability is instantiated in this code. The only attacker-reachable pointer dereference (local->local = 1) is protected by a quoted error arm (find_site_by_name failure returns -EINVAL before the deref), and the only string construction uses bounds-checked snprintf with size-1, preventing overflow and guaranteeing termination. Remaining concerns (ignored find_myself return possibly leaving local NULL, unchecked booth_conf->name before snprintf, lockfile path truncation, disabled libgcrypt secure memory) are speculative or same-privilege robustness issues with no quotable impact chain in this code.

assumptions: cl, local, and booth_conf are globals populated by read_config and command-line parsing whose implementations are not shown; their values were judged at the use sites rather than trusting unquoted producer contracts.
DAEMON/CLIENT/GEOSTORE are internal selection constants; type is not treated as attacker data since it only selects branches and callee arguments, never sizes or indices.
limitations: find_myself's return value is explicitly ignored (comment: 'Set "local" pointer, ignoring errors.'), so local may remain NULL; any dereference would occur in unshown code (check_config or later), and the impact would be a same-privilege daemon crash, not a security impact per discipline 3.
booth_conf->name is not NULL-checked before the snprintf on line 45; a NULL name from a read_config edge case would crash this root-config-owning process (robustness only).
A long configuration name truncates the derived PID file path via the bounded snprintf (functional effect: wrong/short lockfile name), not an overflow.

gcry_control(GCRYCTL_DISABLE_SECMEM, 0) disables libgcrypt secure memory for auth key handling — a hardening weakness in key storage hygiene, but no attacker-controllable trigger or impact class is quotable here.

verdict.summary: The ELF parser consumes attacker-controlled header offsets (e_shoff, e_shstrndx, shnum, sh_offset, d_un.d_val) with no bounds validation against the mapped file size. The only containment check in the code, validated_offset(name, elf_map, elf_map + st.st_size), is applied solely to section-name pointers inside the first section loop; it never guards the section/program header table indexing, the segment-mapping and .dynstr/.dynamic scan name pointers, the possibly-uninitialized dynamic/dynstr indices, or the DT_NEEDED string offset. A crafted ELF therefore produces out-of-bounds reads (shstrtab = shdr[ehdr->e_shstrndx]; shdr[dynamic]; snprintf reading elf_map + shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + d_un.d_val) far past the end of the mmap.

evidence.reason: Root cause and instantiated trigger: e_shoff and e_shstrndx come straight from the attacker-supplied ELF header (full uint domain) and are never compared against st.st_size; with a 100-byte file and e_shoff=0xFFFFFF00, e_shstrndx=1, the read shdr[ehdr->e_shstrndx] dereferences roughly 4GB past the mapping — out-of-bounds read; no validated_offset or range check precedes this use.

dynamic is declared uninitialized (line 335) and assigned only if a section literally named ".dynamic" exists; when it does not, shdr[dynamic] indexes the section table with a garbage stack value, and even when found, sh_offset is an unvalidated uint32 attacker offset — both yield out-of-bounds reads with no guard on this path.

evidence.snippet:
name = elf_map + shdr[dynstr].sh_offset + dyn[i].d_un.d_val;
                    snprintf(value, 50, "Shared library: [%s]", name);
evidence.reason: d_un.d_val is fully attacker-controlled (any representable uint); the computed name pointer is never passed through validated_offset on this path, so snprintf's %s reads an unbounded, out-of-map string when d_val points past the file (e.g. 0xFFFF0000).

assumptions: validated_offset(ptr, base, end) is assumed (not shown) to test pointer containment in [base, end); even granting this, it is quoted only at lines 184-187 and never guards the sinks at 176-178, 323, 338, 349, or 366.
flag2str/flag2str_sh are assumed to write at most 4 bytes into char flag[4]; their bodies are not shown.
limitations: The second machine-name switch tests ehdr->e_type instead of e_machine (copy-paste bug) — an incorrect-display/cosmetic issue, not a security defect.
strcpy(&name[15-6], "[...]") writes into the MAP_PRIVATE copy at offset 9 of a validated >15-byte string — in-bounds of the string, not a write primitive.
No out-of-bounds WRITE primitive was instantiated: the only writes into elf_map occur after the single validated_offset guard or inside a string longer than the 6 bytes copied.

CWE-457 (uninitialized dynstr/dynamic) is folded into the CWE-125 intake-pattern defect rather than emitted as a second CWE; the index garbage and the unchecked offsets produce the same out-of-bounds-read sink.
file is opened with the attacker-supplied path read-only (O_RDONLY); no path-traversal or write impact via the path itself.

verdict.summary: The XCLASS property parameter cc[1], derived from attacker-supplied compiled pattern bytecode, is used directly as an index into fixed-size static Unicode tables (ucp_typerange, ucd_caseless_sets, ucd_boolprop_sets, ucd_script_sets) without any bounds, mask, or range validation, enabling out-of-bounds reads at attacker-scaled offsets and, in the PT_CLIST scan loop, propagation of out-of-bounds-read values into the min/max bounds passed to read_char.

evidence.reason: cc[1] is a raw byte from parsed pattern bytecode consumed with no validation anywhere in the function; the mention sweep shows the only switch default (SLJIT_UNREACHABLE) guards the property *type* (*cc), never the parameter cc[1], so any representable value (e.g. 0xFFFF → index 131070) indexes ucp_typerange out of bounds — an attacker-controlled-offset OOB read at this sink.

Taint origin: same unvalidated property parameter cc[1] is added to the ucd_caseless_sets base pointer during the scan pass; the following while (*other_cases != NOTACHAR) loop then dereferences at the attacker-scaled offset and feeds the read values into min/max, which later parameterize read_char — OOB read with compile-time state propagation.

assumptions: The cc bytecode buffer is produced by the pattern compiler from an untrusted regex pattern; per the width-domain rule the full representable domain of PCRE2_UCHAR values in cc[1] is instantiable.

SUPPORT_UNICODE is enabled (the property-parameter sinks are inside that guard); the codegen while-loops are consumed by the JIT as shown, so table misindexing is a compile-time read, not only a JIT-time read.
limitations: If the upstream pattern compiler (not shown) is treated as a trusted producer that provably only emits valid property parameters in range, the OOB reads are unreachable in practice; per the analysis rules this unquoted contract cannot serve as a guard at this intake point.
SLJIT_ASSERT statements are compiled out in release builds and enforce nothing on cc[1] even in debug builds (they assert other invariants).
SLJIT MEM1-generated runtime dereferences (e.g. ucd_stage2 lookups) are masked (UCD_BLOCK_MASK) and were verified as bounded.

verdict.summary: The only memory sink in this code, ctx->set_output(output_port, shape), is protected by a quoted, verified guard: 'if (output_port < 0 || output_port >= ctx->num_outputs())' rejects output_port < 0 and output_port >= num_outputs at both bounds with the correct operators, and precedes the sink in execution order; the ctx NULL check at line 5 is fail-closed and precedes every ctx deref. The pre-validation call GetUnknownOutputShape(node, output_port) at line 3 uses output_port before the range check, but the callee body is not shown and its behavior with an out-of-range port is not characterizable, so no impact chain is instantiated in this code.

assumptions: output_port and node are attacker-influenced (e.g., derived from a parsed GraphDef), per the width-domain rule: full int domain for output_port, including negative and one-past-limit values.

GetContext and InferenceContext::set_output/num_outputs follow standard TensorFlow semantics: num_outputs() returns the context's output count and set_output(idx, ...) indexes the output array, requiring 0 <= idx < num_outputs().
limitations: GetUnknownOutputShape(node, output_port) is called at line 3 before both the ctx NULL check (line 5) and the output_port range check (line 8). If that not-shown callee indexes or dereferences using output_port, or fetches and dereferences the context when it is NULL, this would be a defect at this call site; the callee's body is not given, so this candidate remains unproven and does not decide the verdict.

The ShapeHandle returned by the unseen GetUnknownOutputShape is passed to ctx->set_output without validation; if that helper builds the handle from a different InferenceContext, cross-context handle confusion could occur — not instantiable from the given code.

verdict.summary: mrb_remove_method contains no reachable security sink: the only pointer consumed from a parameter (c) is dereferenced without a NULL test, but the sole impact is a same-privilege crash unquotable as a security effect; the table pointer h is correctly guarded by 'if (h && mt_del(...))' before its only use, the deletion result is checked, and the method cache is invalidated exactly on the success path.

assumptions: mrb_sym mid is an interned symbol ID whose full uint32 domain is valid as a table key for mt_del and as a format argument for mrb_name_error's internal '%n'/'%C' specifiers (mruby-internal formatting, not C printf).
The literal format string in mrb_name_error is not attacker-controlled.
limitations: If a caller ever passed c == NULL, 'h = c->mt' (and the MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN expansion) would dereference NULL and crash the interpreter; this is a robustness/same-privilege crash with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass, and no statement in this code instantiates such a caller.
Behavior of mt_del, mrb_mc_clear_by_class, and mrb_name_error internals is not shown; no in-domain misuse of their returns occurs here (mt_del's result is checked; no other returns are consumed).

verdict.summary: The graph-controlled scalar from ctx->input(0) is converted from int to std::size_t and used as the buffer position in buf->Peek(index, &tuple) with no range or sign validation anywhere in this code; a negative or oversized value (e.g. -1 -> 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF) is passed as a raw index into the staged-buffer lookup at the intake point.

evidence.reason: Attacker-derived index (read on line 7 from the input tensor, sign-widened to size_t with no range check) is passed unvalidated as the lookup position into the buffer; no bounds, clamp, or sentinel guard exists between the definition and this use.
Origin of the tainted value: attacker-controlled 32-bit signed tensor value converted to std::size_t, so any negative input wraps to a huge out-of-range index.

assumptions: Buffer::Peek consumes its index parameter as a position into the staged queue; its implementation is not shown in this code and no quoted statement bounds the index against the queue length.
OpKernelContext input/output access is assumed reachable with attacker-influenced tensor values as is standard for TF graph ops.
limitations: If input(0) is not a scalar of dtype int32, scalar<int>() triggers a CHECK failure (crash of the same-privileged process) — robustness issue, not promoted.

The actual out-of-bounds read occurs inside Buffer::Peek, which is not shown; per analysis rules the unchecked call site is the defect, but the concrete memory layout of the queue could not be simulated here.
The tuple.size()/num_outputs mismatch check (line 12) correctly guards the output loop and is not a defect.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-data input is the int parameter 'size', consumed solely in pure size arithmetic. For negative 'size' the int-to-size_t conversion wraps (e.g. size=-1 yields computed_size=0, and the MSVC subtraction underflows for size<=-2 producing near-SIZE_MAX values), but this code performs no allocation, copy, indexing, or output construction — every harmful use of the wrapped value (undersized/oversized malloc, subsequent writes) lies in callers not shown, so no direct security impact is instantiated within this code. No guard on 'size' exists, but no sink exists for it to protect.

assumptions: sizeof(dummy) and sizeof(dummy.data[0]) are treated as fixed compile-time constants; the actual TfLiteIntArray layout (flexible array member vs data[1]) is in a header not provided, so the MSVC compensation in line 7 cannot be verified as correct or incorrect from this code alone.
limitations: Speculative (CWE-191/190-style): a negative 'size' (in-domain for an exported API parameter, e.g. size=-1 → computed_size=0; size<=-2 under MSVC → computed_size wraps to ~2^64-4) would yield an undersized or oversized allocation in any caller that passes the return value to malloc and then writes a positive element count — that caller, its NULL check, and the write are not shown and cannot be quoted, so the corruption chain is not instantiated here.

Whether the MSVC branch (line 7) under-compensates (4-byte under-allocation on every call, overflowing the struct's 'size' field in callers) depends on whether TfLiteIntArray uses data[1] on MSVC; the struct definition is not given, so this cannot be evaluated.
For all size >= 0 the computation cannot overflow size_t (max ≈ 2^33), so no positive-domain overflow exists.

verdict.summary: mrb_remove_method is guarded: the short-circuit 'if (h && mt_del(mrb, h, mid))' prevents a NULL method table from reaching mt_del, and a failed deletion correctly falls through to mrb_name_error (fail-closed). The only remaining defect shape is a NULL/garbage 'c' dereference at 'h = c->mt' / MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN(c), which is a same-privilege crash at worst and relies on a caller precondition this code does not quote; no memory-corruption, injection, bypass, or fail-open impact is instantiable.

assumptions: mt_del(mrb, h, mid) has standard hash-delete semantics: it requires a non-NULL table, performs a keyed lookup, and returns a truthy value on successful deletion and a false sentinel on miss; this consumption pattern is characterized by the 'if (h && mt_del(...))' guard and the fall-through to mrb_name_error.

mrb_name_error's '%n' and '%C' format specifiers are engine-internal formatters taking a symbol ID and a class object; the format string is a literal, so no attacker-controlled format string or injection exists.
MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN(c) is assumed to be a pointer-field adjustment on a valid class (standard mruby macro); its expansion is not shown.
limitations: A NULL or corrupted 'struct RClass *c' would dereference at 'h = c->mt' (and inside MRB_CLASS_ORIGIN), causing a crash of the same-privilege scripting engine. Per the impact model this is a robustness issue, not a security verdict: the only instantiator is a caller passing NULL, a precondition this code does not quote or check, and the worst case is a crash with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass.

A garbage (non-NULL) attacker-supplied 'c' could yield out-of-bounds reads via 'c->mt', but instantiating it requires prior memory corruption outside this code; no statement here produces or can produce that state, so the trigger is speculative.

verdict.summary: send_control_msg copies len bytes into a guest-provided scatter-gather buffer (elem.in_sg/elem.in_num, populated by virtqueue_pop from guest DMA descriptors) with no check that the guest's buffer capacity is at least len. A guest that posts an undersized descriptor (e.g., 1 byte) receives a full-length copy request with no local bound, and virtqueue_push then reports len as written even though fewer bytes can have been copied; the code's own TODO (line 14) admits the missing short-buffer detection.

evidence.reason: Sinks len bytes into guest-controlled destination buffers without any capacity check; the copy length is never validated against the total size of the guest-supplied in_sg descriptors, so an undersized guest buffer (e.g., iov_len=1 with len=8) triggers the copy at the call site; the return value (bytes actually written) is also discarded.

Origin of the attacker data: virtqueue_pop fills elem.in_sg/elem.in_num from guest-authored DMA descriptor chains (guest controls each segment's base and length); the code only checks the failure sentinel, never the size of the popped buffers.

The unchecked return of iov_from_buf is consumed here: the requested len is reported to the guest's used ring regardless of how many bytes the guest-sized buffer could actually accept, propagating the unvalidated size relationship.

assumptions: elem.in_sg/in_num are filled by virtqueue_pop from guest-supplied virtqueue descriptors, so per-segment lengths are attacker-controlled across the guest-to-host trust boundary (declared-domain rule; producer not shown).
buf and len originate from host-built control messages; len is a small host-computed struct size, so len itself is not attacker-scaled.
limitations: If iov_from_buf (not shown) internally clamps copies to each segment's iov_len, the realized host-side impact reduces to message truncation plus virtqueue_push reporting more bytes than were written (guest-visible inconsistency), i.e., a robustness/correctness defect; upstream QEMU fixed exactly this by assigning the return value ('len = iov_from_buf(...)'). The verdict rests on the last-line-of-defense rule that an unshown callee contract can neither guard nor dismiss the call site.

The 1-byte-descriptor trigger's worst-case host heap overflow therefore depends on the unshown callee's semantics; if that callee is bounds-safe, the confirmed defect is the unchecked-return consumption at line 17 rather than memory corruption.
virtqueue_push's unsigned length parameter could truncate a size_t len larger than UINT_MAX, but len is host-computed and small here, so this was not instantiated.

verdict.summary: The op stores its input tensor in the session's TensorStore and writes a handle to the output. Both failure-prone operations (tensor store insertion and output allocation) are guarded by OP_REQUIRES_OK before any use of the result; no attacker-controlled size, index, offset, or content reaches any memory, copy, output-construction, or control-flow sink in this code.

assumptions: TensorFlow's OpKernel execution framework guarantees that the inputs declared at op registration (including input 0) are present and arity-correct before Compute is invoked.

The output dtype seen by expected_output_dtype and the allocated output tensor both derive from the single server-side op registration, so the DT_RESOURCE vs legacy tstring branch cannot be made inconsistent by runtime data.
limitations: If this op were ever registered with an output dtype that is neither DT_RESOURCE nor a string type, the legacy path handle->flat<tstring>().setConstant(...) would CHECK-fail (same-privilege crash/robustness issue, not exploitable corruption); registration is C++ server-side and not attacker-instantiable from the shown code.

ctx->input(0) is not locally checked for validity, but the Tensor is only stored by reference (TensorAndKey{val,...}) and never indexed here, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable from this function.

verdict.summary: updateHandshakeState consumes only TLS-stack-exported cipher/parameter handles; every sink is guarded in execution order by an in-function truthiness check, a duplicate-install rejection throw, or a null-sentinel throw before first use. Clearing conn.writableBytesLimit is gated on the 1-RTT read cipher, which the TLS layer exports only after the peer's Finished is verified — fail-closed. Remaining candidates (possible null conn.serverHandshakeLayer, CHECK-invariant aborts) are not attacker-instantiable and crash-only at equal privilege.

assumptions: Cipher/parameter getters on ServerHandshakeLayer follow standard TLS/fizz export semantics: 1-RTT read keys are exported only after the peer's Finished is verified, and cipher/header-cipher pairs derive together (characterizable callee semantics, not an unquoted dismissal).
conn.serverHandshakeLayer and conn.readCodec are assigned by the same server process during connection setup before this handler runs.
limitations: If conn.serverHandshakeLayer could be null when updateHandshakeState runs, `handshakeLayer->getZeroRttReadCipher()` would dereference null — a crash-only abort; no statement here or attacker-reachable path instantiates it.
`CHECK(handshakeReadHeaderCipher)` and `CHECK(conn.oneRttWriteCipher)` abort the process if the fizz-layer pairing invariants were violated; impact is a same-privilege abort with no corruption.
No duplicate-install rejection exists for the 1-RTT read cipher (unlike the write cipher); the codec setter replaces the cipher, so this is at most functional redundancy, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability: the width/height/total_size validation (lines 18-24) provably bounds every downstream multiplication (row sizes, element counts, tensor allocations) at both boundaries, verified against 0, negative, exactly-at-limit, one-past-limit, and uint32-to-int truncation values; all surviving candidates require an unshown producer (decoder channels > 4, out-of-domain data_type_ attribute) to violate a precondition this code does not quote, and are therefore speculative.

assumptions: decode.channels is set by png::CommonInitDecode (not shown) from a successfully-initialized, structurally valid PNG; standard libpng semantics (png_check_IHDR rejects color_type > 6) confine it to {1,2,3,4}, which the line 18-24 arithmetic (channels*width*2 <= 2^31-8; total*4 = 2^31-4) relies on.
channels_ and data_type_ are op attributes whose registration-time validation (channels in {0,1,3,4}; data_type in {uint8,uint16,float}) is not shown in this code.
CommonFinishDecode writes exactly height rows of the row size passed, consistent with the allocated tensor element count.
limitations: decode.channels has no local validation anywhere in this code; if the unshown decoder could emit channels > 4 (e.g. 5 with total_size near 2^29), the int product height*width*decode.channels in new uint16[...] on the DT_FLOAT path would overflow and could under-size the buffer — speculative, requires the not-shown decoder to violate libpng color-type constraints.

If data_type_ were outside {DT_UINT8, DT_UINT16, DT_FLOAT}, no decode branch runs and the allocated output tensor is returned uninitialized (CWE-908) — speculative, requires op registration to accept an unlisted dtype.
On the DecodeBmp and DecodeAndCropJpeg error arms, png::CommonFreeDecode is not called, leaking the libpng structs per call — a resource leak, not memory corruption.

Images at the permitted limit (e.g. ~16384x32768, 4 channels, DT_FLOAT) induce a ~4 GB heap allocation; new uint16[] throwing std::bad_alloc or allocation failure crashes the same-privilege process — accepted risk within the deliberately permitted size limits (resource consumption, not corruption).

verdict.summary: No vulnerability. The only attacker-influenced input is the shape of input(0); the sole indexed access, c->Dim(c->input(0), 1), is guarded by TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR(c->WithRank(c->input(0), 2, &unused)), which enforces rank exactly 2 and returns before the access for any other rank. All other statements manipulate framework-produced symbolic shape handles with no memory, output-construction, or authorization sinks.

assumptions: InferenceContext::WithRank returns an error Status when the shape's rank is not exactly 2, and TF_RETURN_IF_ERROR propagates it before subsequent lines execute — standard TensorFlow semantics.
c->Dim on a rank-2 shape at index 1 is in range; c->Matrix/Vector/set_output construct symbolic metadata only.
limitations: Shape functions produce inference metadata only; even a semantically wrong output shape (e.g., misinterpreting dim 1 as the output rank) is a correctness issue for the graph author who controls the inputs, not a security impact.

verdict.summary: In the JPEG-LS run mode, the run length returned by DecodeRun (attacker-controlled via the entropy-coded scan bitstream) is never bounded against the remaining line width. The fill loop `while(run)` writes one sample per component per iteration via `*lp[cx]++` and only decrements `length` alongside `run`; if the decoded run exceeds the line width, length underflows negative and the loop performs a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-influenced values, and the negative `length` further keeps the outer pixel loop and run-interruption branch writing past the buffer. A `run <= length` clamp or `while(run && length > 0)` bound is absent everywhere in the code.

evidence.reason: Sink: per-iteration write through lp[cx], which points at a line buffer of m_ulWidth[0] LONGs. The enclosing `while(run)` loop (line 69) decrements both run and length (line 77) but never tests length, so a decoded run greater than the line width writes past the end of the buffer (heap out-of-bounds write) with the attacker-influenced value a[cx]<<preshift.

Origin/missing-guard site: DecodeRun returns a value decoded from the attacker's entropy-coded bitstream, and no statement between its return and the fill loop bounds run against `length` (no clamp, no `run > length` test, no `length` term in the loop condition). The comment on line 78 ('As long as there are pixels on the line') shows the intended invariant was never implemented.

assumptions: DecodeRun's implementation is not shown; per the width-domain rule its return is treated as attacker-data over the full LONG domain, since no quoted statement in this code bounds it.

Line buffers behind m_pData are heap/scan-line buffers of m_ulWidth[0] LONGs, the standard layout of this decoder class; the overflow lands in the buffer's own allocation, not an adjacent stack object.
limitations: Secondary candidate: `assert(m_ucCount < 4)` (line 26) is the only bound on m_ucCount for the line[4]/lp[4]/a[4] arrays; with NDEBUG it is absent, and count validation at scan-header parse is not shown, so a component count > 4 could cause a stack OOB — cannot be confirmed from this code alone.

Speculative: if m_ulRemaining[0] ever became negative, `while(--lines)` would iterate on negative values and over-advance `line[cx]->m_pNext` toward NULL; no quoted statement produces a negative remaining count here.

DecodeRun receives `length` as a parameter, so a defensive callee could in principle clamp the run to the line width; that contract is not quotable in this code and cannot dismiss the missing local bound.

verdict.summary: parse_query reads the 4-byte type/class fields via pj_memcpy at p = start + name_part_len without any check that p+4 <= max. An attacker-supplied DNS packet whose query name ends within the last 4 bytes of the buffer makes p reach max, so pj_memcpy reads 2-4 bytes out of bounds past the packet buffer (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: p is set to start + name_part_len with no bounds check against max before the memcpy. When the attacker's query name ends at the packet end, name_part_len == max - start so p == max, and pj_memcpy(&q->type, p, 2) reads 2 bytes out of bounds (the subsequent class read at p+2 extends this to 4 bytes past max). The missing guard `if (p+4 > max) return error;` appears nowhere in the function.

Second sink of the same defect: p has already been advanced 2 bytes (p += 2) with no bounds check, so even a name ending 3 bytes before max leaves p+2 past the buffer end, reading the class field out of bounds.

assumptions: get_name_len returns PJ_SUCCESS with name_part_len up to max - start (i.e., a name occupying bytes through the last packet byte is a valid success case), which is the standard semantics of a DNS name-length parser that receives max as its bound.
pj_memcpy is a memcpy wrapper performing no bounds checking of its own.
pkt/start/max describe a network-received DNS packet, making the packet content attacker-controlled across a trust boundary.
limitations: Integer overflow of name_len+4 in pj_pool_alloc (line 15) would require get_name_len to return a name_len near INT_MAX; get_name_len's expansion limits are not shown, so this candidate is speculative.
NULL-dereference of q->name.ptr if pj_pool_alloc fails is a robustness issue only (pj_pool_alloc failure semantics not shown); no corruption or bypass demonstrated.

The exact amount of data readable past max depends on the caller's buffer layout, which is not shown; the confirmed impact is the out-of-bounds read primitive itself (up to 4 bytes), not a measured disclosure.

verdict.summary: The Unstage-style Compute path checks tuple arity with an exact equality against ctx->num_outputs() before the set_output loop; the guard is positioned before the sink, covers both over- and under-size cases, and uses matching units ((size_t) cast), so the indexing loop's i is provably in-domain. No candidate trigger survived simulation.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES / OP_REQUIRES_OK set an error status and return from Compute on failure (standard TensorFlow macro semantics), so the tuple.size() mismatch path exits before the loop.
Buffer::Tuple behaves as a sized random-access container where size() matches operator[] domain (standard std::vector-like semantics).
limitations: Historical sibling defect: if the OP_REQUIRES equality check between tuple.size() and ctx->num_outputs() were absent, the set_output loop would be an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787); in this variant the guard is present and verified at both bounds.

On the mismatch error path the tuple has already been popped by buf->Get and is silently lost — a functional queue-loss/robustness issue, not a security impact (error status is correctly propagated, no fail-open).
buf->Get's internal copy/allocation behavior is not shown; if it mishandles tuple contents that defect would reside in the callee, and no out-of-domain argument is passed to it here.

verdict.summary: qtm_decompress (Quantum decoder) contains all decisive bounds guards: the match-overrun write check 'if (window_posn + match_length > qtm->window_size) return qtm->error = CL_EFORMAT;' admits exactly window_size and rejects one-past-limit, the wrapped-source read check 'if (j > (int) qtm->window_size)' bounds j at both edges, and 'if (j < i)' prevents the classic i-=j underflow; arithmetic on out_bytes/flush lengths cannot produce a negative length or pointer back-step within representable state. Remaining concerns (frame_end 32-bit truncation hang for out_bytes >= 2^32, and the literal write relying on the window_size frame-alignment invariant established in the not-shown qtm_init) are speculative, requiring an unshown producer, and are recorded as limitations.

assumptions: QTM_RESTORE_BITS/QTM_GET_SYMBOL/QTM_READ_BITS macros (not shown) refill the input bitstream with bounds checks against i_end and propagate errors, and QTM_FRAME_SIZE divides every window_size admitted by qtm_init (not shown) so frame_start stays frame-aligned and frame_end <= window_size, keeping the literal write 'window[window_posn++] = sym;' in bounds.

qtm->window_size is at most the libmspack/ClamAV maximum (0x200000), so window_posn + match_length and (int) window_size casts cannot wrap or go negative; if init admitted larger values the (int) cast in the j check still fails safe (rejects).
limitations: A caller passing out_bytes >= 2^32 (not shown; full off_t domain) makes frame_end = (unsigned)(window_posn + out_bytes - stored) truncate to <= window_posn, skipping the inner decode loop and spinning the outer loop forever (CPU denial of service, no memory corruption); trigger needs an unshown caller, so not confirmed.

The literal-write path window[window_posn++] = sym has no direct check against qtm->window_size in this function; its safety rests on the frame-alignment guard 'if ((window_posn - frame_start) != QTM_FRAME_SIZE) return qtm->error = CL_EFORMAT;' plus the unquoted qtm_init contract that window_size is a multiple of QTM_FRAME_SIZE.
The QTM_* bit-reading macros and mspack_write internals are not shown; their error/bounds behavior could not be quoted.

verdict.summary: In the run-mode branch of ParseMCU, the value returned by DecodeRun (attacker-controlled via the compressed bitstream) is copied into the target line by 'while(run) { *lp++ = a << preshift; run--,length--; }' without any check that run <= length. The loop condition tests only 'run', so when the decoded run exceeds the remaining line width, length goes negative and lp writes past the end of the line buffer (sized m_ulWidth[0]), producing a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced LONG values. The missing guard is a clamp such as 'if (run > length) run = length;' between the DecodeRun call and the while loop; the only length test, 'if (length)', appears after the loop and never gates the writes.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: the loop terminates only when 'run' reaches zero; 'length' (initialized to m_ulWidth[0]) is decremented alongside but never tested, so a decoded run larger than the line width makes lp advance past the end of line->m_pData and write attacker-influenced LONG values out of bounds (CWE-787). Trigger: a crafted bitstream whose run-mode section yields run > width, e.g. width=32, run=132 → 100 LONGs written past the heap buffer.

Origin of the tainted value: DecodeRun decodes the run length directly from the attacker-supplied compressed bitstream; its return is consumed without any local clamp to the remaining line length ('if (run > length) run = length;' appears nowhere in the function), so the full decoded value reaches the unbounded write loop.

assumptions: The line buffer line->m_pData is allocated with m_ulWidth[0] elements elsewhere (not shown); the OOB direction and extent follow from that standard allocation and from lp advancing once per run iteration.
DecodeRun's return derives from the compressed bitstream (attacker-instantiable domain); the callee body is not shown, so no internal clamping could be quoted and none was credited.
limitations: If ParseMCU is invoked when m_ulRemaining[0] <= 0 (caller not shown), 'while(--lines)' with lines==0 or negative would loop ~2^31-2^32 times, walking line->m_pNext past the line list — a potential second OOB/DoS, but the caller-side stop condition on m_ulRemaining is not in this code, so it stays speculative.
line->m_pNext could be NULL if fewer than 'lines' (up to 8) lines are allocated; the allocation logic is not shown, so a NULL deref there could not be instantiated here.
assert() statements (lines 11, 15, 25) vanish under NDEBUG and were not treated as guards.
The run-interruption and regular-mode writes at 'lp' are in-bounds only if 'run' is clamped; they share the same root cause and do not constitute an independent defect.

verdict.summary: btrfs_rm_device dereferences the attacker-supplied device_path pointer without a NULL check: when the caller resolves a device by devid alone (device_path == NULL, as the BTRFS_IOC_RM_DEV_V2 by-id form supplies) and the devid lookup misses, btrfs_find_device_by_devspec returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT), the code enters the ENOENT arm, and evaluates strcmp(NULL, "missing"), causing a NULL-pointer dereference (kernel oops / denial of service) triggered by an ioctl argument.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing NULL guard on the pointer parameter device_path before its first dereference. Trigger: device_path == NULL (devid-only removal) and btrfs_find_device_by_devspec returns ERR_PTR(-ENOENT); both && operands then evaluate strcmp(NULL, "missing"), dereferencing NULL.

Origin of the tainted control flow: the attacker-influenced lookup (attacker-chosen u64 devid, possibly-NULL path) whose -ENOENT failure sentinel is explicitly handled by the following branch, proving that arm is reachable; no NULL validation of device_path occurs before the strcmp.

assumptions: btrfs_find_device_by_devspec performs a lookup whose miss returns the ERR_PTR(-ENOENT) sentinel the code itself handles at lines 20-25, and accepts a NULL device_path when devid identifies the device (this is the signature's designed devid-only mode).
limitations: The u64 expression `num_devices - 1` (line 14) would wrap to U64_MAX if num_devices were 0, weakening the RAID-min check; a mounted filesystem was assumed to always report >= 1 device, so no concrete trigger was instantiated.

The code's own TODO comment acknowledges that write_all_supers() is not locked out while the superblock num_devices counter is stale after the uuid_mutex is dropped around btrfs_shrink_device(); this race window could not be simulated to a concrete corruption with the statements given.

Dereference of device->name->str in the btrfs_scratch_superblocks call was not instantiable as a NULL-name case because a device with WRITEABLE set is presumed to have an initialized name; no attack value was proven.
The ioctl path requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which limits the attacker population but does not eliminate the trust boundary.

verdict.summary: Examples::Initialize validates the sizes of sparse_example_indices, sparse_feature_indices, and sparse_feature_values input lists against the corresponding attacker-controlled feature counts, but never validates dense_features_inputs.size() against num_dense_features before passing both to CreateDenseFeatureRepresentation; a graph/feed author supplying fewer dense tensors than num_dense_features causes the callee to index the input-list vector out of bounds (OOB read of Tensor pointers, crash/DoS of the TF process).

verdict.summary: This isoffin process loop consumes attacker-controlled MP4 sample metadata (ch->sample->dataLength, subsample and SAI buffers, NTP/fragment info), but its only raw memory-write sink, memcpy(data, ch->sample->data, ch->sample->dataLength), is guarded by an allocation sized from the exact same expression (gf_filter_pck_new_alloc(ch->pid, ch->sample->dataLength, &data)) with a NULL-sentinel check (if (!pck) return GF_OUT_OF_MEM;) before first use; all other callee results (subs_buf, sai_buffer, tfrf, pck from new_shared) are sentinel-checked or consumed as matched pointer+size pairs, and no command/SQL/path/URL/format-string construction from attacker data exists in this code.

assumptions: gf_filter_pck_new_alloc allocates a buffer of exactly the requested size (standard allocation semantics per discipline 3).
isor_reader_get_sample / gf_isom_* populate ch->sample->data and ch->sample->dataLength consistently (pointer and size produced by the same callee).
limitations: The actual parsing of attacker-supplied ISO-BMFF/DASH data occurs in not-shown callees (isor_reader_get_sample, gf_isom_refresh_fragmented, gf_isom_sample_get_subsamples_buffer, isoffin_push_buffer); defects inside those functions cannot be evaluated here.

dep_flags (u8) packing of isLeading/dependsOn/dependedOn/redundant can silently truncate bits from attacker-influenced trun flags, but the value only feeds a packet metadata property with no memory or indexing use — functional, not a security impact.

ch returned by gf_list_get(read->channels, i) is not NULL-checked; the channel list is internal filter state populated by this filter's own configure path, so a NULL ch was not instantiable from attacker data in this code.
assert(ch->sai_buffer_size) may be compiled out in release builds; a zero-size SAI property is benign (empty property, no out-of-bounds access).

verdict.summary: setup_config builds the default lockfile (pidfile) path by interpolating booth_conf->name — a string parsed from the configuration file — into snprintf("%s/%s.pid", BOOTH_RUN_DIR, booth_conf->name) with no canonicalization or component validation, so a config-supplied name containing '/' or '..' (e.g. "../../tmp/evil") produces a lockfile path outside BOOTH_RUN_DIR; the tainted path construction is itself the vulnerability.

verdict.summary: The AddManySparseToTensorsMap Compute path validates every attacker-controlled value before its consuming sink: shape/dimension consistency is enforced by the two dim_size equality OP_REQUIRES, `rank > 1` guards the element-0 read of input_shape_vec and the `NumElements()-1` underflow, and the decisive guard `b > -1 && b < N` (backstopped by `input_st.IndicesValid()` executed before the group loop) provably keeps the batch index b inside the N-element `sparse_handles` tensor at both boundaries (b=-1 and b=N rejected, b=0 and b=N-1 admitted and in-bounds), so the OOB write candidate `sparse_handles_t(b) = handle` is not reachable. Residual issues (int loop counter vs int64 num_entries wrap requiring >32GB inputs, TensorShape CHECK-fail on huge N, int rank truncation) are recorded as limitations, not primary defects.

assumptions: TensorShape::BuildTensorShape rejects negative dimension entries (standard TF semantics), so `N = input_shape_vec(0)` is non-negative by the time `TensorShape({N})` is constructed.
SparseTensor::Create and IndicesValid have standard TF semantics: IndicesValid validates every index component against tensor_input_shape, whose dim 0 equals N.
limitations: The inner loop uses `int i` against `int64_t num_entries`; a group with >= 2^31 entries would wrap i at INT_MAX and cause an out-of-bounds access. The trigger requires the caller to materialize >2^31-row input tensors (~32+ GB), a resource-scale precondition no statement of this code produces; recorded as speculative.
`Tensor sparse_handles(DT_INT64, TensorShape({N}))` with a very large N causes allocation failure and a TF CHECK-fail abort (same-privilege crash/DoS), not memory corruption.

`int rank = input_shape->NumElements()` can truncate if NumElements exceeds INT_MAX, but that requires a >=16 GB shape vector plus indices with >2^31 columns, and SparseTensor::Create's order-size/ndims consistency check would reject before the truncated value reaches an indexing use.

verdict.summary: No unguarded sink found. The primary copy sink (memcpy of ch->sample->data) is protected because gf_filter_pck_new_alloc is sized from the exact same expression (ch->sample->dataLength) as the memcpy length, and the allocation result is NULL-checked (if (!pck) return GF_OUT_OF_MEM) before data is used. All callee returns (subs_buf, tfrf, prop, pck, gf_list_get with i<count) are sentinel-checked before use, and the u64 subtraction (min_offset_plus_one-1) is guarded by the non-zero test (read->mem_load_mode && min_offset_plus_one). No output construction from attacker data exists in this function.

assumptions: gf_filter_pck_new_alloc allocates a buffer of at least the requested size and sets *data to it (standard GPAC semantics).
gf_list_get returns a valid non-NULL element for i < gf_list_count, and read->channels is not mutated during the channel loop.
isor_reader_get_sample / isor_reader_get_sample_from_item leave ch->sample consistent with ch->sample->dataLength / data as produced by the ISOBMFF parser (callee not shown).
limitations: dep_flags is a u8 built with three <<=2 shifts from ch->isLeading; if the unshown parser stores isLeading > 3, the value truncates — functional flag corruption only, no memory-safety impact.
assert(ch->sai_buffer_size) compiles out in release builds; a non-NULL sai_buffer with size 0 would produce an empty CENC SAI property, not a demonstrated memory error.

Potential defects inside unshown callees (isoffin_push_buffer with attacker-controlled data_size, isor_reader_get_sample internals, tfrf lifetime under PROP_POINTER ownership) could not be evaluated from this code.
The while(nb_pck) loop's continue path (stsd mismatch) does not decrement nb_pck, but each iteration releases and fetches the next sample, bounding iterations by the file's sample count.

verdict.summary: In STATE_REP, a REP item from the spell/aff file is applied to fword without any check that the replacement fits: fl = STRLEN(ftp->ft_from), tl = STRLEN(ftp->ft_to) are attacker-chosen lengths, and STRMOVE(p + tl, p + fl) / mch_memmove(p, ftp->ft_to, tl) can write past the end of the caller's fixed fword buffer, corrupting adjacent stack memory. No statement in the function bounds the write extent (the only length-ish test, try_split = (sp->ts_fidx - repextra < su->su_badlen), compares different variables in a different unit and runs after the write).

evidence.reason: Root cause: no bound on the REP replacement extent. ftp->ft_from/ft_to come from the spell file's REP/SAL list (attacker-controlled if the .spl/.aff is untrusted); fl and tl are their arbitrary string lengths, p = fword + sp->ts_fidx points into the fixed-size fword buffer. Instantiated trigger: ft_from of length 1 matching fword[0] and ft_to of length 200 while fword holds a 250-byte word: STRMOVE(p+200, p+1) copies ~250 bytes starting at fword+200, and mch_memmove writes 200 bytes at fword[0] — both beyond the buffer end. The mention sweep found no statement comparing tl/fl or the write offset against any buffer size; repextra is only ever adjusted (+=/-=), never bounded.

Origin context: taint source chain — fword (parameter, bad word from the document) and ftp->ft_from/ft_to (slang REP items loaded from the spell file) both cross a trust boundary into this function with no local validation of their lengths before the STATE_REP sink.

assumptions: The spell file (.spl/.aff) supplying slang->sl_rep / sl_repsal entries and the trie is treated as attacker-controlled input (per the width-domain rule: no validation of REP entry lengths is quoted in this code).
fword is a fixed-size buffer (MAXWLEN-sized or su_badlen-sized) owned by the caller; its capacity is not checked against the REP replacement extent anywhere in this function.
limitations: compflags[sp->ts_complen + 1] = NUL could write one byte past compflags[MAXWLEN] if ts_complen reaches MAXWLEN-1, but ts_complen only increments inside TRY_DEEPER-guarded pushes whose macro body is not shown, so the depth ceiling cannot be fully verified here (speculative).
The TRY_DEEPER macro body is not shown, so stack[depth] overflow depends on it containing a depth check; the primary finding does not rely on it.
Exact line numbers for the evidence may be off by a small constant due to the length of the excerpt; the snippets are copied verbatim from the STATE_REP block and the taint-origin context.

verdict.summary: Attacker-controlled username (and ip_source) from the JSON request body is interpolated verbatim into security/audit log lines via y_log_message with no content validation or encoding; the only username check (json_string_length) verifies non-emptiness, never content. A failed login with a username containing newlines injects forged entries (e.g., fake 'Event - User authenticated' records) into the authentication audit log.

evidence.snippet: y_log_message(Y_LOG_LEVEL_WARNING, "Security - Authorization invalid for username %s at IP Address %s", json_string_value(json_object_get(j_param, "username")), ip_source);
evidence.reason: Unguarded log-line construction: the raw attacker-supplied username from the JSON body is written into the security audit log with %s and no encoding; the trigger is any non-empty username containing \n (e.g., "bob\n... Event - User 'admin' authenticated with password") with a wrong password, reaching this line with check_result_value(j_result, G_ERROR_UNAUTHORIZED) true and forging log entries. The same unvalidated construction repeats at lines 28 and 74.

evidence.snippet: json_t * j_param = ulfius_get_json_body_request(request, NULL), * j_result = NULL;
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted value: j_param is the raw JSON request body from the network client; the username field consumed by the log sinks is read from it with no content validation anywhere between intake and the y_log_message sinks.

assumptions: y_log_message writes its formatted output to the server log without stripping newline/control characters from %s arguments (standard printf-style logging semantics).
limitations: Line 53: user_session_update is called with u_map_get(request->map_cookie, config->session_key) while the validation (get_users_for_session) was performed on session_uid from get_session_id — a validate-one/use-another mismatch; impact could not be instantiated because both get_session_id and user_session_update are not shown, so divergence of the two values and harmful update semantics are unproven.

Line 37: the failed-authentication branch passes the attempted, unauthenticated username into user_session_update for an existing session; if the unshown callee does not verify the username belongs to the session, this would allow session-user substitution (authz bypass), but callee semantics are not quoted here.
Set-Cookie responses embed cookie-derived session_uid (ulfius_add_cookie_to_response); header-splitting impact depends on unshown ulfius encoding and was not instantiated.
get_ip_source may derive its value from attacker-supplied X-Forwarded-For, adding a second injection vector into the same log lines; same CWE-117 finding.

verdict.summary: The Compute kernel loops hs/ws over height_cum_seq.size()-1 / width_cum_seq.size()-1 (attacker-influenced returns of GeneratePoolingSequence, whose size is never validated against output_size), but indexes out_mat with out_offset = (b*output_size[1]+hs)*output_size[2]+ws. When the returned sequence is longer than output_size+1 (or empty, making size()-1 wrap to SIZE_MAX), out_offset exceeds the allocated output tensor's column count and out_mat.col(out_offset) writes out of bounds on the heap. The single missing guard is OP_REQUIRES(height_cum_seq.size() == output_size[1]+1) (and the width analog); the only nearby check, DCHECK_GT(output_size[i], 0), is a release-mode no-op on a different variable.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop bound is the unvalidated size of GeneratePoolingSequence's return (attacker-data via seed_/pseudo_random_/input shape) instead of output_size[1]; no statement ties the sequence size to the allocated output dimension, and if the sequence is empty, size()-1 wraps to SIZE_MAX.

Sink: with hs ≥ output_size[1] (sequence longer than output_size[1]+1), out_offset = (b*output_size[1]+hs)*output_size[2]+ws exceeds the output tensor's column count and this statement performs a heap out-of-bounds write of attacker-influenced values.

assumptions: GeneratePoolingSequence is not shown, so its return (vector<int64_t> size and content) is treated as attacker-data with the full domain of its declared type per the width-domain rule; it is steered by the attacker-controlled seed_, seed2_, pseudo_random_ attributes and input shape.
TensorFlow release builds compile DCHECK_GT (line 24) to a no-op, so output_size is effectively unvalidated at runtime.
limitations: Trigger instantiation relies on the unshown callee returning a sequence whose size differs from output_size+1 or is empty; the exact conditions are in-domain for its return type but not quotable here.

Secondary speculative effects noted but not promoted: negative sequence values would make height_start/in_offset negative (OOB read on in_mat), and pooling_ratio_[i]==0 causes a division-by-zero/inf-to-int cast UB (CWE-190); both share the same unvalidated-callee-return/missing-validation root as the primary finding.
Only a heap OOB write via out_mat.col(out_offset) was confirmed as the primary defect; no independent second primary defect with its own quoted trigger was established, so a single CWE is emitted.

verdict.summary: All memory-relevant sinks are guarded: node.input(0) is protected by 'if (node.input_size() < 1) return false;' (verified at both bounds, precedes uses), and *input is protected by an explicit nullptr check before first dereference. The remaining candidates — the unchecked 'consumer' pointer from GetOutputs (crash-only, not provably null in this code), the 'node.input_size() > 1' gate that weakens Retval/Merge protection for single-input Identities, and the input(0)-only inspection for multi-input IdentityN — have consequences that materialize only in the unshown graph-rewiring code, so no primary vulnerability is instantiated in this snippet.

assumptions: node and node_map_ derive from a GraphDef loaded from an untrusted model file, so op strings, input lists, and node names are attacker-data across a trust boundary.
NodeMap::GetNode is a lookup whose miss sentinel is nullptr (checked at line 18); NodeMap::GetOutputs is a lookup whose miss form is an empty container.
limitations: Lines 26-29: 'consumer' from node_map_->GetOutputs() is dereferenced (IsRetval(*consumer), consumer->input()) without a null check. A null element is not instantiable from the shown code (depends on unshown NodeMap internals), and even then the result is only a same-privilege NULL-dereference crash induced by the model loader's own input — a robustness issue (CWE-476), not a primary vulnerability.

Line 26: 'node.input_size() > 1 && (IsRetval(*consumer) || IsMerge(*consumer))' gates the Retval/Merge protection, so a single-input Identity feeding _Retval or Merge is deemed removable; whether that removal is unsafe depends entirely on the rewire logic outside this snippet (same for input(0)-only Variable/Recv/Switch inspection when input_size()>1). These are optimizer-correctness candidates whose impact could not be instantiated in STEP 4.

If a not-shown caller invokes SafeToRemoveIdentity on non-Identity nodes and treats 'true' as a general removal authorization, the early 'return true' (lines 2-4) would be fail-open; no such caller is visible here.

verdict.summary: xQueueGenericCreate sizes the heap allocation with sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes without checking the addition for 32-bit wrap. The quoted configASSERT on line 17 verifies only the multiplication uxQueueLength*uxItemSize, so a queue created with uxQueueLength=1 and uxItemSize=0xFFFFFFC4 passes every check, wraps the sum to a tiny size, and yields an undersized heap block whose Queue_t metadata and 4 GB storage area are written out of bounds (heap corruption on initialization and on every subsequent send).

evidence.snippet: pxNewQueue = ( Queue_t * ) pvPortMalloc( sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes ); /*lint !e9087 !e9079 see comment above. */
evidence.reason: The allocation size sizeof( Queue_t ) + xQueueSizeInBytes is computed in size_t with no overflow check; with attacker-chosen uxQueueLength=1, uxItemSize=0xFFFFFFC4 the sum wraps to ~64 bytes while the queue records a ~4 GB item size, so the returned block is far smaller than the storage written through pucQueueStorage (pxNewQueue+sizeof(Queue_t)) and by prvInitialiseNewQueue — integer overflow leading to undersized allocation and out-of-bounds heap writes.

evidence.snippet: xQueueSizeInBytes = ( size_t ) ( uxQueueLength * uxItemSize ); /*lint !e961 MISRA exception as the casts are only redundant for some ports. */
evidence.reason: Origin of the tainted size: xQueueSizeInBytes is derived from attacker-supplied uxQueueLength/uxItemSize; the subsequent assert (line 17) checks only this multiplication, not the addition on line 28.

assumptions: 32-bit size_t and UBaseType_t (typical FreeRTOS targets); sizeof(Queue_t) > 0, which holds on every port.

prvInitialiseNewQueue stores uxQueueLength/uxItemSize into the Queue_t at pxNewQueue and points the storage at the supplied pucQueueStorage, per FreeRTOS queue semantics; pvPortMalloc returns a suitably sized non-NULL block for small requests.
limitations: The actual out-of-bounds write executes in prvInitialiseNewQueue and the queue send/copy paths, which are not shown; the undersized allocation, wrapped size, and out-of-block storage pointer are fully quoted here.

The multiplication-overflow assert on line 17 and the uxQueueLength>0 assert on line 9 enforce only when configASSERT is defined as fail-stop; in builds where configASSERT compiles to a no-op, uxQueueLength*uxItemSize wrap is also unguarded — a wider instance of the same class, not needed for this verdict.

Exploitation additionally requires a caller that passes attacker-controlled creation parameters across a trust boundary; per the width-domain rule the full UBaseType_t domain is instantiable at this exported API.

verdict.summary: All tensor acquisition and the quantized kernel path are guarded fail-closed (TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK, and an explicit error return for unsupported output types); no memory, copy, division, or output-construction statement in this function is reachable with an unvalidated attacker value. The only residual concern — the discarded return of EvalDiv at line 16 — cannot be instantiated because EvalDiv's signature and failure modes are not shown and are not characterizable from standard-function semantics.

assumptions: TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK and GetInputSafe/GetOutputSafe follow their standard TFLite semantics: on a non-OK status the macro returns early, and the Safe accessors handle missing/optional tensors, so input1/input2/output are non-NULL on the guarded paths.
node->builtin_data and node->user_data are populated by the framework's Prepare pass, which is not shown in this code.
limitations: Line 16: the return value of EvalDiv<kernel_type>(...) is discarded while the sibling call EvalQuantized is wrapped in TF_LITE_ENSURE_OK. If EvalDiv returns TfLiteStatus, a kernel error would be swallowed and Eval would report kTfLiteOk (fail-open, CWE-451/754 shape). Not confirmed: EvalDiv's return type is not shown; in the canonical TFLite div.cc this template returns void, which makes the discard correct. Trigger not instantiated within the given code.

params (node->builtin_data) and data (node->user_data) are reinterpret_cast without local NULL checks; a NULL from an incomplete Prepare pass would at most crash the same-privilege process (CWE-476), with the producer not shown.
Dispatch validates only output->type; validation of input tensor types (and any division-by-zero handling, CWE-369) occurs entirely inside the not-shown EvalDiv/EvalQuantized kernels.

verdict.summary: SetupWriters validates only SampleSize, ChunkOffset and SampleToChunk in the stbl guard but dereferences stbl->TimeToSample (and trak->Media->mediaHeader) without any NULL check, so a crafted MP4 lacking the stts (or mdia header) box crashes the process ingesting the file (denial of service at the parser intake point).

evidence.reason: NULL-pointer dereference: the guard on line 17 checks !stbl || !stbl->SampleSize || !stbl->ChunkOffset || !stbl->SampleToChunk but never validates stbl->TimeToSample, so a crafted MP4 whose stbl omits the TimeToSample (stts) box reaches this dereference with TimeToSample==NULL, crashing the process parsing the untrusted file.

Second independent instance of the same missing NULL check: no statement in the function tests trak->Media->mediaHeader before this dereference, so a crafted MP4 track missing the media header box crashes the writer setup.
