A NULL 'dev' would dereference at dev->name, but no statement in this code can produce that and the caller contract is outside the shown code — speculative.

verdict.summary: All memory sinks are guarded by in-code branches: the key buffer is allocated at cipher key length and zero-padded only when password_len < keylen, ctx key length never exceeds the key buffer in either branch (including EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length failure on fixed-length ciphers), and outbuf is sized from the same data_len + block_size expression that bounds EncryptUpdate/EncryptFinal output, leaving a verified 2-byte margin. The only reachable anomaly, signed overflow of data_len + block_size, requires a ~2GB attacker string and results in a fatal emalloc bailout (same-privilege DoS), not corruption.

assumptions: emalloc fatal-errors (bails out) on allocation failure per standard PHP semantics, so outbuf/key are never NULL at use.
EVP_EncryptUpdate/EVP_EncryptFinal obey their documented output bounds (single Update call: combined output <= inl + block_size), and *outl is assigned on all return paths.
php_openssl_validate_iv returns the ownership flag consumed by `if (free_iv) efree(iv);`.
limitations: IV length/content validation is delegated to the unshown php_openssl_validate_iv; an over-read at EVP_EncryptInit_ex (iv shorter than max_iv_len) or an overflow inside the callee cannot be assessed from this code.

Signed overflow of outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type) is triggerable only with a ~2GB input string (data_len near INT_MAX) and results in a failed huge allocation / fatal error, i.e. same-privilege DoS, not memory corruption.

Return values of EVP_EncryptInit, EVP_EncryptInit_ex, EVP_EncryptUpdate and EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length are unchecked; for all in-domain inputs the consequences are benign (failed set_key_length leaves ctx key_len <= key buffer size), but a future cipher with nonstandard output bounds would surface here.
Warning-then-proceed on empty IV and use of the raw password as key (no KDF) are the documented openssl_encrypt API contract, not fail-open verification bypasses.

verdict.summary: All attacker-data sinks in this CDF property parser are guarded in execution order: offs is bounded (offs > UINT32_MAX / 4), the section length is range-checked and stream-validated (sh.sh_len > CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT, cdf_check_stream_offset), property count is bounded (CDF_PROP_LIMIT) with the inp allocation sized from the same expression, p<e and e-in-stream are checked before the loop, the property-position lookup NULL sentinel is tested before the id read, left>=4 / left>=8 gate the type and vector-length reads, nelements is range-checked, and every inner-loop string read and buffer pointer is gated by 'o4 + sizeof(uint32_t) > left' and 'o4 + l > left' with inner writes capped by 'i < sh.sh_properties' in the loop condition before each write. No missing-guard candidate with an in-code impact chain survives; the only residual issue (32-bit unsigned wrap of o4+l passing the length check with l=0xFFFFFFFC) requires an ILP32 build and an unshown downstream consumer of the oversized s_len, so it is not instantiated here.

assumptions: CDF_GETUINT32(p, off) reads a 4-byte value at byte offset off*sizeof(uint32_t), so CDF_GETUINT32(p, i << 1) reads p + i*8.

cdf_get_property_info_pos returns a position within [p, e] or NULL on out-of-bounds; its NULL sentinel is tested before the first use of the returned pointer (and before the pi_id read that follows it in execution order).

cdf_check_stream_offset, cdf_grow_info, and cdf_copy_info have the standard sentinel semantics implied by their tested return values (-1, NULL, 0); the allocation from cdf_grow_info covers *count + requested elements.
The target is a 64-bit (LP64) build where size_t is 64 bits; under that width the arithmetic in the quoted guards cannot wrap.
limitations: On a 32-bit build, 'if (o4 + l > left)' can wrap: with o4=4 and l=0xFFFFFFFC the sum wraps to 0, passing the check and storing pi_str.s_len=0xFFFFFFFC with s_buf=&q[8]; the resulting over-read would occur only in the (not shown) string consumer that iterates s_len bytes, so the impact chain is not instantiated in this code. A wrap-safe form such as 'if (l > left - o4)' would close it.

'if (l & 1) l++;' wraps when l==0xFFFFFFFF (uint32_t) back to 0, causing the inner loop to re-read the same length word; iterations remain bounded by 'j < nelements && i < sh.sh_properties' and all writes stay in the grown buffer, so no security impact was identified.

No explicit check ties sh_properties to sh_len (e.g., sh_properties*8 <= sh_len-8), but every dereference derived from sh_properties is individually guarded by the q-sentinel test and the left-based checks, so no unguarded read path exists.
Constants CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT, CDF_PROP_LIMIT, and CDF_ELEMENT_LIMIT are not shown; their values are assumed to keep the corresponding loops and allocations within size_t and memory limits.

verdict.summary: In do_arg_all(), the second loop indexes the argument list with AARGLIST(alist)[i] using a loop bound (count, clamped to opened_len, a snapshot of ARGCOUNT taken before any autocommand ran) without re-checking i against the current alist->al_ga.ga_len. Autocommands fired by do_ecmd/win_split can shrink or replace the argument list mid-loop (the code's own comments acknowledge ARGCOUNT may change), so a subsequent iteration reads one-past-the-end of the reallocated aentry_T array and alist_name() then dereferences the out-of-bounds entry's pointer field: a heap out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Sink: AARGLIST(alist)[i] is indexed with i bounded only by count (= opened_len, a stale snapshot of ARGCOUNT taken at line 43 before any autocommand executed). The twin access in the first loop is guarded by 'if (i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' (line 84); no equivalent ga_len check exists anywhere between the loop entry (line 196) and this sink. Trigger: an autocommand (BufRead/BufNewFile via do_ecmd) runs :argdel/:args during iteration i=0, shrinking al_ga.ga_len below i; iteration i=1 then reads past the reallocated aentry_T array and alist_name() dereferences the OOB-read filename pointer — heap out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

Origin of the stale bound: count was clamped to opened_len (line 179), the ARGCOUNT value captured at line 43 before autocommands ran; this loop therefore permits i up to the pre-autocmd argument count even after al_ga.ga_len has shrunk, reaching the unguarded AARGLIST(alist)[i] use at line 252.

assumptions: AARGLIST(alist) expands to indexing (alist->al_ga.ga_data) as an aentry_T array sized by al_ga.ga_len (standard Vim semantics), so an index >= current ga_len is out of bounds.

do_ecmd triggers file-reading autocommands (autocmd_no_enter/leave only suppress Win/Buf Enter/Leave events), which can execute :argdel/:args — the possibility is explicitly acknowledged by this code's own comments at lines 48-50 and 176-177.
limitations: opened[i] accesses are safe: opened[] is allocated with opened_len (line 44, NULL-checked at line 45) and both loops bound i by opened_len or count <= opened_len.

Exploitation requires an autocommand (from a vimrc, plugin, or filetype autocmd) that mutates the argument list while :all/:tab drop is running; this matches Vim's established threat model for autocmd-triggered memory bugs.

The defect is a read (the entry's filename pointer is then dereferenced by alist_name/do_ecmd), so impact is out-of-bounds read/crash/potential information exposure rather than direct memory corruption.

verdict.summary: The sole memory-safety candidate, memcpy(usb_msg.data, cf->data, usb_msg.dlc) at line 45, is guarded in execution order by the standard CAN-frame validation at lines 14-15 (can_dropped_invalid_skb drops any frame with cf->len > 8 before the copy, and the copy length equals the checked length in the same units). All other tainted uses are bit-masked to their destination widths, and callee sentinels (ctx NULL, xmit err) are tested before use.

assumptions: can_dropped_invalid_skb is the standard kernel CAN helper whose characterizable semantics reject any classic CAN frame with len > CAN_MAX_DLEN (8) or invalid can_id bits, returning true so the function returns before the memcpy.
struct mcba_usb_msg_can.data is 8 bytes (MCBA_USB_CAN_DATA_MAX), matching the guarded maximum copy length of 8.
limitations: If a kernel build were used where can_dropped_invalid_skb did not validate cf->len (not the case for the standard helper), the memcpy at line 45 would be an out-of-bounds write of up to 247 bytes past data[8]; with the standard helper present, no candidate survived STEP 4.

verdict.summary: No primary vulnerability. The only candidate — idx accumulating past buf[NUMBUFLEN + MB_MAXBYTES] because 'continue' on a partial end-code match retains idx — is provably bounded: the quoted guard 'if (end != NULL && STRLEN(end) >= NUMBUFLEN) end = NULL;' caps STRLEN(end) at NUMBUFLEN-1, so the continue path holds idx <= NUMBUFLEN-2 before each write, and a multi-byte write plus the NUL terminator lands at index <= NUMBUFLEN-2+MB_MAXBYTES, inside the buffer. The end[idx] read is likewise only reachable with idx <= STRLEN(end). All other sinks (ga_grow-checked memmove, cmdline insert) carry quoted sentinel checks.

verdict.summary: Untrusted parameters fname and backup are passed directly as the format string to asprintf (with idstring as the only variadic argument), allowing attacker-controlled conversion specifiers such as %n or %s to read and write arbitrary memory.

evidence.reason: fname is used as the format string rather than as a %s argument. With fname = "%n" (any string representable in the parameter's domain), the printf engine consumes variadic slots beyond the single idstring argument and writes through garbage pointers — an attacker-controlled write primitive. No statement anywhere validates or literal-wraps fname.

Second instantiation of the same defect: backup is used as the format string. The only nearby check, `if (backup && *backup)` (line 8), tests non-NULL/non-empty only and does not constrain content, so backup = "%s%s%s" reaches the format engine and reads/writes beyond the supplied variadic argument.

assumptions: asprintf follows standard printf formatting semantics, including %n writes, on the target platform.
limitations: Memory leaks of suffix/oldLog on the FatalError paths are non-security robustness issues (FatalError presumably terminates).

The returned logFileName is passed to rename/remove with caller-derived path content; this is the function's intended file-management behavior, and no path-escape impact beyond the caller's own supplied paths is instantiated in this code.

verdict.summary: This io_uring read path re-fetches req->async_data only after the quoted sentinel test 'if (ret2) return ret2;' on io_setup_async_rw, NULL-tests rw at entry ('if (rw)'), bounds the retry loop with 'while (ret > 0 && ret < io_size)' where io_size only decreases by consumed bytes, performs rw_verify_area before reading, and hands iovec ownership off explicitly (iovec = NULL) before any return that skips the final kfree. Every candidate memory-safety trigger requires an unshown callee to violate its characterizable contract (a read returning more than the iov_iter supplied, an importer exceeding SSIZE_MAX, or a setup helper failing without its -ENOMEM sentinel).

assumptions: io_import_iovec (unshown standard importer) rejects iovecs whose total length exceeds MAX_RW_COUNT, so io_size = iov_iter_count(iter) is a small positive value; no quoted statement here bounds it below SSIZE_MAX but none can produce a larger value either.

io_iter_do_read consumes at most the current iov_iter count and returns at most that many bytes (characterizable read(2)-style semantics), so 'io_size -= ret' cannot underflow and 'io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)' passed to iov_iter_revert is always in [0, io_size].

io_setup_async_rw returns a nonzero errno on its allocation-failure arm and only returns 0 after req->async_data is allocated and populated; 'if (ret2) return ret2;' is therefore an effective NULL guard for the subsequent 'rw = req->async_data' deref.

io_setup_async_rw(..., true) takes ownership of the imported iovec (the code's own 'iovec = NULL;' bookkeeping and the comment-free return 'return ret ?: -EAGAIN' path are consistent with the transfer), so no double-free or leak is provable from this code.
limitations: Candidate (leak): 'if (ret2) return ret2;' after io_setup_async_rw has no kfree(iovec); if the unshown io_setup_async_rw fails without taking ownership, the kmalloc'd iovec could leak (CWE-401). Whether the error arm frees or adopts iovec is decided entirely inside the not-shown callee, so the trigger is not instantiated here.

Candidate (underflow): 'io_size -= ret' would go negative if a read returned more bytes than requested (ret > io_size passes the entry else-if chain, which only tests 'ret == io_size'). This needs a file/driver violating its buffer contract; not instantiable from characterizable callee semantics.
Candidate (bytes_done accounting): an over-returning read would also inflate rw->bytes_done and req->result accounting, but with no memory unsafety this is a robustness/accounting issue only.

Callee internals (io_import_iovec, io_setup_async_rw, io_iter_do_read, rw_verify_area, kiocb_done) are not shown; their memory-safety properties are assumed per standard kernel-function semantics, which is why confidence is not high.

verdict.summary: memslot_get_virt uses off-by-one bound checks (`>` instead of `>=`) for both group_id and slot_id, so exactly-at-limit values (group_id == num_memslots_groups, slot_id == num_memslots) pass and are used to index info->mem_slots one element out of bounds at `slot = &info->mem_slots[group_id][slot_id];`; slot->generation and slot->address_delta are then read from out-of-bounds memory and address_delta is added to the returned host pointer. QXLPHYSICAL addr/group_id come from the guest across the trust boundary, giving a guest-induced host out-of-bounds read.

evidence.reason: Off-by-one bound check: with num_memslots = N, slot_id = N yields `N > N` == false, so the one-past-the-end index passes validation and is used at line 22 to form `&info->mem_slots[group_id][N]`, reading slot->generation (line 25) and slot->address_delta (line 29) out of bounds; slot_id is derived from guest-controlled addr. Correct guard is `slot_id >= info->num_memslots`.

Sink: attacker-influenced indices (group_id parameter, slot_id derived from guest addr) are used to index mem_slots with no in-range check covering the exactly-at-limit value; the resulting OOB pointer is dereferenced for generation and address_delta before memslot_validate_virt runs.

Same off-by-one on the other index: group_id == num_memslots_groups passes (`g > g` false) and indexes mem_slots one row out of bounds at line 22; the guard must be `group_id >= info->num_memslots_groups` (plus a negative-value check).

assumptions: memslot_get_id/memslot_get_generation derive slot_id and generation from the guest-supplied addr, as in upstream spice-server; addr is guest-controlled across the VM trust boundary.
num_memslots / num_memslots_groups describe the actual row counts of info->mem_slots, so the exactly-at-limit index is one past the end.
limitations: A negative slot_id from the unshown memslot_get_id would also pass `slot_id > info->num_memslots`; upstream masks slot_id to nonnegative, which is not quotable here, so this variant is not counted as a separate defect.

The returned h_virt is consumed by callers not shown; whether the OOB-derived address_delta yields writes or disclosure beyond the direct OOB read of slot->generation/address_delta is outside this code.
A NULL `info` would crash the same-privilege process; no quoted contract, but this is a robustness issue at most.

verdict.summary: This static probe-helper allocates a control device with a checked kzalloc sentinel and a correct error arm. No attacker-data (no sizes, indices, offsets, strings, or protocol fields) reaches any sink; the only unchecked value, vdev->priv, is set by the same-file caller and its worst-case failure is a same-privilege NULL deref, which is a robustness issue, not a security impact.

assumptions: This static function is called only from rpmsg_virtio_probe in the same file, which assigns vdev->priv before the call; the assignment is not shown but the function is not part of the exported/callback/handler surface of discipline 4.

rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device follows the device_register contract: on failure it drops the last device reference, invoking rpdev_ctrl->dev.release (virtio_rpmsg_release_device), which frees vch — matching the in-code comment on the error path.
limitations: Candidate C1: vrp = vdev->priv is dereferenced without a NULL check; if a caller ever passed a virtio_device with NULL priv it would crash the kernel. The trigger is not instantiable from the given code, and the impact is a same-privilege crash with no corruption or disclosure, so it is a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

Candidate C2: if rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device failed without dropping the device reference, vch would leak on the error path; this depends on unshown callee behavior and is a bounded one-shot leak on a probe error path, not attacker-scalable.

verdict.summary: fname (and backup) are used directly as asprintf format strings; the code's own comment confirms the format string is user-controlled, giving an attacker a full %n/%s format-string primitive (memory corruption, arbitrary reads, unbounded allocation) at lines 7 and 17, with no guard anywhere in the function.

evidence.snippet:
if (asprintf(&logFileName, fname, idstring) == -1)
        FatalError("Cannot allocate space for the log file name\n");
evidence.reason: Root cause: user-controlled fname is passed as the asprintf format argument (the code comments admit it, lines 5-6). Trigger: fname containing %n/%s/%99999999d executes attacker format directives, enabling memory writes via %n, arbitrary pointer reads, and attacker-scaled allocation; the == -1 test guards only allocation failure, and no mention sweep statement validates fname.

Same defect, second sink: user-controlled backup (only NULL/emptiness-checked at line 10, never format-validated) is used as the format string, giving the identical attacker-controlled format-string primitive.

assumptions: The code's own comment (lines 5-6) is taken as authoritative: 'the format string below is controlled by the user' — no unquoted caller contract was used to dismiss the candidate.
asprintf is attributed GNU/vfprintf semantics: %n and %s process attacker directives and write/read through the varargs.
limitations: Memory leak of suffix if the second asprintf fails before free(suffix) at line 21 is a robustness issue, not a security impact.

Potential path manipulation of the remove/rename targets (lines 23, 31) is dominated by, and dependent on, the same attacker-controlled fname/backup inputs; it is not counted as an independent primary defect.

verdict.summary: mkiss_close correctly guards NULL (if (!ax) return;), synchronizes concurrent users via refcount_dec_and_test + wait_for_completion, and frees the AX.25 buffers only after unregister_netdev returns, which is the fixed ordering that prevents the historical double free of rbuff/xbuff between ndo_uninit and close. No attacker-representable input reaches an unguarded sink in this function.

assumptions: ax->dev/rbuff/xbuff are allocated in the not-shown mkiss_open path and are either all valid or the open failed without publishing disc_data.
ax->dead is completed by the final refcount holder in the not-shown receive/transmit put path, matching standard refcount+completion ldisc teardown semantics.
limitations: The historical double-free variant of this function (kfree before unregister_netdev) is not present here; this code shows the post-fix safe twin.

Potential races with concurrent receive/transmit paths (mkiss_receive_buf, mkiss_xmit) cannot be fully verified because those functions are not shown; the in-code synchronization protocol (write_lock_irq on disc_data, refcount_dec_and_test, wait_for_completion) is assumed to be mirrored there by ax_hold/ax_put.
A NULL ax->dev would crash, but no statement in this code can produce that state and it is not attacker-instantiable; at most a same-privilege robustness issue.

verdict.summary: mkiss_close() correctly guards every free-path use: ax is NULL-checked (line 10) before first dereference, and the quoted refcount_dec_and_test + wait_for_completion pair (lines 17-18) runs in execution order before netif_stop_queue, unregister_netdev, the kfree calls, and free_netdev, so no concurrent holder can exist when ax and its buffers are released. This code is the safe twin of the historical mkiss use-after-free; the missing guard that would make it vulnerable appears nowhere, and none is needed.

assumptions: ax->refcnt is initialized and incremented only by code paths that first obtain ax under disc_data_lock (mkiss_open/other mkiss entry points, not shown); the detach under write_lock_irq at lines 5-8 is the exclusion point this relies on.
The last refcount holder signals completion of ax->dead; ax is allocated as the netdev private area so free_netdev(ax->dev) releases ax itself.
limitations: If a holder-side path existed that used ax without taking a reference, the failure mode here would be an indefinite wait at wait_for_completion (hang), not a premature free, because free_netdev is only reached after refcount_dec_and_test returns true or the completion fires; that holder-side contract is in code not shown and cannot be verified here.

A historical variant of this function without the refcount/completion wait had a use-after-free on tty->disc_data; the quoted guard at lines 17-18 is that fix, so this snippet is judged as the safe twin.

verdict.summary: In the second argument-opening loop, do_arg_all() indexes AARGLIST(alist)[i] via alist_name() inside the do_ecmd() call using a bound (count/opened_len) snapshotted before the loop, while the argument list length (alist->al_ga.ga_len) can shrink when the autocommands fired by win_split()/do_ecmd() modify the arglist — a scenario this code itself anticipates. The first loop guards the identical access with 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len', but that check is absent on the path to line 254, yielding an out-of-bounds (and potentially use-after-free) read of an argentry whose ae_fname pointer is then dereferenced.

evidence.reason: Unguarded array access: i is bounded only by count/opened_len (clamped at lines 180-181 to opened_len, the ARGCOUNT snapshot), never against the live alist->al_ga.ga_len, although the do_ecmd() call on this very line and win_split() at line 239 run attacker-influenced autocommands that can remove arglist entries. With ga_len shrunk to 1 after iteration i=0, iteration i=1 reads AARGLIST(alist)[1] past the live array and dereferences its (possibly freed) ae_fname via alist_name(). The safe twin guard 'i < alist->al_ga.ga_len' (line 86) exists in the first loop but not here.

Origin of the stale bound: opened_len snapshots ARGCOUNT (ga_len) before any autocommands run; the comments at lines 49-51 and 179 ('ARGCOUNT may change while doing this, because of autocommands') confirm the live ga_len can drop below this snapshot during the loop, making every later i < count <= opened_len access to AARGLIST(alist)[i] out of bounds.

assumptions: autowrite(), win_close(), win_split() and do_ecmd() execute user-defined autocommands (standard vim semantics), so vimscript in loaded files/plugins is the attacker across the trust boundary.

When autocommands remove argument-list entries, the stale entry read past ga_len may hold an ae_fname pointer freed at removal time, making the read a potential UAF; the plain OOB read stands regardless.
limitations: Whether the not-shown arglist-mutation routines (e.g., :argdel handlers) honor arglist_locked (set at line 54) cannot be quoted from this code; per the last-line-of-defense rule this unquoted contract does not dismiss the defect, but it lowers confidence.
win_enter(lastwin, FALSE) at line 188 lacks a win_valid() check, but no concrete stale-pointer state could be instantiated from the given statements — not promoted.

Removing entries may only decrement ga_len without shrinking ga_data; in that case the read stays within the allocation but still consumes a stale/possibly-freed ae_fname, which keeps the impact a memory-safety read rather than a pure logic error.

verdict.summary: memslot_get_virt validates only the upper bound of the signed int parameter group_id ('group_id >= info->num_memslots_groups'); a negative group_id passes the check and indexes info->mem_slots[group_id][slot_id] out of bounds, causing OOB reads of slot->generation and slot->address_delta and returning an attacker-influenced host pointer derived from OOB memory.

evidence.reason: Sink: with group_id = -1 (representable in the signed int parameter's domain), the pointer is computed before mem_slots, and slot->generation (line 25) and slot->address_delta (line 34) are read out of bounds; the resulting h_virt is returned at line 41.

Origin of the defect: this is the only check on group_id and it tests only the upper bound; -1 >= num is false, so every negative value is admitted. The missing guard is a group_id < 0 test (or unsigned comparison).

assumptions: group_id originates from a guest/protocol command across the spice trust boundary, so its full signed int domain is instantiable per the width-domain rule.
memslot_get_id/memslot_get_generation return values derived from addr are treated per discipline 4; only group_id's trigger is fully instantiated within this code.
limitations: A negative slot_id from the unshown memslot_get_id(info, addr) would also bypass the line 16 upper-bound-only check, but the producer's range is not shown, so this stays speculative.
Whether callers write through the returned h_virt (potential OOB write) is not shown; the confirmed in-code impact is the OOB read of slot fields.

verdict.summary: No attacker-instantiable defect in this code. The array index ji->active_ag is guarded against its in-code sentinel (-1) before use, and the JFS allocation code that sets active_ag and sizes db_active is not shown, so an out-of-range index cannot be triggered by any statement quoted here.

assumptions: inode and its lifetime invariants are supplied by the trusted VFS layer; on-disk-derived fields (nlink, fileset) are consumed only through equality/sentinel checks that are present and correct.

ji->active_ag is maintained by the JFS allocator (not shown), which sizes db_active consistently with the AG index range it stores; no attacker-reachable producer of an out-of-range value is quoted in this code.
limitations: Speculative: db_active[ji->active_ag] (line 35) has no upper-bound check in this function; if any unshown code path could store an out-of-range active_ag, this would be an out-of-bounds atomic decrement — the producing statement and array sizing are outside the given code and could not be instantiated.
BUG_ON(!list_empty(&ji->anon_inode_list)) is a kernel panic on an internal invariant violation; triggering it requires an unshown lifetime bug, so it is robustness-only here.
Potential refcount underflow of db_active via mismatched increment/decrement across unshown allocation/eviction paths could not be evaluated from this snippet.

verdict.summary: The jfs_evict_inode handler validates every security-relevant use: the ipimap dereference and diFree call are protected by the quoted NULL test 'if (ipimap && JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap)', and the db_active[active_ag] decrement is protected by the sentinel test 'if (ji->active_ag != -1)' with active_ag produced only by in-kernel allocation paths. No attacker-data path (on-disk fileset/commit flags only steer between benign branches) reaches any sink unguarded, and no memory-corruption, disclosure, bypass, or scalable-consumption impact is instantiated.

assumptions: ji->active_ag is an in-memory field initialized to -1 at inode allocation and assigned only by kernel allocation paths (agno bounded by the block map), never read from disk; if a path existed that loaded it from attacker-controlled on-disk data, the check at 'if (ji->active_ag != -1)' would be insufficient (it tests only the sentinel, not the upper bound).
JFS_SBI(inode->i_sb)->bmap and ->ipimap are mount-lifetime objects freed only during unmount after all inodes are evicted, so a NULL bmap at line 38 is not instantiable from this code.
limitations: If ipimap is NULL (e.g., partially failed mount), diFree is skipped, leaking the inode's imap slot — a resource-accounting leak on an already-corrupt filesystem, not an attacker-scalable consumption primitive; no memory-safety consequence.

The worst-case on-disk 'fileset' value outside FILESYSTEM_I only causes the code to take the truncate-only branch; a leaked-inode DoS on a crafted filesystem was judged non-primary because no unbounded consumption loop is quoted.
The BUG_ON(!list_empty(&ji->anon_inode_list)) is an intentional kernel assertion on an internal list; it cannot be triggered by data shown in this code.

verdict.summary: This is the hardened form of Vim's do_cmdline(): every attacker-data sink reachable from statements in this code is protected by a quotable guard — loop-line indexing is bounded by 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0 && current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' (correct at both bounds, current_line provably >= 0 from 'cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] >= 0'), the :endwhile jump-back is guarded by the full 'cs_idx >= 0 && CSF_WHILE|CSF_FOR && cs_line >= 0 && CSF_ACTIVE' chain, fgetline/vim_strsave/do_one_cmd returns are NULL/FAIL-tested before use, breakpoint/dbg_tick pointer writes are NULL-guarded, and recursion is capped at 'call_depth >= 200'. The only unguarded statement, STRMOVE(cmdline_copy, next_cmdline), cannot be shown to overflow because the containment of do_one_cmd's return pointer within the cmdline_copy allocation is a callee contract not visible in this code, so its trigger is not instantiable here.

assumptions: cmdline content and fgetline-returned lines originate from the user/script author across a trust boundary (attacker-data).
STRMOVE is Vim's memmove-based overlapping-safe string move; the copy length equals strlen(next_cmdline)+1.
limitations: STRMOVE(cmdline_copy, next_cmdline): a heap overflow would require do_one_cmd to return a pointer outside the cmdline_copy allocation (or a string overrunning it); no statement in this code produces that state and do_one_cmd is not shown, so the trigger is speculative on an unshown callee.

cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx] = current_line_before is written with no local upper bound on cs_idx; cs_idx is only incremented inside do_one_cmd (not shown), so a stack-depth overflow is not instantiable from this code.

current_line is reassigned from cmd_loop_cookie.current_line (maintained by get_loop_line, not shown); a negative value from that callee would defeat the '< lines_ga.ga_len' guard's implicit lower bound, but no such value is producible here.
Unbalanced ++recursive/--recursive on a longjmp out of do_one_cmd would be a robustness issue only (same-privilege crash/reset), not a security impact.

verdict.summary: vsnprintf's return value (the would-be untruncated length) is stored in len without clamping to the 256-byte print_buffer, and the line-wrapping loop advances ptr by cut+1 while decrementing len by only cut, so for any formatted message longer than the buffer ptr walks past the end of the stack array; ptr[cut] (line 21) and fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) (line 25) then read and disclose out-of-bounds stack memory.

verdict.summary: The vhost-user GET_INFLIGHT_FD handler reads num_queues and queue_size directly from the socket message and computes mmap_size = num_queues * pervq_inflight_size without any upper-bound validation (no check against dev->nr_vring or a maximum queue size). A peer across the trust boundary can supply e.g. num_queues=65535, queue_size=2048 to request a ~4.3 GB mapping (up to ~137 GB at max field values); the NULL check on the allocation result passes for sparse mappings and memset(addr, 0, mmap_size) then forces every page resident, exhausting host memory of the vhost-backend process (attacker-scalable denial of service).

evidence.snippet:
mmap_size = num_queues * pervq_inflight_size;
	addr = inflight_mem_alloc(dev, "vhost-inflight", mmap_size, &fd);
evidence.reason: mmap_size is computed from fully attacker-controlled uint16 message fields with no bound check anywhere in the function (mention sweep found only fd-count, payload-size, NULL, and fd>=0 checks); the same unbounded value sizes the mapping and is consumed by memset(addr, 0, mmap_size) at line 60, forcing up to ~137 GB (65535 queues x 65535 descriptors) of resident memory — OOM/DoS of the host backend triggered by a socket peer.

Origin of the tainted values: both are read from the vhost-user message payload (full uint16 domain, instantiable by the socket peer) and no validation is applied between this assignment and their use as allocation/copy sizing.

assumptions: inflight_mem_alloc creates a sparse anonymous/memfd mapping sized to the requested mmap_size, which succeeds for multi-GB sizes under standard Linux semantics, so the !addr check does not fire; the memset then faults pages in (standard memset semantics).
get_pervq_shm_size_packed/split return sizeof(header) + queue_size*sizeof(desc-entry) per DPDK semantics, making the packed init loop exactly allocation-consistent (no OOB inside this function).
limitations: Possible out-of-bounds access if a later SET_VRING_NUM configures a vring larger than the queue_size used here — the consumer code (vhost_user_set_inflight_fd / vring processing) is not shown, so this cannot be instantiated in this code.
dev->virtqueue[0] could theoretically be NULL when nr_vring > 0; treated as crash-only same-privilege robustness, not a security verdict.
dev->ifname is printed with %s (no format-string defect); any log-forging impact depends on how ifname is set elsewhere and is not shown.

verdict.summary: cdf_read_property_info validates every attacker-derived value before use: offs is capped by 'offs > UINT32_MAX / 4' and cdf_check_stream_offset; sh_len is capped by CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT and stream-checked (e re-validated, p >= e rejected); sh_properties is capped by CDF_PROP_LIMIT and the inp array is grown from the same expression with NULL checked; property positions come from the checked cdf_get_property_info_pos with NULL tested before first use; the string loop guards 'o4 + sizeof(uint32_t) > left' before each length read and 'o4 + l > left' before publishing s_buf/s_len, which on 64-bit size_t provably confines all reads and string regions to [q, e). No primary trigger could be instantiated.

assumptions: size_t is 64-bit (LP64); on ILP32 the check 'o4 + l > left' could wrap for l near 0xFFFFFFFF with small o4, admitting a bogus s_len, but the wrap point is not representable in the modeled 64-bit size_t domain.
cdf_get_property_info_pos (not shown) validates the returned position q against the passed end pointer e and returns NULL otherwise; its NULL sentinel is checked here before first use.
CDF_SHLEN_LIMIT and CDF_PROP_LIMIT are compile-time constants small enough that left and o4 stay far below size_t wrap; cdf_grow_info reallocs with a NULL-failure sentinel that is checked.
cdf_copy_info is a bounds-checked helper receiving the end pointer e and returning failure, which this code tests.
limitations: C1 (speculative): on a 32-bit size_t platform, 'o4 + l > left' can wrap (e.g., o4=0x14, l=0xFFFFFFF8 -> 0xC <= left), storing pi_str.s_len ~4GB with an in-bounds s_buf; the out-of-bounds read would occur in downstream consumers of s_buf/s_len, which are not shown.

C2 (speculative): if cdf_get_property_info_pos ever returned q > e, 'left = e - q' would underflow to a huge size_t and defeat every later bound; this requires callee behavior contradicting its e-parameter contract and cannot be instantiated from the given code.

C3 (speculative): nelements up to 0xFFFFFFFF is passed to cdf_grow_info, causing a transiently huge allocation attempt; the NULL return is checked, so the worst case here is a failed allocation, and the write loop is capped by i < sh.sh_properties.
Downstream consumers of the returned info array (string printing, count handling) are outside this code and were not analyzed.

verdict.summary: No primary vulnerability: the disconnect teardown is correctly ordered (shutdown flag, cancel_delayed_work_sync, usb_kill_anchored_urbs/usb_kill_urb all precede the corresponding frees), and no attacker-controlled data, size, index, or output construction exists in this function. The only unguarded use is the unchecked return of usb_get_intfdata dereferenced at the first statement, a NULL-deref crash at most, on a speculative precondition, with no corruption, disclosure, or bypass impact.

assumptions: atusb and its fields (usb_dev, work, rx_urbs, tx_urb, hw) are initialized by a prior successful probe call not shown; disconnect is invoked by the USB driver core only after probe completion.
Standard callee semantics assumed: cancel_delayed_work_sync waits for completion, usb_kill_anchored_urbs/usb_kill_urb synchronize and reference the urb safely, usb_get_intfdata may return NULL.
limitations: Line 4 dereferences the usb_get_intfdata return without a NULL check; if disconnect could run without a successful probe, this is a kernel NULL-deref crash (CWE-476). Dismissed as speculative and same-privilege crash-only per the impact model.
The atusb_free_urbs, ieee802154_unregister_hw, and ieee802154_free_hw callees are not shown; any defect entirely inside them with no out-of-domain argument passed from here is out of scope.

verdict.summary: No fully instantiated vulnerability found. The dangerous sinks in this substitute implementation (the sub_firstline[matchcol] index at the lastone computation, the do_join call in the :s/\n// fast path, the needed_len allocation sizing, and the regmatch column arithmetic) are each covered by a quoted, execution-order-verified guard: sub_firstline is allocated and NULL-checked (goto outofmem) before any skip_match path can reach the index, joined_lines_count is gated by 'joined_lines_count > 1' rejecting zero/negative counts, new_start_len is sized from the same needed_len expression that bounds the subsequent memmove, and the exmode cursor column is clamped to 0. Remaining candidates require a malloc failure (unchecked vim_strsave result in the nmatch>1 path) or a ~2^31-byte line to wrap the int needed_len; both are OOM-robustness or unreachable-scale issues recorded in limitations.

assumptions: vim_regexec_multi/vim_regsub_multi keep regmatch.endpos[0].col within the length of the matched line and startpos[0].lnum within nmatch; this is standard-function semantics of the regex engine, not a quoted statement in this code.

getdigits parses only decimal digits, so its result is non-negative; the i<=0 handling at lines 354-357 with the 'e' flag or eap->skip can only yield an inverted (empty) line range, not a negative line count reaching a memory sink.
limitations: Speculative: 'needed_len' (int) = copy_len + (STRLEN(p1) - endpos[0].col) + sublen + 1 could signed-overflow if a single buffer line plus an inflated sublen (e.g. via a \= expression expanding the substitute) approaches 2^31 bytes; no quoted statement caps the line length or sublen, but the trigger needs an unexhibited wrap scale, so it is not confirmed.

Robustness: in the nmatch > 1 branch, sub_firstline = vim_strsave(ml_get(sub_firstlnum)) at line 592 is not NULL-checked; on malloc failure sub_firstline becomes NULL and is later indexed in the lastone computation. This requires an allocation failure sentinel and only crashes the same-privilege process (no corruption/disclosure), so per impact rules it is a robustness issue, not a verdict-deciding vulnerability.

The matchcol = (colnr_T)STRLEN(sub_firstline) - matchcol subtractions (lines 798-803) could wrap if matchcol exceeded the line length; that requires the regex engine to return an out-of-range endpos, which could not be instantiated without violating the callee contract noted above.

Behavioral quirk: ':s/pat//e 0' bypasses the positive-count error (do_error FALSE) and sets line2 = line1 - 1, producing an empty range with no memory-sink impact; treated as functional, not security.

verdict.summary: The ut32 accumulator total_slide_infos wraps when attacker-supplied slide-info counts (read raw from the dyld cache file) are summed, causing an undersized allocation while the inner loops keep writing infos[k] entries beyond it — a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled count and content.

evidence.reason: Unchecked ut32 addition of file-derived counts (rz_buf_read_le32_at at 0x13c+hdr_offset, full ut32 domain) wraps: e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF + 2 = 1, and this wrapped value sizes the allocation at RZ_NEWS0(..., total_slide_infos).

Heap out-of-bounds write: k is incremented for every crafted valid cache_mapping_slide entry bounded only by the unwrapped per-header count n_slide_infos[i]; no statement bounds k against total_slide_infos before these writes (the only k check, 'if (k < total_slide_infos)', executes after all writes). With the wrapped total = 1 and n_slide_infos[0] = 0xFFFFFFFF, infos[1], infos[2], ... are written past the single-entry allocation.

assumptions: rz_buf_read_le32_at and rz_buf_fread_at perform their own buffer bounds checking (they return failure sentinels that this code tests), so the read offsets are safe.
RZ_NEW0/RZ_NEWS0 return NULL on failure; all such returns are NULL-checked in this code.
limitations: cache->maps[1] is indexed when cache->hdr->mappingCount > 1, but the code that populates cache->maps from mappingCount is not shown, so an out-of-bounds read there could not be instantiated from the given code.

The inner loop breaks when the buffer read fails, so the OOB write requires the attacker to supply sufficiently many well-formed cache_mapping_slide records; this is fully attacker-controlled in the parsed file.
get_rebase_info internals are not shown; no defect was attributed to it.

verdict.summary: The vsnprintf return value (would-be length, unbounded up to INT_MAX) is used unclamped as loop/pointer-advance control over a 256-byte stack buffer; a formatted message longer than 255 bytes drives ptr past print_buffer, causing out-of-bounds stack reads via ptr[cut] and fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) whose contents are written to the output stream (information disclosure).

evidence.reason: Origin of the defect: vsnprintf returns the would-be formatted length (may far exceed sizeof(print_buffer)-1 = 255) while only 255 bytes are stored; no subsequent statement clamps len to the buffer size before it drives pointer advancement.

Out-of-bounds read sink: with len > 255 (e.g., a 1000-byte formatted message), the loop at lines 15/31 advances ptr by ~cut+1 per iteration past print_buffer+255 while len stays > 0, so ptr[cut] and the subsequent fwrite(ptr, cut+1, ...) at line 29 read stack memory beyond the 256-byte buffer and write it to config->errors.

assumptions: WARN_TEXTWIDTH is a positive constant (curl default 79); only its relative magnitude vs buffer size matters to the simulation.

The va_list arguments and fmt originate from callers not shown; per the width-domain rule, a formatted result of any length up to INT_MAX is treated as instantiable, which the standard semantics of vsnprintf fully support.
limitations: Double va_start(ap, fmt) at lines 9-10 without an intervening va_end is undefined behavior per the C standard; on common ABIs it merely re-initializes ap with no security impact, so it is not a primary finding.
config->errors is never NULL-checked before fputs/fwrite (lines 16/29/30/35); whether it can be NULL depends on unshown caller initialization, so no verdict is drawn from it.
The accounting mismatch (ptr += cut+1 but len -= cut, lines 31-32) over-extends the loop by one byte per iteration; it compounds the primary defect rather than constituting an independent one.
No write primitive beyond the 256-byte buffer exists; the impact is limited to out-of-bounds reading and disclosure of adjacent stack contents to the error stream.

verdict.summary: The only memory sink, r_anal_op(core->anal, &op, cur, buf + i, iend - i, ...), is fully guarded: the allocation malloc((size_t)iend + 2), the fill r_io_read_at(..., buf, iend + 1), and the sink length iend - i all use the same iend, which is bounded to [0, MAX_SCAN_SIZE] by 'if (iend < 0) return;' and 'if (iend > MAX_SCAN_SIZE) ... return;'. Every path that increases i (i += minopsize - 1, i += op.size - 1, get_next_i) reaches 'if (i >= iend) break;' before re-entering, and the sink is preceded in execution order by 'if (i > iend) { goto repeat; }'; even the boundary i == iend yields an in-bounds pointer with length 0, and the ut64-to-int truncation of iend cannot desynchronize i from iend because i is compared against the same truncated iend at full size_t width. All format strings are fixed; xref targets are validated with myvalid/r_io_is_valid_offset; callee failure sentinels (malloc, r_anal_get_fcn_in, r_syscall_get, r_reg_get_name) are tested. Residual issues are non-scalable error-path leaks and a stale ESIL hook/user pointer whose corruption use lies outside this code.

assumptions: MAX_SCAN_SIZE is a compile-time constant below INT_MAX-2 so that iend+1 and iend+2 cannot overflow int/size_t.
r_anal_op, when given len = 0, reads no bytes from buf, matching the standard decoder contract that it accesses at most buf[0..len-1].
get_next_i sets i within the range implied by ictx {start, end, fcn}; any value it produces is still caught by 'if (i > iend)' before the sink, so the conclusion does not depend on this assumption.
limitations: Early return on the kpcname path ('if (!kpcname || !*kpcname) ... return;') leaves ESIL->cb.hook_* installed and ESIL->user pointing at the dead stack frame ctx, and leaks buf and spname (CWE-401/562-style). The dangling-pointer corruption requires a later ESIL hook invocation not shown in this code, and the leak is a one-shot error path triggered by a register profile lacking a PC alias, so no fully instantiated security impact in this snippet.

ESIL is reassigned after r_core_cmd0(core, "aeim") without a NULL recheck; harm requires 'aeim' to destroy the ESIL instance that 'aei' just created — unshown callee behavior, no quoted statement produces NULL there.
core->anal->cur->arch is dereferenced without a NULL check ('if (!strcmp (core->anal->cur->arch, "arm"))'); with no arch plugin loaded this is a same-privilege NULL-deref crash, not corruption.

A decoder returning op.size far larger than the supplied length would make the 'for (fcn_i = i_old + 1; fcn_i <= i; fcn_i++)' loop at repeat: iterate op.size times before the i >= iend break — a potential slowdown (CWE-400), but depends on unshown decoder behavior.

The ut64-to-int truncation 'iend = end - start' (e.g., a function or length of 0x100000005) yields a truncated iend and thus analysis of the wrong/wrong-sized region; simulated values show all buffer accesses stay in bounds because the guard, allocation, and sink all share the truncated iend.
r_anal_op is called with len 0 when i == iend (guard uses '>' not '>='); the pointer buf+iend is within the iend+2 allocation and a len-0 read touches nothing, so no out-of-bounds access results.

verdict.summary: do_cmdline() defensively checks every sentinel (vim_strsave, fgetline, store_loop_line) with quoted failure arms that break before use; the lines_ga indexing sinks are covered by the in-execution-order guards 'cstack.cs_looplevel > 0 && current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' and 'lines_ga.ga_len > 0', and recursion is bounded by the verified 'call_depth >= 200 && call_depth >= p_mfd'. The two remaining unguarded-looking reads (breakpoint lines_ga[current_line] after jump-back, cs_pending[cs_idx] in the :finally branch) have no instantiable out-of-domain value from any statement shown in this code.

assumptions: store_loop_line()/get_loop_line() (not shown) append to lines_ga without shrinking it while cs_looplevel > 0; this monotonicity underpins the safety of the jump-back breakpoint read at '((wcmd_T *)lines_ga.ga_data)[current_line].lnum-1', which lacks a local 'current_line < lines_ga.ga_len' check.

CSL_HAD_FINA is only set by do_one_cmd (not shown) while executing ':finally' inside a ':try', i.e. with cstack.cs_idx >= 0, making the unchecked 'cstack.cs_pending[cstack.cs_idx]' read in the CSL_HAD_FINA branch safe in practice.
rewind_conditionals() and cleanup_conditionals() handle idx = -1 (from 'if (idx >= 0) --idx;') as a rewind-all sentinel per upstream semantics.
limitations: The breakpoint read '((wcmd_T *)lines_ga.ga_data)[current_line].lnum-1' after 'current_line = cstack.cs_line[cstack.cs_idx]' checks only '>= 0', not '< lines_ga.ga_len'; a defensive upper-bound check there would remove the dependence on unshown store_loop_line/rewind_conditionals contracts, but no concrete over-limit cs_line value could be instantiated from this code.

'current_line = cmd_loop_cookie.current_line' trusts do_one_cmd/get_loop_line (not shown) to keep the value in range; the next iteration's top-of-loop guard would still prevent an OOB access at the .line/.lnum read.

DOCMD_REPEAT can keep the do/while loop running as long as commands produce continuations (unbounded execution by design, e.g. :global); line_breakcheck()/got_int provide the user interrupt path, so no attacker-scalable consumption defect beyond normal script semantics.

A crash-only NULL-deref scenario at lines_ga.ga_data with ga_len == 0 in the jump-back block is unreachable because store_loop_line stores the :while line before looplevel > 0 can trigger the jump-back.

verdict.summary: atusb_disconnect consumes the return of usb_get_intfdata(interface) without any NULL sentinel check and dereferences it (first unconditional use: atusb->shutdown = 1), causing a NULL-offset read/write and kernel oops (denial of service) when disconnect runs with unset interface data.

evidence.reason: Sink: unconditional write through atusb, which is never checked for NULL; with atusb == NULL this writes at a fixed offset from NULL (kernel oops/DoS). The mention sweep found no `if (!atusb)` guard anywhere between the assignment and this first use.
Origin: unchecked callee return whose declared domain includes NULL; the value flows directly to the dereference at line 7 with no local sentinel test.

limitations: In practice the USB core serializes probe/disconnect per interface and does not call disconnect after a failed probe, so reaching atusb == NULL requires a lifecycle state guarded by an unshown caller contract; under the last-line-of-defense rule this unquoted contract cannot dismiss the unchecked sentinel.
dev_dbg at line 5 dereferences atusb->usb_dev only when debugging is enabled; the unconditional defect is the write at line 7, so the finding does not depend on debug configuration.
The write is a constant at a fixed struct offset from NULL; no attacker-controlled data or address is written, so impact is denial of service (kernel oops), not memory corruption.

verdict.summary: In get_lisp_indent(), the column-advance loop uses pos->col (a byte index of the matching bracket) as an iteration count while lbr_chartabsize_adv() advances the pointer by one multi-byte character per call. With multibyte characters on the bracket line the loop can exhaust the line and exit with *that == NUL; the else arm then executes 'that++' with no NUL check, moving one byte past the line's NUL terminator, and subsequent VIM_ISWHITE(*that) / *that reads and lbr_chartabsize* advances walk out of bounds through the heap line buffer (out-of-bounds read, CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Sink: 'that++' advances past the buffer when the preceding loop (line 97) exits with *that == NUL; VIM_ISWHITE(*that) and the following loops then read and advance out of bounds. Trigger instantiated: bracket line "é(" in UTF-8 gives pos->col=2 bytes but only 2 characters, so the loop consumes the NUL before col reaches 0; no NUL check exists between the loop exit and this increment.

Origin of the harmful value: col is pos->col, a byte index, but lbr_chartabsize_adv advances 'that' by one character (mb_ptr2len) per iteration, so the loop can run past the bracket to the line's NUL terminator and exit with *that == NUL while col > 0; the loop condition permits this exit state.

assumptions: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated heap buffer of the line, and lbr_chartabsize_adv advances the pointer by exactly one multi-byte character (vim semantics: *pp += mb_ptr2len(*pp)).
findmatch returns the byte-column of the actual bracket character, and get_lisp_indent runs on the originator-supplied buffer contents with 'lisp' indenting enabled.
limitations: Impact is limited to out-of-bounds reads (heap-buffer-overflow read / potential crash); no out-of-bounds write path was found.
The mis-indentation caused by the same byte-vs-character mismatch when the loop overshoots the bracket without hitting NUL is functional, not a security defect.
The quote/backslash skipping loops (lines 45-69) were checked and each escape step re-tests NUL before the outer for-increment; no defect found there.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled header values reach their sinks only through quoted, verified guards: user_length is bounded against GetBlobSize and the profile buffer is allocated from the identical expression as the read length; columns*rows is checked (cast-to-64-bit before multiply, no wrap) against blob size before SetImageExtent; the offset skip loop is EOF-bounded and re-checked; every callee sentinel (profile, quantum_info, q, SetImageExtent status, count!=length) is tested before use; all string copies are length-bounded and format strings are literals. The only residual candidates (quantum scratch buffer sizing for depth=0/>64) are decided inside unshown AcquireQuantumInfo/GetBytesPerRow and cannot be instantiated here.

assumptions: Standard ImageMagick API semantics: ReadBlob never writes more than the requested count; CopyMagickString copies at most length-1 bytes from the source regardless of source NUL; ThrowReaderException returns after destroying the image list.

AcquireQuantumInfo/SetQuantumPad size the quantum pixel buffer from the same image->columns/depth values used to compute `length`, so the ReadBlobStream sink is presumed adequately sized; this contract is not quotable in the given code.
limitations: A heap-overflow candidate in `ReadBlobStream(image,length,pixels,&count)` for extreme bits_per_pixel (e.g. 0 or 255) was not confirmable: the buffer extent and GetBytesPerRow behavior live in unshown quantum.c internals, so the impact chain could not be instantiated — recorded as speculative, not real.
The film-data section is additionally gated on `cin.file.user_length != 0`, which can skip parsing film metadata for otherwise-valid files; parse-skip only, no security impact.
`image->chromaticity.red_primary.x` is set from green_primary_chromaticity[0] (apparent upstream copy-paste quirk); cosmetic, not security-relevant.

verdict.summary: The archive-supplied entry name (odata->current_file->data) flows through _g_path_get_relative_basename into g_file_get_child as a raw path component with no NULL, absolute-path, or '..' traversal validation in this code; the constructed destination path can escape odata->edata->destination, and per the output-construction rule the tainted path construction itself is the vulnerability.

evidence.reason: Sink: an extraction destination path is constructed from base_name, derived from the attacker-controlled archive entry name odata->current_file->data, with no traversal/containment check (no rejection of NULL, absolute paths, or '..' components) anywhere between producer and sink; g_file_get_child appends the attacker string to the destination directory, allowing a name such as '../../.bashrc' to escape the extraction directory, and the resulting path is then queried and drives the overwrite decision via query_info_ready_for_overwrite_dialog_cb.

Taint origin: the archive entry name (attacker-data across the parsed-archive trust boundary) is the sole input to base_name; the callee is not shown and no statement in this code constrains its return to a traversal-free single path component.

assumptions: odata->current_file->data is an archive-supplied entry name (attacker-data per discipline 4: originator of a parsed file); the extraction flow with FR_OVERWRITE_ASK is reachable via normal archive extraction.
_g_path_get_relative_basename's behavior is not shown, so per discipline 1 it cannot be credited as a sanitizer guard.
limitations: A NULL return from _g_path_get_relative_basename would make g_file_get_child return NULL and cause a GLib warning/possible crash in query_info_async; this depends on an unshown callee returning NULL (CWE-476 robustness, same-privilege crash), not instantiated here.

The FR_OVERWRITE_ASK guarantee is silently forced to FR_OVERWRITE_YES at line 33 when current_file == NULL while file_list != NULL (fail-open of the ask-before-overwrite control), but this code contains no statement that produces that inconsistent state; the trigger could not be instantiated from the shown code alone.
Whether the traversing path also reaches an actual file write depends on the not-shown extraction command and callback; the verdict rests on the output-construction rule for the path built at line 8.
base_name is never freed (memory leak) — non-security.

verdict.summary: The extraction destination path is constructed via g_file_get_child(odata->edata->destination, base_name) from an archive-supplied filename whose content is never validated in this code; the only quoted guard (base_name != NULL) checks the failure sentinel, not path traversal, so a '../'-bearing archive entry yields a destination GFile escaping the intended extraction directory (path construction is itself the impact per the output-construction rule).

evidence.reason: Sink: file path built from attacker-influenced base_name (archive entry name) with no local traversal/containment validation; the NULL check at line 10 does not constrain path content, so an entry such as '../../.bashrc' instantiates a destination outside edata->destination.

Origin of the tainted value: attacker-controlled archive filename flows into base_name via a not-shown callee; per the last-line-of-defense rule its presumed sanitization is an unquotable contract and cannot serve as a guard.

assumptions: _g_path_get_relative_basename_safe and the async/callback extraction path are not shown; their sanitization and write behavior are assumed absent because they are not quotable in this code.
limitations: The actual file write occurs in the not-shown callback/extract path; per the output-construction rule the tainted path construction is treated as the impact, but exploitability of the write depends on that consumer.

Speculative: if current_file == NULL while overwrite == FR_OVERWRITE_ASK, overwrite is silently forced to FR_OVERWRITE_YES and extraction proceeds without asking — dismissed because no quoted statement produces that caller state.
base_name is never freed (minor memory leak, not a security impact).

verdict.summary: In the PseudoClass path, colormap_index is allocated with only MagickMax(image->colors+1, MaxMap) elements (line 26), but the final remap loop indexes it with ScaleQuantumToMap(GetPixelIndex(...)) whose domain is [0, MaxMap] inclusive — index MaxMap is a one-past-the-end heap out-of-bounds read; because the memset that initializes colormap_index runs only in the != PseudoClass branch, out-of-range pixel indices also read uninitialized heap into the output image. The sibling else-branch correctly allocates MaxColormapSize+1 entries, confirming the off-by-one.

evidence.reason: Origin: for PseudoClass images the buffer is sized MagickMax(image->colors+1, MaxMap) — when image->colors+1 <= MaxMap this yields only MaxMap elements (valid indices 0..MaxMap-1), one element short of the [0, MaxMap] inclusive index domain consumed at the sink. The else branch (line 29) uses MaxColormapSize+1, the safe twin.

Sink: for a PseudoClass image with image->colors=256 and a stored pixel index mapping to MaxMap (e.g. QuantumRange), ScaleQuantumToMap returns 65535 and colormap_index[65535] reads one ssize_t past the 65535-element heap buffer; indices in [colors, MaxMap-1] were never initialized (memset is skipped for PseudoClass), leaking uninitialized heap into the image output. No bounds check on this index exists anywhere in the function.

assumptions: Standard ImageMagick definitions: MaxMap = MaxColormapSize-1 (65535 for Q16) and ScaleQuantumToMap maps a Quantum into [0, MaxMap] inclusive, so the maximum index consumed at line 149 is MaxMap.

image->colormap was allocated by the decoder with at least image->colors entries (PseudoClass path, lines 99-111); this is an unquoted contract but does not affect the confirmed off-by-one at lines 26-27/149.
IntensityCompare only reorders colormap entries without modifying .alpha, so line 119 indexes stay within [0, colors-1].
limitations: Candidate dismissed as speculative: if image->colors==0 (e.g., zero-row image), line 111 writes colormap[0] into a zero-sized AcquireQuantumMemory result — trigger requires a 0-color image that decoders normally reject and is not quotable here.

The OOB read is a single ssize_t past the buffer (attacker-chosen index, value copied into pixel data); the uninitialized-read variant exposes a wider region but its disclosure value depends on heap layout not shown.

Severity limited to read/info-leak: the only OOB write in the pixel loop (line 81, colormap_index[intensity]) is reachable only in the != PseudoClass branch, whose allocation of MaxColormapSize+1 entries provably contains every reachable intensity.

verdict.summary: The BGP dynamic-capability parser validates every attacker-controlled length before use: the loop bound (pnt < end) covers each iteration's first read, pnt+3 > end guards the 3-byte header, hdr->length < sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) enforces a minimum capability length of 4, and pnt + hdr->length + 3 > end bounds the 4-byte memcpy. Simulating every representable hdr->length (0-255), including the boundary values 4 and exactly-at-limit remainders, no out-of-bounds read or write is reachable; the advance pnt += hdr->length + 3 guarantees loop progress. The remaining concerns (caller-provided length matching the buffer, bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int producing in-range afi/safi on success) rest on unshown code and are recorded as limitations, not primary findings.

assumptions: bgp_size_t is a 16-bit unsigned type and the caller passes a length that matches the actual message buffer size; the code consistently uses pnt+length as its sole bound.

bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int returns nonzero on invalid input and only writes afi/safi values that are valid indices into peer->afc_recv/afc/afc_nego when it returns 0; this code correctly tests the return and skips on failure.
limitations: If the caller passed a length larger than the actual buffer, reads such as action = *pnt would go out of bounds; no local guard can check buffer size, and this depends on the not-shown caller (bgp_capability_msg_parse is not the intake point for the raw stream).

If bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int could return 0 while writing out-of-range afi/safi, peer->afc_recv[afi][safi] would be an out-of-bounds write; this requires the unshown callee to violate its contract and is speculative.

The hdr->length < sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) error path returns BGP_Stop without calling bgp_notify_send, unlike the other error paths; this is a functional inconsistency, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: bgp_capability_msg_parse copies a fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) (4) bytes from pnt+3 while the only bounds check (line 43) validates just hdr->length attacker-controlled bytes; with a truncated capability (hdr->length=0, message ending at pnt+3) the memcpy reads 4 bytes past the end of the peer-supplied buffer (heap out-of-bounds read).

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: memcpy consumes a fixed 4 bytes at pnt+3 while the preceding check guarantees only hdr->length bytes; trigger = capability with hdr->length=0 and end==pnt+3, so 4 bytes are read past the attacker-controlled buffer end.

Origin of the defect: this check bounds the capability by the attacker-supplied hdr->length (0..255) instead of the fixed sizeof(struct capability_mp_data); it admits hdr->length < 4, leaving the subsequent 4-byte memcpy under-validated.

assumptions: sizeof(struct capability_mp_data) == 4 (2-byte afi, reserved, safi) per the struct's field usage (ntohs(mpc.afi), mpc.safi) and the known BGP capability layout.
hdr->length is a uint8_t (capability_header), so pnt + hdr->length + 3 cannot pointer-overflow.
limitations: Indexing peer->afc[afi][safi] relies on bgp_map_afi_safi_iana2int producing in-range internal afi/safi; its implementation is not shown (failure is checked at line 59 before use), so no finding is derived from it.
The 4-byte over-read is bounded and the leaked bytes are only used as afi/safi values for mapping and debug strings; no larger disclosure primitive is present in this code.

verdict.summary: No vulnerability: len is clamped to 400 before sizing the len+1 allocation, the fread length is bounded by the allocation, and the compaction loop plus terminator write provably stay in bounds for both even and odd lengths; all failure sentinels (malloc NULL, short read) are checked before use.

assumptions: cli_malloc behaves as a standard allocator: returns NULL on failure, allocates the requested size, per its usage here.
The FILE* f refers to the attacker-supplied scanned file, so any mis-located read via unchecked fseek stays within attacker-owned data.
limitations: The return value of fseek(f, ptr, SEEK_SET) is unchecked; on failure the string is read from the current stream position. This is a robustness/parsing-accuracy issue only (worst case wrong bytes from the same scanned file or a clean NULL return via the fread check), not a security impact.

For odd lengths the terminator is written at index (len+1)/2 rather than (len-1)/2, leaving one possibly-uncompacted region below it, but the index is provably in bounds and the string is NUL-terminated.

verdict.summary: This is the post-TALOS-CAN-0063 hardened version of ntpdc cookedprint: every write to bn/bv goes through atoascii with both a source cap (MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN) and an explicit destination size, the appended output_raw byte and NUL fit within bv[2*MAXVALLEN] by arithmetic (len <= 2*MAXVALLEN-2 so bv[len+1] <= last index), decodeuint's uval>3 check bounds the LP writes, snprintf bounds the OC case, and all decoder failure sentinels are tested before first use. No unguarded sink reachable with attacker-controlled ntpd response data was found.

assumptions: atoascii(src, src_cap, dst, dst_size) is a bounded, NUL-terminating converter respecting dst_size (its size parameter exists for this purpose); contract of an unshown callee.
decodearr caps the number of entries it writes to the 8-element lfparr it is given, per its (unshown) implementation.
nextvar yields NUL-terminated name/value tokens within the response buffer.
limitations: Speculative: decodearr receives lfparr[8] and &narr without an array-size parameter; if the unshown callee writes more than 8 entries, outputarr would read past lfparr. Trigger not instantiable from this code.
Speculative: if atoascii failed to NUL-terminate within dst_size, strlen(bv) could read out of bounds and bv[len+1] write out of bounds; contract not exhibited.
No caller is shown; analysis treats datatype/length/data/status as fully attacker-controlled per the width-domain rule, which only strengthens the guarded sinks.

verdict.summary: extract_archive_thread extracts archives (attacker-authored content) and passes archive_entry_symlink(entry) — an attacker-controlled symlink target string — verbatim to g_file_make_symbolic_link, with no relativization, containment check, '..' rejection, or absolute-path rejection. This lets an archive create a symlink inside the extraction destination pointing anywhere on the filesystem; subsequent parent-directory creation (g_file_make_directory_with_parents) and file replacement resolve intermediate path components through that symlink, so archive-controlled bytes can be written outside the destination.

evidence.reason: archive_entry_symlink(entry) is attacker-controlled archive content; a mention sweep shows this is its ONLY occurrence in the function, so no statement between production and use validates, relativizes, or bounds it (unlike pathname at line 44 and linkname at line 135, which are both routed through _g_path_get_relative_basename). Trigger: an archive entry {pathname:"evil", AE_IFLNK, symlink target:"/etc"} reaches this line with target = "/etc" verbatim, creating destination/evil -> /etc; later AE_IFREG entries under "evil/..." then create directories and write files through the symlink (g_file_make_directory_with_parents at line 106 follows symlinks in intermediate components; G_FILE_CREATE_REPLACE_DESTINATION at line 188 protects only the final component), writing attacker-controlled bytes outside the extraction destination — CWE-22.

Origin of the primary taint flow: this switch arm selects the unvalidated symlink-target path; archive_entry_symlink's value enters here directly from the parsed archive header with its full declared domain (any string) and no prior constraint in this code.

assumptions: The archive being read (via archive_read_open/load_data_read) originates from an untrusted party, so all archive_entry_* fields are attacker-data across a trust boundary.

verdict.summary: The buffer-size bound at `long long allocate = (long long) (size*count + pad+20)` is computed entirely in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic before the cast, so attacker-controlled TIFF `count` and type-derived `size` wrap mod 2^32 and produce an undersized DataBuf; the file-backed read `io.read(buf.pData_,count*size)` and the element-print loops then write/read out of bounds, yielding heap overflow with attacker-controlled content.

evidence.reason: Root cause: size*count + pad+20 is evaluated in uint32_t (size and count are uint32_t) and the (long long) cast applies after the wrap. With size=1 and count=0xFFFFFFFF, allocate wraps to 19. The undersized buffer is then used at the sinks below.

verdict.summary: cookedprint() appends two bytes to the fixed stack buffer bv[2*MAXVALLEN] using len = strlen(bv) with no bound 'len + 1 < sizeof(bv)'. bv is filled from attacker-controlled value (parsed from a remote server's mode-7 response by nextvar) via atoascii(value, MAXVALLEN, bv, sizeof(bv)), the only capacity bound this code supplies being sizeof(bv). evidence.reason: Two-byte append into the fixed stack buffer bv (char bv[2*MAXVALLEN], line 22) with no bounds check on len against sizeof(bv). Trigger: a remote server supplies a variable value that atoascii fills to the passed capacity sizeof(bv); with len = strlen(bv) = 2*MAXVALLEN-1, bv[len] overwrites the terminating NUL at the last in-bounds byte and bv[len+1] = '\0' writes one byte past the end of the array — an out-of-bounds stack write. The single missing guard is 'len + 1 < sizeof(bv)', which appears nowhere in the code.

Origin of the tainted buffer content: value is an attacker-chosen string extracted from the remote response by nextvar (line 31); this call fills bv with the only capacity constraint this code itself imposing being sizeof(bv), and no post-condition on strlen(bv) is checked before the append at lines 121-123.

assumptions: The attacker is the remote NTP server whose response is parsed: data/length are function parameters and name/value are nextvar out-params with no quoted contract, so their content and length are attacker-chosen (full width-domain model).
MAXVARLEN and MAXVALLEN are positive compile-time constants (not defined in the snippet), so bv holds 2*MAXVALLEN bytes and its capacity exceeds the MAXVALLEN source cap by MAXVALLEN bytes.
limitations: atoascii() internals are not shown; the exact maximum strlen(bv) depends on its implementation. Under a callee that strictly caps output at the src_len argument (MAXVALLEN characters), the append at lines 122-123 would remain in bounds; however, this code hands the callee the full sizeof(bv) capacity and performs the append with no local check, so per the last-line-of-defense rule the missing 'len + 1 < sizeof(bv)' guard is judged here.

Line 100 outputarr(fp, name, narr, lfparr) consumes the callee-produced out-param narr as a count over l_fp lfparr[8] without passing or checking the array capacity 8; if decodearr ever returns narr > 8 this is an out-of-bounds read, but the harmful indexing occurs entirely inside the not-shown outputarr, so it is recorded as a secondary concern, not the verdict driver.

If nextvar can return a NULL name or value, the decoders (decodets/decodenetnum/decodeuint) would dereference NULL; this is a same-privilege crash (robustness) only, not a security impact per discipline 3.

The out-of-bounds byte written is a NUL (or '?' for bv[len] at the last in-bounds index), so practical exploitability depends on stack layout; NTP rated the corresponding historical issue low severity.

verdict.summary: LZWDecodeCompat's interrupted-decode restart path copies decoded bytes with `do { *--tp = codep->value; ... } while (--occ);` without ever validating that occ (from the attacker-influenced tmsize_t parameter occ0) is positive. Origin/missing-check site: this is the only validation of occ before the restart copy loop, and it only rejects values that do not round-trip through long; it accepts occ0 == 0 (and, on 64-bit builds, negative occ0), so no statement constrains occ to the positive domain the copy loops require.

assumptions: The decoder is invoked by the TIFF read path with occ0 derived from attacker-controlled image/strip dimensions, so occ0 = 0 is instantiable per the parameter's declared tmsize_t domain; no caller-side rejection of occ0 == 0 is quotable in this code.

LZWCodecState (sp) fields persist between decode calls of the same TIFF read, so the dec_restart/dec_codep state set by a previous call is attacker-arrangeable via a crafted LZW stream (quoted statements: `sp->dec_codep = codep;` and `sp->dec_restart = occ;`).

Chain walks (`while (codep->length > occ);` and the restart walks) dereference codep->next without NULL checks; under a corrupted table this can dereference NULL, but the writes are otherwise bounded, so this is at worst a same-privilege crash given the corrupted-table precondition, not the primary defect.
The main-loop copy paths were verified safe: `while (occ > 0)`, `if(codep->length == 0)`, and `if (codep->length > occ)` correctly bound all writes there, including the exact boundary length == occ.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: if setuid() fails (e.g. EAGAIN under an attacker-set RLIMIT_NPROC), the code only logs and continues, and then unconditionally executes 'current_user.euid = current_user.uid', recording the de-privileged identity while the kernel effective uid remains elevated. The only abort path is compile-time optional (#if EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) and covers only EAGAIN; setgid() failure has no abort at all.

No conditional, sentinel test, or abort protects these assignments.

Origin of the trigger: setuid() failure (attacker-forced, e.g. EAGAIN by exhausting RLIMIT_NPROC) is only logged; the sole exit arm is compile-time optional and restricted to EAGAIN, so any other errno — and every setgid failure (line 14, which has no exit at all) — falls through with privileges retained.

assumptions: disable_priv_mode is invoked to drop privileges from an elevated effective uid (setuid-installed shell), as the function name, current_user.euid field, and historical bash usage (CVE-2002-0572) indicate; under that context the failure sentinel of setuid is attacker-instantiable by a local unprivileged user.
limitations: If compiled with EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE, the EAGAIN setuid case is mitigated; the finding survives via setgid (no abort path at all) and any non-EAGAIN setuid errno.
current_user.uid/gid/euid values originate outside this snippet; only the failure-sentinel handling of the setuid/setgid returns, which is fully shown, drives the verdict.

verdict.summary: When a TGS request carries no server principal name, tgs_build_reply calls _kdc_set_e_text(r, "No server in request") passing the attacker-controlled request realm buffer (r = b->realm, a char*) in place of the function's const char **e_text output parameter.
