The referral 'goto server_lookup' retry could loop if the HDB backend repeatedly returns HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM for the reconstructed krbtgt principals; requires unshown backend behavior.
clientdb/s4u2self_impersonated_clientdb rely on _kdc_db_fetch setting its out-parameters on success; all uses are gated by client != NULL, so no instantiated defect.
The overflow content is a read-only string-literal pointer rather than attacker-chosen bytes; exploitability depends on heap layout, but the out-of-bounds write itself is fully instantiated.

verdict.summary: PHP's openssl_decrypt consumes fully attacker-controlled data, method, password, and IV, but every memory sink is sized from the same expression as the copy (outbuf = data_len + block_size + 1 for a decrypt output that cannot exceed data_len), the key-padding branch provably copies password_len bytes only when keylen > password_len, and the later EVP_CIPHER_CTX_set_key_length(password_len) is reachable only in the branch where key aliases a password_len-byte buffer. Remaining issues (unchecked emalloc results, unchecked EVP_DecryptUpdate return, IV length validation delegated to php_openssl_validate_iv, ~2GB int overflow in outlen) are not instantiable with in-domain attacker input without an unshown callee contract violation or produce at most a same-privilege crash.

assumptions: php_base64_decode always writes its out-param base64_str_len (standard API contract relied on by all callers); a NULL return therefore yields data_len = 0, which is inert at EVP_DecryptUpdate.

php_openssl_validate_iv (same module, unshown) pads or validates iv to EVP_CIPHER_iv_length before returning; the free_iv/efree(iv) protocol evidences this, but its postcondition is not quotable here.
Stock OpenSSL EVP semantics: decrypt update+final combined output never exceeds input length, and EVP_DecryptUpdate sets *outl on all in-domain (inl >= 0) paths for EVP_get_cipherbyname ciphers.
limitations: emalloc return values (key, outbuf) and the php_base64_decode NULL return are not checked; on allocation failure this is a NULL-dereference crash of the same-privileged process handling the request (robustness, not corruption), and a NULL base64 result only yields data_len = 0.

If php_openssl_validate_iv failed to pad a short attacker-supplied IV, EVP_DecryptInit_ex would over-read the IV buffer (heap over-read); the helper's behavior is not shown, so this candidate could not be instantiated from this code alone.

data_len near INT_MAX (~2GB input) could wrap outlen = data_len + block_size before emalloc; building such a string already costs ~2GB attacker memory and the wrapped huge allocation fails before any write, so no overflow primitive is instantiated.
EVP_DecryptUpdate/EVP_DecryptInit_ex return values are unchecked; no in-domain input (data_len >= 0, standard ciphers) reaches a failure path that leaves the out-length i unset in stock OpenSSL.
Zero-padding short passwords to keylen is weak-crypto-by-design (user-supplied key material), not a defect introduced here.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode() continues execution and unconditionally records 'privileges dropped' (current_user.euid = current_user.uid; current_user.egid = current_user.gid) even when setresuid/setuid or setresgid/setgid fails; only an optional, EAGAIN-only exit exists on the uid failure path, so on any other failure errno (or a build without EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE, or any gid failure) the process keeps running with elevated effective privileges while its internal state claims de-escalation — a fail-open security-state misrepresentation.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the de-escalated state is written unconditionally after the set*id failure blocks (lines 10-17, 23) which only log via sys_error; the sole exit arm (lines 13-15) is compile-time optional and restricted to errno == EAGAIN. Trigger: a setuid-root shell where setresuid fails (e.g. EPERM, or EAGAIN on a build without EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE) — control reaches lines 25-26, so current_user.euid/egid claim the real ids while the kernel still holds euid 0, causing all privilege checks keyed on current_user.euid to fail open.

assumptions: current_user is bash's global user state struct; current_user.uid/gid are trusted values obtained at startup.
sys_error is a logging wrapper that does not terminate the process (no exit/abort quoted in this code).
limitations: Actual exploitation requires the program to be running with elevated effective privileges (e.g. a setuid-root bash) and an environment that makes setresuid/setuid fail; the escalation of the misreported state depends on downstream consumers of current_user.euid not shown here, but the fail-open state write itself is the defect.

If the deployment always compiles with EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE and errno can only ever be EAGAIN on failure, the uid path would exit; the gid path at line 19-23 still falls through on any failure, so the defect persists.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode indexes the CDEF box's ents[] array with a loop bounded by dec->numchans (derived from the code stream or CMAP box, independent of the CDEF box's own entry count) and indexes the BPCC box's bpcs[] array with a loop bounded by the image component count while the only cross-check merely warns; both produce heap out-of-bounds reads on attacker-supplied JP2 files.

evidence.reason: Root cause: the loop bound dec->numchans is the image/CMAP channel count, not the CDEF box's own entry count; no statement in the file compares i (or dec->numchans) to dec->cdef->data.cdef.numchans. Trigger: a JP2 file whose code stream yields 100 components (dec->numchans=100) and a CDEF box declaring numchans=1 makes iterations i>=1 read ents[i] out of bounds; the >= check at line 309 tests the already-out-of-bounds value, and passing values cause further OOB reads of .type/.assoc at lines 316-317.

Origin of the tainted loop bound: dec->numchans is derived from the attacker-controlled CMAP box or code-stream component count, fully independent of the CDEF box's own numchans/entry allocation, and is later used at line 307 to index dec->cdef->data.cdef.ents[].

Root cause: the loop bound is the image component count while bpcs[] is sized by the BPCC box's own numcmpts; the only cross-check (line 172) prints a warning without returning. Trigger: a BPCC box with numcmpts=1 plus a code stream of 10 mixed-precision components makes samedtype false, and i=1..9 read bpcs[i] out of bounds.

assumptions: The not-shown box parser (jp2_box_get and per-box data loaders) sizes the ents[] and bpcs[] arrays from each box's own declared count fields (standard JasPer box semantics); this code itself performs no such sizing, so the mismatch between dec->numchans/numcmpts and the box arrays is unvalidated at these sinks.
jpc_decode returns an image whose numcmpts and per-component dtypes are fully attacker-controlled via the embedded code stream.
limitations: Direct CMAP mapping (line 272) stores channo into dec->chantocmptlut while line 240 validates only cmptno, so with cmap.numchans > image numcmpts an out-of-range component index can be passed to jas_image_setcmpttype (lines 313/321); the memory use occurs inside the not-shown callee with no quotable bounds contract, so it is not instantiated as a primary finding here.

lutents (line 274) is the unchecked return of jas_alloc2 used as the write target at line 276 — a NULL dereference on allocation failure only; same-privilege crash, no corruption/bypass, robustness issue.
assert(dec->image->cmprof_) at line 212 aborts (or vanishes under NDEBUG) when jas_cmprof_createfromiccprof returns NULL — robustness issue only.
cdefd = &dec->cdef->data.cdef at line 268 computes an address through a possibly-NULL dec->cdef pointer but performs no memory access and is used only inside the compiled-out #if 0 block.

verdict.summary: tccp->maxrlvls is set directly from the attacker-controlled encoder option string via atoi() with no upper bound anywhere in the function, then used as the loop bound writing the fixed-size arrays tccp->prcwidthexpns[]/prcheightexpns[]; the only validation, 'if (cp->tccp.maxrlvls < 1)', checks the wrong direction and executes after the writes, allowing a heap out-of-bounds write of up to attacker-chosen length.

evidence.reason: Loop bound tccp->maxrlvls is a raw attacker-controlled int (option numrlvls=1000 → 1000) with no upper-bound guard; it indexes fixed-size array members of the heap-allocated jpc_enc_cp_t, so every iteration past JPC_MAXRLVLS writes out of bounds (CWE-787). The later check at line 376 only rejects maxrlvls < 1 and runs after the loop.
Origin of the tainted loop bound: the encoder options string value is converted with atoi() (full int domain, e.g. 1000) and stored into tccp->maxrlvls with no range validation at the intake point.

assumptions: prcwidthexpns[]/prcheightexpns[] are fixed-size members of jpc_enc_tccp_t declared in jpc_enc.h (JPC_MAXRLVLS entries); any fixed bound is exceeded by an attacker-supplied int.
optstr is attacker-influenced (application-supplied encoder options), so its values fall under the full parseable domain.
limitations: cp->numtiles = cp->numhtiles * cp->numvtiles (line 317) can overflow uint_fast32_t, and unsigned wraps in 'cp->tilegrdoffx + cp->tilewidth < cp->imgareatlx' (line 305) and in imgareatlx *= hsteplcm can be induced, but their consuming sinks (tile allocation) lie in code not shown here.
cp->tccp.numgbits is validated only with '> 8' (line 382); negative values pass, but the shift/consuming use is outside this function.

jpc_atoaf-supplied ilyrrates are matched exactly by the jas_alloc2 count, so the ilyrrates copy loops are within bounds; the numlyrs > 16384 check occurring after the copy is harmless because allocation and copy use the same count.

verdict.summary: cp_create() parses the attacker-supplied options string and stores OPT_MAXRLVLS via atoi without a lower-bound check (`if(tccp->maxrlvls > JPC_MAXRLVLS)` passes every negative value). The negative maxrlvls then becomes the loop bound in `for (rlvlno = 0; rlvlno < tccp->maxrlvls; ++rlvlno)` where rlvlno is uint_fast16_t: the signed -1 converts to a huge unsigned value, so writes of prcwidthexpns[rlvlno]/prcheightexpns[rlvlno] proceed far past the 33-element arrays inside the heap-allocated cp, a heap out-of-bounds write. The existing `maxrlvls < 1` rejection at line 380 executes only after the overflowing loop and cannot protect the sink.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write sink: rlvlno (uint_fast16_t) compared against attacker-controlled signed maxrlvls; with maxrlvls = -1 (numrlvls=-1 in optstr) the comparison converts to unsigned (0xFFFFFFFF) and the loop writes past the JPC_MAXRLVLS-element prcwidthexpns/prcheightexpns arrays in the jas_malloc'd cp, corrupting the heap.

Origin of the tainted value and the defective one-sided guard: atoi can return -1 (or any negative), which passes the upper-bound-only check `> JPC_MAXRLVLS`; the lower-bound rejection (`maxrlvls < 1`, line 380) is unreachable before the loop at lines 286-289 executes.

assumptions: The struct fields maxrlvls, prcwidthexpns, and prcheightexpns are declared signed int and sized JPC_MAXRLVLS respectively (implied by the code's own signed comparisons `maxrlvls > JPC_MAXRLVLS` and `maxrlvls < 1`, but the struct definition is not shown).
JPC_MAXRLVLS is 33, the standard JasPer constant.
optstr is attacker-influenced (encoder options supplied by the caller of the public encode API / CLI).
limitations: numgbits set via atoi is checked only with `> 8`; a negative value passes and is consumed by later encoding stages not shown in this code — downstream impact not instantiated here.
tilewidth/tileheight via atoi and the numhtiles*numvtiles multiplication (line 321) can wrap or go negative; any resulting miscalculation is consumed by encoding code not shown.
cp->imgareatlx *= hsteplcm can overflow unsigned, but exploitation requires downstream behavior not shown.
Repeated OPT_ILYRRATES options leak the previously allocated ilyrrates buffer; memory leak only, no security impact instantiated.

verdict.summary: In the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write and I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL paths, the attacker-supplied SMBus byte count data->block[0] (u8, 0-255) is never bounds-checked before being used as the memcpy length into the fixed DMA scratch buffer, unlike the I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA case which clamps it to I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX. With block[0]=255 the u8 assignment dma_size = data->block[0] + 1 wraps to 0 and dma_size - 1 becomes SIZE_MAX, producing a massive out-of-bounds write/read (kernel memory corruption); with intermediate values the copy overflows the ~33-byte DMA buffer and reads past the 34-byte i2c_smbus_data union.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled byte count data->block[0] (full u8 domain 0-255 via the SMBus API) is used as the DMA copy length with no bounds check on this path; at 255 the u8 store truncates 256 to 0, setting up the wrapped length at the sink.

Sink: with data->block[0]=255, dma_size=0 so dma_size-1 converts to (size_t)-1 and memcpy copies SIZE_MAX bytes into the fixed DMA buffer — unbounded out-of-bounds write and read. With block[0] between 33 and 254 the copy of up to 255 bytes overflows the ~33-byte buffer and reads past the 34-byte union. No statement on this path constrains block[0]; the clamp exists only in the unreachable I2C_SMBUS_I2C_BLOCK_DATA case.

Second instance of the same missing guard: in I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_PROC_CALL the raw attacker value data->block[0] (up to 255) is used directly as the memcpy length into the DMA scratch buffer sized for I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX (32) byte transfers, an out-of-bounds write of up to ~220 bytes into adjacent ismt_priv state.

assumptions: data->block[0] originates from the i2c SMBus request path (e.g. userspace i2c-dev ioctl) and is bounded only by its u8 width; no validation is performed in this function.
union i2c_smbus_data.block is I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX+2 = 34 bytes per the standard i2c header; memcpy semantics (copies exactly n bytes) per discipline 3.
limitations: sizeof(priv->buffer) is defined outside this snippet; for buffer sizes below 256 bytes the overflow is concrete, and the block[0]=255 truncation to a SIZE_MAX-length memcpy is an unconditional corruption primitive regardless of buffer size.
Post-processing of received block data inside ismt_process_desc (not shown) may contain additional length handling; out of scope of this code.

verdict.summary: decode_errcode_attr derives the copy length from the attacker-controlled 16-bit attribute length (hdr.length - 4) and passes it to pj_strdup, which copies that many bytes from the message buffer. Only a negative-length clamp exists; nothing bounds the length against the actual message buffer size (msghdr is explicitly unused), so a declared length up to 65535 on a short message causes a heap out-of-bounds read of up to ~64KB, with the over-read data stored into attr->reason (potential disclosure) or a crash.

evidence.reason: Sink: pj_strdup allocates and memcpy's value.slen bytes from value.ptr (buf+8). With a truncated STUN message declaring attribute length 0xFFFF, slen = 65531 and the copy reads ~64KB past the message buffer — out-of-bounds read. No statement bounds slen against the message size; the only check (line 21 'if (value.slen < 0)') clamps negatives only.

Origin: slen is computed directly from the attacker-controlled 16-bit attribute length (0-65535) with no upper-bound validation; the following clamp handles only length<4, so the in-range attack value 65531 flows unchanged to pj_strdup.

assumptions: GETATTRHDR reads the attribute header from buf, setting hdr.length from a 16-bit field (standard pjnlib semantics); full domain 0-65535 is instantiable by a network peer.
pj_strdup allocates slen bytes and copies exactly slen bytes from value.ptr (standard pjnlib/pj_str semantics).
limitations: The upstream pjnlib message parser (not shown) typically validates attribute length against the remaining message size before dispatching to attribute decoders; if that check exists, the OOB read is unreachable in the full program. Per analysis rules this unquoted contract cannot dismiss the defect at this intake point, but it reduces confidence.

attr->err_code = buf[6]*100 + buf[7] can exceed 699 (buf[6] up to 255) and buf[6]/buf[7] are read even when length < 4; these are functional value-correctness issues, not security impacts, so they do not affect the verdict.
The negative-length case (length < 4) is correctly handled by the quoted clamp 'if (value.slen < 0) value.slen = 0;'.

verdict.summary: Thin packet-dispatch wrapper: buf/size (guest-derived) are only passed through to qemu_send_packet or the loopback receive callback; no local memory access, sizing, arithmetic, or output construction consumes them, and the register test uses a compile-time-constant index. No defective use exists in this code.

assumptions: s->macregs[MAC_XIFCFG >> 2] is indexed with a compile-time-constant register offset, so the array access is fixed and safe.

buf/size arrive as an already-formed packet (pointer,length) pair, which is the in-domain argument type of qemu_send_packet and NetClientState.receive; the packet is assembled/DMA'd in code not shown here.
limitations: nc from qemu_get_queue(s->nic) is dereferenced at nc->info->receive without a sentinel test (line 7); if the NIC were unattached this would NULL-deref, but s->nic attachment is producer state not shown and the worst case is a same-privilege crash, so it is a robustness note, not a verdict.

Validation of size against the guest TX descriptor / NET_BUFSIZE happens in the packet-assembly code, which is not part of this snippet; if that (not-shown) code fails to bound size, the overflow would land inside the callee, not here — cannot be instantiated from this code.

verdict.summary: In the GLOB_TILDE ~user expansion, the user_name buffer is sized end_name - dirname (bytes up to the first '/'), but the backslash-unescape loop copies until the string's NUL terminator, writing everything after that '/' past the end of the buffer. A pattern like "~a\b/CCCCCCCC/d" passed to glob() with GLOB_TILDE and escapes enabled causes an attacker-length, attacker-content out-of-bounds write (heap via malloc for large sizes, stack via alloca for small ones).

verdict.summary: The bookmark command line is built for execution by /bin/sh -c with title, description, and feed_title inserted into single-quoted shell slots after only stfl::quote (an unquoted stfl-UI quoting helper); unlike url (line 12), their single quotes are never neutralized, so a feed-supplied title containing ' closes the shell quoting and injects arbitrary commands (CWE-78).

evidence.snippet:
std::string cmdline = strprintf::fmt("%s '%s' %s %s %s",
		                                       bookmark_cmd,
		                                       utils::replace_all(url,"'", "%27"),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(title)),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(description)),
		                                       quote_empty(stfl::quote(feed_title)));
evidence.reason: Shell command constructed from attacker-controlled feed fields: url has its single quotes replaced with %27 (line 12), but title, description, and feed_title are only passed through stfl::quote/quote_empty, which are not shell quoting and are not shown to remove single quotes. A title like "'; cmd; '" breaks out of the '%s' single-quoted context, and the resulting cmdline is executed by /bin/sh -c (lines 27-29), yielding arbitrary command injection.
Sink: the tainted cmdline (containing unneutralized single quotes from feed title/description/feed_title) is executed via /bin/sh -c, instantiating the command-injection impact.

assumptions: stfl::quote and quote_empty are not shown; they are stfl UI-layer helpers with no quoted shell-escaping guarantee, so per guard-anchoring rules they cannot serve as guards for single-quoted shell context.
bookmark-cmd is user configuration and assumed non-empty and attacker-uninfluenced; url is sanitized at line 12 and excluded from the trigger.
limitations: The interactive path (utils::run_interactively, line 22) executes the same tainted cmdline and is equally affected; only one CWE is reported since it is the same defect.
The DEBUG log of cmdline (line 17) could enable log forging but is a consequence of the same construction, not an independent defect.

verdict.summary: The libcurl header callback treats the delivered network buffer `ptr` as a NUL-terminated C string while never bounding any read by the delivered length (`nmemb`). curl header-callback data is not NUL-terminated, so strncasecmp (lines 11/13), sscanf (line 16), and snprintf's %s (line 22) read past the end of the delivered chunk into adjacent heap memory; the over-read bytes are copied into url->errormsg (line 22), an info-disclosure sink, and the prefix comparisons can read attacker-chosen lengths past the buffer.

evidence.reason: Primary sink: ptr is the non-NUL-terminated header chunk delivered by the network peer; the %s source is read up to sizeof(errormsg) bytes from ptr+22 with no bound by nmemb, copying heap memory past the chunk into url->errormsg (out-of-bounds read / disclosure). Trigger: a response line 'icecast-auth-message: x\r\n' shorter than sizeof(errormsg), no NUL in the delivered data.

Secondary sink of the same defect: strncasecmp reads up to config-controlled auth_header_len bytes from the delivered chunk with no check that nmemb >= auth_header_len and no NUL terminator; a header line shorter than auth_header_len causes a read past the buffer.

Origin of the taint and the sole mention of nmemb: attacker-controlled, non-NUL-terminated response bytes (ptr) and their length (nmemb) enter here; bytes = size*nmemb is computed and returned but never used to bound any read of ptr, which is the exact missing guard.

assumptions: The callback is installed as a libcurl CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION, whose documented contract delivers data that is not NUL-terminated and whose length is exactly size*nmemb; this standard-API semantic, not a quoted line, establishes the missing-termination premise.
limitations: size * nmemb (line 4) can theoretically wrap, but curl invokes header callbacks with size==1 and a wrap would only misreport consumed bytes and abort the transfer, with no memory-safety impact.

sscanf %u at line 16 lets the peer set discon_time via a up-to-2^32-1 value; this is a functional/integrity nuisance on an already-authenticated session, part of the same unbounded-read pattern, not a separate primary defect.
If stream (auth_user) were NULL the function crashes, but stream is supplied by the local caller configuration, not across a trust boundary; same-privilege robustness issue only.

A full auth bypass via the strncasecmp over-read would additionally require adjacent heap bytes to match the expected header text, which is a low-probability instance of the same OOB-read primitive, not a separate finding.

verdict.summary: STUN ERROR-CODE attribute decoder computes value.slen = attr->hdr.length - 4 without any minimum-length check; an attacker-supplied attribute length of 0-3 underflows to a negative pj_slen_t, which pj_strdup treats as non-zero and passes to pj_pool_alloc/pj_memcpy as a huge unsigned size, causing massive heap out-of-bounds read/write and remote crash of the STUN-handling process.

evidence.reason: Root cause: attacker-controlled 16-bit attribute length (read at line 13 via GETATTRHDR, no lower-bound check anywhere) is decremented by 4 with no guard; length=0 yields slen=-4, which the copy at line 22 converts to a huge unsigned size.
Origin of the tainted value: reads the attribute length directly from the attacker-controlled network buffer with no validation; with hdr.length < 4 the subsequent subtraction at line 19 underflows.
Sink: pj_strdup sees non-zero slen (-4), allocates (size_t)-4 bytes and memcpys that many bytes from buf+8, producing a giant out-of-bounds read/write and crash on a single malformed STUN message.

assumptions: pj_strdup/pj_pool_alloc follow standard pjlib semantics: a non-zero (including negative) slen drives allocation and memcpy of that many bytes after conversion to unsigned pj_size_t.
pj_str_t.slen is a signed type (pj_ssize_t), so length - 4 for length < 4 stays negative rather than wrapping small.
limitations: Reading buf[6]/buf[7] when hdr.length < 4 can read up to a few bytes past the attribute value area (usually STUN padding); it is a minor consequence of the same missing check, not a separate finding.

If the parent message decoder (not shown) rejects attributes with length < 4, this trigger would be blocked, but no such check is quotable in this code and this function is the intake point for the attribute value.

The practical impact is a huge failing allocation followed by an enormous memcpy; depending on pool allocator behavior this manifests as a failed allocation with NULL-dereference/crash or direct heap corruption — both are remotely triggerable.

verdict.summary: In LZWDecodeCompat, the 'restart interrupted output' path performs a backward copy with a post-tested do-while (`do { *--tp = codep->value; codep = codep->next; } while (--occ);`) without any occ>0/emptiness check. The main decode loop is guarded by `while (occ > 0)`, but the restart block runs before it and returns at line 46, so a decode call with occ==0 (in-domain for the tmsize_t handler parameter) while dec_restart != 0 makes tp = op + 0 and the first iteration write op[-1] — an out-of-bounds heap write of attacker-influenced decoded bytes before the output buffer (then a NULL deref when the chain ends).

verdict.summary: hdr.nSubrects (32-bit, server-controlled) is bounds-checked against RFB_BUFFER_SIZE only through a wrapping 32-bit multiplication; a value such as 0x20000000 (BPP=32) wraps the product to 0 (or a small value), bypassing the check, so the decode loop reads far past client->buffer (out-of-bounds read) and passes the results to GotFillRect.

evidence.reason: The only bounds guard on the attacker-controlled nSubrects uses a 32-bit unsigned multiplication that wraps: for BPP=32 and nSubrects=0x20000000, 0x20000000*8 = 0x100000000 truncates to 0, so 0 > RFB_BUFFER_SIZE is false and the small wrapped size is passed to ReadFromRFBServer; the loop at line 24 then iterates 2^29 times reading past client->buffer.
Attacker-data origin: nSubrects is read from the RFB server (line 9) and byte-swapped here with no range validation; its full uint32 domain is instantiable by a malicious server.

Sink: the loop bound is the unvalidated nSubrects and ptr has no bounds check; once the wrapped check at line 19 is bypassed, ptr walks past the RFB_BUFFER_SIZE-byte client->buffer, causing a heap out-of-bounds read for up to ~2^29 iterations.

assumptions: client->buffer is RFB_BUFFER_SIZE bytes, so the guard's size constant matches the allocation (standard LibVNCClient layout).
limitations: GotFillRect receives rx+x, ry+y, w, h without local clipping (x,y,w,h are uint8_t so bounded to 0-255); whether that causes a framebuffer OOB write depends on the not-shown callee's clipping, so it is recorded as a secondary concern, not the verdict driver.

On typical builds where the wrapped product is exactly 0, ReadFromRFBServer's behavior with a zero length is not shown; the trigger uses nSubrects = 0x20000005 (product 40) so the read succeeds regardless.

verdict.summary: All attacker-controlled values in this CIN parser are guarded at or before their sinks: image_offset is floored at 712 and re-checked after the skip loop with an EOF break; user_length is capped by GetBlobSize and its allocation NULL-checked; columns/rows are capped by the 64-bit-cast blob-size comparison, validated by SetImageExtent (status-checked), and every row is length-verified via 'count != length' before use. The one unvalidated value, bits_per_pixel (image->depth, 0-255), flows into length=GetBytesPerRow(...) and the ReadBlobStream copy into the quantum scratch buffer, but that buffer is allocated by AcquireQuantumInfo(image_info,image) from the same image->columns/image->depth expressions with a MaxPixelChannels (>=64 vs 3 used) headroom that provably dominates the copy length for every representable depth; ImportQuantumPixels consumption likewise stays within length. String fields are zero-filled by memset(&cin,0,...) and copied with bounded CopyMagickString. No primary vulnerability could be instantiated.

assumptions: AcquireQuantumInfo -> SetQuantumDepth sizes the quantum scratch buffer (returned by GetQuantumPixels) from the same image->columns/image->depth that also determine length=GetBytesPerRow(...), with a per-column headroom of at least MaxPixelChannels (64) sample slots versus the 3 (or 1) samples actually used, and clamps quantum_info->depth to <=64; under this, extent >= columns*512 >= columns*3*32 >= length for all depth in 0..255.
ImportQuantumPixels consumes at most columns*channels*ceil(min(depth,64)/8) bytes from 'stream', which is <= length, so the per-row 'count != length' verification also bounds the import read.

CopyMagickString and AcquireStringInfo/BlobToStringInfo are bounded/zero-initializing by their documented semantics; ReadBlob never writes more than its length argument into the caller buffer and returns fewer bytes at EOF (handled by count checks).
limitations: If AcquireQuantumInfo's scratch-buffer sizing in the unshown quantum core did NOT derive from image->columns/image->depth with the assumed headroom, the unvalidated bits_per_pixel (up to 255) would make length exceed the GetQuantumPixels buffer in ReadBlobStream (heap OOB write, CWE-787); the sizing code is not in the given snippet, so this could not be fully verified here.

The ping path ('image_info->ping != MagickFalse') returns the image before any validation of columns/rows/depth, so a pinged image can carry arbitrary dimensions (up to 0xFFFFFFFF); any memory or resource impact depends on downstream consumers not shown in this code and is therefore speculative.

The blob-size check 'columns*rows/8 > GetBlobSize' does not account for image->depth, so files with depth > 8 can claim more pixel data than the file holds; the consequence is only early loop termination ('count != length' break) plus the EOFBlob exception, not an out-of-bounds access.
Cosmetic defect: cin.image.green_primary_chromaticity[0] is assigned to image->chromaticity.red_primary.x (copy-paste); non-security metadata issue only.

verdict.summary: pcs->status.write_pos - pcs->status.read_pos is an unsigned subtraction with no local check that read_pos <= write_pos; when the (elsewhere-set) status fields hold read_pos > write_pos, the difference wraps to ~4G, min() selects max_data, and memcpy performs an out-of-bounds read of up to max_data bytes from buffer + read_pos, disclosing out-of-bounds memory to the caller.

evidence.reason: Unsigned underflow at the origin: write_pos - read_pos wraps when read_pos > write_pos (e.g. 0 - 8 = 0xFFFFFFF8), so count becomes max_data instead of 0; no statement checks read_pos <= write_pos before this subtraction.

Sink: with count = max_data (1024) and read_pos = 8 > write_pos = 0, memcpy reads 1024 bytes from beyond the valid buffer region into the caller's buffer; 'if (count)' only tests non-emptiness and min() bounds only the destination, never the source-side valid bytes.

assumptions: pcs->status.buffer/write_pos/read_pos are struct fields whose producers are not shown in this code; per the width-domain rule their surface is the full uint domain, so read_pos > write_pos is an instantiable state.
The caller-provided data buffer is sized max_data bytes (count never exceeds max_data, so the destination cannot overflow).
limitations: Within this function alone the invariant read_pos <= write_pos is preserved (count never pushes read_pos past write_pos); the trigger requires other, unshown code that mutates status.write_pos/read_pos to violate it — real but not demonstrable from this snippet alone.
If buffer == NULL while positions are stale and unequal, memcpy dereferences buffer + read_pos — crash-only of the same-privilege process, no corruption primitive shown.
Repeated calls after the free path call gs_free_object on NULL (positions zeroed with buffer); non-security allocator behavior.

verdict.summary: pfkey_register correctly bounds the attacker-controlled 8-bit sadb_msg_satype with 'if (hdr->sadb_msg_satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX) return -EINVAL;' before every '1<<satype' use, and NULL-checks the compose_sadb_supported() return before use. All simulated boundary values (satype 0, 8, 9, 255; NULL skb) are rejected or in-domain.

assumptions: SADB_SATYPE_MAX is 8 (PF_KEY v2), so the admitted satype range is 0..8 and the maximum shift 1<<8=256 fits the 32-bit pfk->registered bitmask.
struct pfkey_sock::registered is a 32-bit field, per the standard kernel definition.
limitations: The historical defect this function class carried (an unbounded u8 satype reaching 1<<satype, causing shift-width undefined behavior) is neutralized by the line-6 range check; if that check were absent, satype=255 would be the trigger.
compose_sadb_supported and pfkey_broadcast are not shown; their internal handling of hdr is outside this analysis, but this code passes no out-of-domain size, index, or pointer to them.

verdict.summary: sungem_send_packet is a pure dispatcher: it forwards the guest-originated (buf, size) pair to qemu_receive_packet or qemu_send_packet without any local memory access, copy, arithmetic, or output construction. The only potential issue — an unvalidated size reaching a copy primitive — lives entirely in the not-shown caller (descriptor parsing / buffer allocation) and callees (packet send/receive), so no out-of-bounds or other impact can be instantiated from this code alone.

assumptions: buf and size are guest-derived TX data (device transmit handler), so size's input surface is treated as the full signed int domain; no local narrowing is present.
qemu_get_queue(s->nic) returning NULL is not attacker-instantiable from this code, since s->nic is internal device state initialized elsewhere.
limitations: Candidate A (speculative): qemu_receive_packet(nc, buf, size) / qemu_send_packet(nc, buf, size) receive size unchecked; if the unseen caller does not clamp the TX descriptor length to buf's extent, an oversized or negative size could cause an out-of-bounds read inside the not-shown callee. Both the buffer allocation and the caller-side size validation are outside this snippet, so this cannot be confirmed or rejected here.
The loopback bit MAC_XIFCFG_LBCK merely selects between two call targets; both branches consume the same unvalidated (buf, size), so it is not a security-relevant decision.

verdict.summary: simplestring_addn never validates that add_len is positive or that target->len + add_len + 1 does not overflow signed int. The only bounds check (target->len + add_len + 1 > target->size) evaluates false for negative add_len and for values that wrap the int sum, so the realloc is skipped and memcpy at the sink copies an attacker-chosen length — negative add_len converts to near-SIZE_MAX bytes, and add_len near INT_MAX copies ~2GB — into an undersized heap buffer: a directly attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write (secondary signed integer overflow in the guard itself).

evidence.reason: Unguarded sink: add_len is an attacker-controlled int parameter with no sign or range validation. With add_len = -1 and len=0, the line-6 check (0-1+1=0 > size) is false, no realloc occurs, and memcpy copies (size_t)(-1) = SIZE_MAX bytes past the buffer — an attacker-sized out-of-bounds heap write. With add_len = INT_MAX the guard's signed overflow makes the sum negative, again skipping realloc and copying ~2GB into the small buffer.

Origin of the defect: the sole bounds guard under-admits. It contains no add_len >= 0 test, and its arithmetic target->len + add_len + 1 overflows signed int for large add_len, so the comparison yields false and the allocation (and the check itself) is bypassed, leaving the memcpy sink unbounded. The required guard — rejecting add_len <= 0 and add_len > INT_MAX - target->len - 1 before line 20 — appears nowhere in the code.

assumptions: add_len is treated as attacker-data per the width-domain rule: it is a data-carrying parameter of a non-static exported function, so any int value including negatives and INT_MAX is instantiable.

The simplestring struct's len/size are assumed to be plain signed ints as used here; the negative-add_len trigger (add_len = -1, len = 0) works for any non-negative initial len/size, so no struct detail is load-bearing.
limitations: Potential division-by-zero at 'newsize % incr' when target->size == 0 is speculative: size becomes 0 only on realloc failure (line 15), which also sets str to NULL so line 18 skips the sink, and simplestring_init_str's behavior on re-init is not shown.

The signed overflow in 'target->len + add_len + 1' is technically undefined behavior in C; the analysis assumes the common two's-complement wrap, but the negative-add_len trigger alone fully instantiates the out-of-bounds write without relying on UB.
Whether callers in a larger program can pass a negative add_len is not shown, but per the intake-point rule the missing local validation at the use is itself the defect.

verdict.summary: HandleCoRREBPP decodes sub-rectangle coordinates x,y and sizes w,h (each attacker-controlled 0-255 bytes from the VNC server) and passes rx+x, ry+y, w, h to the framebuffer fill callback with no bounds check against the framebuffer dimensions, allowing a malicious VNC server to drive an out-of-bounds heap write with attacker-chosen pixel data.

evidence.snippet: client->GotFillRect(client, rx+x, ry+y, w, h, pix);
evidence.reason: Sink: rx+x, ry+y, w, h are attacker-derived (server bytes plus server rectangle origin) and are passed to a memory-writing fill callback with no bounds/clip check anywhere in the function. Trigger: x=255, w=255 with rx at the framebuffer edge makes the fill write columns 354..608 of a 100-wide framebuffer — out-of-bounds heap write (CWE-787).

Origin of the tainted values: x, y, w, h are raw bytes read from the server-controlled client->buffer (filled at line 19), each spanning the full 0-255 domain, never validated against framebuffer bounds before use.

assumptions: client->GotFillRect writes the rectangle into client->framebuffer (its standard role in libvncclient consumers); the overflow lands in that callback, but the unchecked pass of raw offsets/sizes is the defect at the call site.
rx, ry, rw, rh originate from the attacker-controlled RFB framebuffer-update rectangle header (unvalidated at line 17, same defect class).
limitations: The line-19 guard `hdr.nSubrects > RFB_BUFFER_SIZE / (4 + (BPP / 8))` was verified sufficient for the client->buffer read (max admitted product equals RFB_BUFFER_SIZE; loop consumes exactly 4+BPP/8 bytes per iteration), so the buffer copy itself is not vulnerable.
Line 17 uses unvalidated rx/ry/rw/rh in the same callback; it is the same defect pattern as the primary finding rather than an independent one.
Coordinate magnitudes are bounded by 255 per component, limiting overflow reach from the rectangle origin.

verdict.summary: cgroup_release_agent_write is the post-CVE-2022-0492 hardened variant: the opener's user namespace is checked against init_user_ns plus capable(CAP_SYS_ADMIN) before the release agent path can be written, blocking container-root privilege escalation; the path copy is bounded by strlcpy with sizeof(release_agent_path) (guaranteed >= PATH_MAX by BUILD_BUG_ON), and the cgroup_kn_lock_live NULL sentinel is tested before dereference. No unguarded sink for attacker data was found.

assumptions: buf is the kernfs write buffer, assumed NUL-terminated by the kernfs write path (standard kernfs_fop_write behavior); even without termination, strlcpy's explicit size argument bounds the copy, so the conclusion does not depend on this assumption.
limitations: cgroup_kn_lock_live, capable, and strstrip semantics are consumed per standard kernel semantics (lock returns NULL for dead/absent cgroup; capable checks init_user_ns credentials); if any had nonstandard behavior the analysis would need revisiting, but the bounded strlcpy and the user_ns check stand on their own.

The historic CVE-2022-0492 defect (writing cgroup.release_agent from a non-init user namespace to gain host-capability code execution) is present in the sibling variant that omits the 'of->file->f_cred->user_ns != &init_user_ns' clause; this code includes that clause, so it is not vulnerable.

verdict.summary: Test-harness setup function that initializes an OPC UA secure channel with dummy fixtures and constants; no attacker-reachable input, memory operation, or security decision exists in this code, so no vulnerability is present.

assumptions: dummyPolicy, dummyCertificate, keySizes, testingConnection, sentData, testChannel are static test fixtures with no attacker-controlled content, per naming convention of a unit-test setup function.
createDummyConnection and TestingPolicy are in-file test doubles whose behavior is fixed for the tests; their implementations were not shown.
limitations: testChannel.state is set to UA_SECURECHANNELSTATE_OPEN without a handshake; in production channel code this pattern would be a fail-open concern (CWE-451/863), but here it is fixture initialization with no verification decision or untrusted consumer — speculative.

The return value of createDummyConnection is not checked for NULL before UA_Connection_attachSecureChannel; if the test double could fail, line 7 would receive a bad pointer — robustness only, no attacker trigger and no dereference in this code.

verdict.summary: No reachable memory-safety or injection defect. Every pointer advance over attacker-controlled line text is gated by a quoted NUL check: the string-skip uses '*(that + 1) != NUL' entry guard plus 'if (*that == NUL) break;' and in-escape NUL breaks; the backslash double-advance in the token loop is gated by 'if (*that == '\' && *(that+1) != NUL)' (exactly the guard that fixes the historical end-of-line overflow in this function); the column walk is gated by 'while (*that && col)'; the post-paren increment by 'if (*that != NUL)'; and findmatch's NULL sentinel is tested at 'if ((pos = findmatch(NULL, '(')) == NULL)' / 'if (pos != NULL)'. Simulated end-of-line edge cases (trailing backslash, unterminated string, escaped last char, oversized pos->col, NULL findmatch) are all blocked at execution order; remaining behavior is indent-accuracy logic, not a security impact.

assumptions: Standard Vim callee semantics: ml_get_curline() returns a NUL-terminated line for a valid lnum; lbr_chartabsize_adv() advances exactly one character and never steps over the terminating NUL (utf/dbcs ptr2len clamp to length 1 at a non-continuation byte); findmatch() returns NULL or a position within the buffer at or before the cursor line; lisp_match() reads only a NUL-terminated alphabetic prefix.
Attacker-data is the text of the buffer being indented; its full domain (any bytes, any length up to Vim's line limits, arbitrary parens/quotes/backslashes/semicolons) was used in the simulations.
limitations: Neutralized candidates, all blocked by quoted guards: (1) end-of-line backslash in the big token loop causing an advance past NUL — blocked by 'if (*that == \\ && *(that+1) != NUL)'; (2) unterminated-string / escaped-last-char walks in the first line scan — blocked by 'if (*that == NUL) break;' and the '*(that + 1) != NUL' entry check; (3) col walk overshooting pos->col with multibyte prefixes — blocked by the '*that' term of 'while (*that && col)' (worst case is a mis-chosen indent, not memory access); (4) unchecked findmatch failure — blocked by explicit NULL tests; (5) lnum underflow below 1 — impossible because findmatch returns pos->lnum >= 1 and <= cursor lnum, making '>= pos->lnum' the loop bound.

Defects internal to the not-shown callees (findmatch, get_indent, lbr_chartabsize internals) could not be audited here; the analysis treats them per standard-function semantics, which is sufficient because each in-caller use is independently NUL/sentinel-guarded.
Pure indent-accuracy quirks (e.g., trailing escaped quote treated as unterminated string, quote-aware paren counting order) were observed but have no security impact and are not reported.

verdict.summary: This is a unit-test setup fixture for a UA SecureChannel. It consumes no attacker-controlled input (no parameters, no parsed/network data), performs no memory operations, no output construction, and no security decisions. Setting testChannel.state = UA_SECURECHANNELSTATE_OPEN is deliberate test scaffolding, not a fail-open security-state misrepresentation in production logic. No vulnerability is present.

assumptions: The identifiers dummyPolicy, dummyCertificate, fCalled, keySizes, sentData, and testingConnection are test-fixture globals/locals as their names and usage indicate; none is populated from a trust boundary within this code.
UA_ConnectionConfig_default is a library-supplied default configuration constant.
limitations: The unchecked return of createDummyConnection could yield a NULL testingConnection passed to UA_Connection_attachSecureChannel; this is a robustness issue only — no attacker can induce the failure, the worst case is a same-privilege test-process crash, and no corruption or bypass follows.

If this setup pattern were copied into production code that marks a channel OPEN before completing the actual handshake, it would constitute CWE-451 fail-open state misrepresentation; within the given test-harness context no such impact is instantiated.

Callee implementations (TestingPolicy, createDummyConnection, UA_SecureChannel_*) are not shown; no defect could be located inside them from this excerpt, and no in-domain violation is passed to them by this code.

verdict.summary: In the USB_DT_OTG handler, when cdev->config is NULL the code takes config = list_first_entry(&cdev->configs, ...) without checking that the list is non-empty. list_first_entry on an empty list returns a non-NULL bogus pointer, so the guard `if (!config) goto done;` never fires, and memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value) then dereferences an out-of-bounds pointer and copies up to otg_desc_len bytes into the ep0 reply, leaking kernel memory to the USB host or crashing the gadget driver.

evidence.reason: Sink: config is a bogus pointer obtained from list_first_entry on an empty configs list; config->descriptors[0] is an out-of-bounds read and the memcpy copies from the resulting garbage pointer into req->buf, which is queued back to the host. Trigger: host GET_DESCRIPTOR(USB_DT_OTG) with cdev->config == NULL and empty cdev->configs; the `if (!config)` check cannot catch the non-NULL bogus pointer.

Origin of the tainted pointer: list_first_entry on a possibly empty list yields container_of(&cdev->configs, ...), which is never NULL, defeating the subsequent `if (!config) goto done;` guard; the missing check is list_empty(&cdev->configs).

assumptions: req->buf (cdev->req) and os_desc_req buffers are allocated with at least USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ / USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ by the composite framework, matching the clamps in this code.
gadget_is_otg() is true for some gadget configurations where no configuration is bound yet, which is the state the OTG branch must tolerate; this is a runtime state, not a caller contract.
limitations: cdev = get_gadget_data(gadget) could be NULL for an unregistered gadget, causing a NULL dereference at `req = cdev->req`; no host-triggerable path with cdev == NULL was instantiated here, so it is not confirmed.

If otg_rev >= 0x0200 selects sizeof(struct usb_otg20_descriptor) bytes but descriptors[0] is a shorter legacy OTG descriptor, memcpy over-reads by up to 5 bytes; this depends on how the configuration registers descriptors (not shown) and is a weaker variant of the primary finding.
NULL dereference crashes of the same-privilege process alone are treated as robustness issues per discipline 3; the confirmed finding is an out-of-bounds read, not a mere crash.

verdict.summary: All host-controlled fields (wLength, wIndex, wValue) are bounded before every sink: w_length is clamped to USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ at function entry (and to USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ before the OS-descriptor memset), intf is checked with 'intf >= MAX_CONFIG_INTERFACES' at all five interface-array uses, and the endpoint index is mask-bounded to 0-31. No attacker-instantiable out-of-bounds or injection path survives simulation.

assumptions: req->buf and cdev->os_desc_req->buf are allocated by the gadget framework with at least USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ and USB_COMP_EP0_OS_DESC_BUFSIZ bytes respectively (constant-named buffer sizes referenced by the clamps).
f->endpoints is a bitmap covering indices 0-31, matching the computed maximum of ((w_index & 0x80) >> 3) | (w_index & 0x0f) = 31.
Function-driver callbacks (set_alt, get_alt, get_status, func_suspend, setup, req_match) are in-tree trusted drivers; their returns are checked for negative sentinels before use.
limitations: OTG descriptor path: 'memcpy(req->buf, config->descriptors[0], value)' with value = min(w_length, otg_desc_len) trusts that the gadget driver's config->descriptors[0] is at least as large as otg_desc_len (8 or 10 bytes per otg_caps->otg_rev). A driver supplying an 8-byte OTG descriptor while setting otg_rev >= 0x0200 would cause a 2-byte over-read of driver-controlled kernel data; not attacker-instantiable from this code and the source is internal-trusted, so speculative.
GET_INTERFACE stores 'value' from f->get_alt into a u8 without an upper-bound check; only a trusted driver returning >255 could truncate, which is a robustness issue in the driver, not this code.
The '*temp = cpu_to_le16(USB_COMP_EP0_BUFSIZ)' write deliberately mutates the const ctrl buffer; this is the intended upstream fix behavior, not a defect.

verdict.summary: cgroup_release_agent_write is the write handler for the release_agent file but performs no capability/authorization check before storing attacker-supplied buf (via strstrip(buf)) into root->release_agent_path (lines 12-13). Any writer with access to a cgroup-v1 mount — e.g. a container-root process unprivileged in the init user namespace — can set an arbitrary path that the kernel later executes as a root usermode-helper command when a cgroup is released, yielding host-level privilege escalation / container escape (CVE-2022-0492 pattern). Memory safety of the store itself is fine: strlcpy is bounded by sizeof(cgrp->root->release_agent_path), which BUILD_BUG_ON (line 6) proves is >= PATH_MAX, and strlcpy always NUL-terminates; the defect is the missing authorization gate, not the copy.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unvalidated storage of attacker-controlled buf into the privileged release_agent_path with no capability check on any path in this function. Trigger: unprivileged (init-namespace) writer on a cgroup-v1 mount passes any path string as buf; the only guards executed are the compile-time size check (line 6), the liveness check cgroup_kn_lock_live/if (!cgrp) (lines 8-10), and spin locks — none constrains writer privilege. The stored value is later executed as a root command by the kernel's release_agent mechanism, an authorization bypass with arbitrary root command execution.

assumptions: buf arrives via the kernel's standard kernfs write path for the cgroup-v1 release_agent file, so its full string domain is attacker-instantiable by any process with write access to that file.
The stored release_agent_path is executed by the kernel as a root usermode helper on cgroup release, per the standard, well-known semantics of the cgroup-v1 release_agent feature (code not shown).
limitations: The out-of-bounds-copy candidate was dismissed on a quoted guard: strlcpy's size argument is sizeof(cgrp->root->release_agent_path) — the destination's own size — and BUILD_BUG_ON(sizeof(cgrp->root->release_agent_path) < PATH_MAX) (line 6) guarantees the destination is at least PATH_MAX; strlcpy copies at most size-1 bytes and always NUL-terminates, so no overflow or CWE-170 is possible.
The exact upstream remediation (a capable()/user-namespace check at function entry) is described from memory of the CVE-2022-0492 fix; the analysis itself relies only on the code shown.

verdict.summary: This function only forwards opaque handles and a compile-time-constant error string (with its exact matching sizeof) to sctp_sf_abort_violation; no attacker-controlled data is read, sized, indexed, or constructed locally, so no reachable sink exists in this code.

assumptions: sctp_sf_abort_violation is a standard SCTP helper that reports the error string and aborts; its internals are not shown but no out-of-domain argument is passed from this site.
limitations: The decision to invoke this violation handler (parameter-length validation of the SCTP chunk) and the callee sctp_sf_abort_violation are outside the given code; any defect there is not analyzable or attributable here.

verdict.summary: All callee returns are sentinel-checked in execution order (kvzalloc NULL check, two err checks before first use), the WQ-init loop is bounded by mlx5_cqwq_get_size, and inlen is sized from the same npages expression consumed by mlx5_fill_page_frag_array. The only concrete defects are non-primary: a one-shot memory leak of 'in' when mlx5_vector2eqn fails (kvfree skipped by the early goto err_cqwq), and the unvalidated cq_size parameter whose 0/negative value would cause undefined behavior in roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 — but cq_size's producer is not shown and this static helper is not an intake point for untrusted data, so the trigger is not instantiated in this code.

assumptions: cq_size is treated as internal-trusted for verdict purposes because this is a static driver helper and its caller (same translation unit, not shown) is assumed to pass the fixed positive CQ size used by mlx5 FPGA connection setup; per the width-domain rule its full int domain was nevertheless swept in STEP 2 and no guard exists.
mlx5_fill_page_frag_array is assumed to write exactly npages u64 entries matching the inlen allocation, per the standard MLX5_CMD buffer-layout semantics.
limitations: Memory leak (CWE-401): on the mlx5_vector2eqn failure path, 'goto err_cqwq' at line 29 skips kvfree(in), leaking the allocation made at line 21; not attacker-scalable (vector2eqn failure is a kernel/IRQ topology condition, not attacker-triggered at scale), so not a primary finding.

Undefined behavior for cq_size <= 0: roundup_pow_of_two(0) computes a shift by fls_long(-1)=64 (UB) and ilog2 of a non-positive value is invalid; no guard exists in this code, but instantiating it requires a caller (not shown) to pass 0 or a negative int, which is an unquoted precondition violation — speculative.
out[] is uninitialized stack passed to mlx5_core_create_cq, but only as a command-output buffer filled by the callee; no uninitialized read reaches control flow or output in this code.

verdict.summary: No reachable vulnerability: every attacker-influenced value (io_size, read return, imported iovec) passes a quoted, in-order sentinel or range check before its first use — io_import_iovec return checked with 'if (ret < 0) return ret;', negative/oversized io_size rejected by the quoted rw_verify_area error arm 'if (unlikely(ret)) { kfree(iovec); return ret; }' before any read or revert arithmetic, loop decrement 'io_size -= ret' only executes with ret in {0, positive partial bounded by iter->count} enforced by 'while (ret > 0 && ret < io_size)', and the revert expression 'io_size - iov_iter_count(iter)' is paired with 'iov_iter_reexpand(iter, iter->count + iter->truncated)' restoring the pre-read count. Remaining concerns (io_import_iovec possibly leaving *iovec pointing at the stack array inline_vecs before kfree(iovec), and io_setup_async_rw ownership of iovec on the early-punt path) are decided entirely inside unshown io_uring-internal helpers and could not be instantiated.

assumptions: Standard kernel helper semantics for unshown callees: rw_verify_area rejects negative counts; import_iovec/rw_copy_check_uvector clamp total iovec length to MAX_RW_COUNT; kiocb_done handles negative and partial ret including accumulated rw->bytes_done.
io_iter_do_read cannot return more bytes than the current iov_iter count, bounding each partial read ret to the remaining io_size.
The code matches upstream Linux io_uring io_read (fs/io_uring/rw.c) as shipped, which is the safe twin of any near-identical variant.
limitations: C3 (potential kfree of the stack array inline_vecs if io_import_iovec leaves *iovec == inline_vecs on the fast path) is decided inside io_import_iovec/__import_iovec, which is not shown; could not be instantiated from this code, so it remains speculative.
C4 (potential iovec ownership/double-free on the early-punt path 'return ret ?: -EAGAIN' where io_setup_async_rw consumes iovec) depends on io_setup_async_rw internals not shown.

C1 (negative revert count if iter->count could exceed the io_size snapshot after iov_iter_reexpand) requires iov_iter.c behavior not shown; the quoted reexpand/revert pair is the standard restore sequence and no in-code statement produces the harmful value.
C6 (ret == -EAGAIN reaching 'done:' and kiocb_done) relies on kiocb_done semantics for negative ret, not shown.

verdict.summary: Kernel driver helper mlx5_fpga_conn_create_cq validates every fallible operation it performs: kvzalloc is NULL-checked before the MLX5_SET/frag-array writes, all three error-returning callees (mlx5_cqwq_create, mlx5_vector2eqn, mlx5_core_create_cq) have their err checked before dependent state is touched, the CQE-init loop is bounded by the same mlx5_cqwq_get_size that sized the work queue, and inlen is computed from the same npages that mlx5_fill_page_frag_array consumes. No attacker-data crosses a trust boundary into this static function, so no trigger is instantiable in this code.

assumptions: mlx5_cqwq_get_size returns the entry count the wq allocator created from the same log_cq_size set from cq_size, so the init loop's bound matches the allocation.
MLX5_SET/SET64 mask written values to the declared firmware bitfield widths.
mlx5_core_create_cq (standard cmdif) fills the out buffer before any consumer reads it; out is not read in this function.
mlx5_fill_page_frag_array writes exactly wq_ctrl.buf.npages entries, the same expression used to size inlen.
limitations: cq_size (int) is unvalidated: cq_size <= 0 makes roundup_pow_of_two/ilog2 undefined and values > 2^30 would not fit the 5-bit log_cq_size field; the trigger requires a caller (not shown) passing such a value, and no trust boundary or attacker input reaches this static helper, so it is speculative here.
The uninitialized stack array out is passed to mlx5_core_create_cq; if that callee failed to fill it and its result were later consumed, that use occurs in code not shown.
Teardown of the tasklet/CQ on later failure paths lives outside this function and was not audited.

verdict.summary: Thin wrapper that forwards its arguments to sctp_sf_abort_violation along with a static, NUL-terminated error string and its exact compile-time size (sizeof(err_str)). No attacker-controlled data is dereferenced, sized, copied, or indexed in this code; no callee return is consumed. Any defect would have to reside in the not-shown callee, which receives only in-domain arguments here.

assumptions: sctp_sf_abort_violation is the standard kernel helper whose signature matches this call; its body is not shown and no assumption is made about its internals.
limitations: If the callee sctp_sf_abort_violation mishandles the forwarded 'arg' chunk pointer or the length parameter, that defect is outside the given code and cannot be evaluated here; this analysis covers only the wrapper, which passes an in-domain static string, its exact size, and untouched forwarded pointers.
No NULL checks on ep/asoc/commands appear here, but none of these pointers is dereferenced in this code, so per discipline 3 that is not a security finding in this snippet.

verdict.summary: The only attacker-controlled scalar, hdr->sadb_msg_satype (u8, full domain 0-255), is validated at the top of pfkey_register by 'if (hdr->sadb_msg_satype > SADB_SATYPE_MAX) return -EINVAL;' (SADB_SATYPE_MAX = 10). This early-return guard precedes every use in execution order, so the shifts and bit operations '1 << hdr->sadb_msg_satype' on pfk->registered (32-bit) only ever see satype in [1,10]; 1<<10 = 0x400 fits the mask with no sign overflow. The error rollback path and the SADB_SATYPE_UNSPEC branch are likewise covered. No unguarded sink on attacker data remains.

assumptions: SADB_SATYPE_MAX is 10 per include/uapi/linux/pfkeyv2.h (UNSPEC=0, AH=2, ESP=3, RSVP=5, OSPFV2=6, RIPV2=7, MIP=8, IPCOMP=9, MAX=10), and struct pfkey_sock::registered is a 32-bit integer field, so 1 << satype for satype <= 10 is in-range.
sk is a valid PF_KEY socket supplied by the kernel dispatch table, so pfkey_sk(sk) is not an attacker-NULL.
limitations: pfk->registered is read-modified-written outside pfkey_mutex (the mutex is taken after the bit is set). A concurrent register on the same socket could race the check-then-set, but no interleaving window is exhibited by this code and the worst effect is a duplicated registration bit / lost -EEXIST, not memory corruption — speculative, not a finding.

compose_sadb_supported() and pfkey_broadcast() internals are not shown; satype (bounded <= 10) and the freshly composed skb are passed to them in-domain, so no out-of-domain argument is passed at this call site, but their internal handling cannot be audited from this snippet.
Satype values 1, 4-8, and 10 are admitted by the guard despite having no registered algorithm handler; this is at most a functional oddity (a set bit with no effect), not a security impact.

verdict.summary: handle_returned_header passes a non-NUL-terminated libcurl header buffer into sscanf: input = ptr + timelimit_header_len has only len-total-header bytes guaranteed, and sscanf reads until NUL, so an auth-backend header with an empty/whitespace timelimit value drives %u's scan past the end of the delivered buffer — an out-of-bounds read. The code NUL-terminates or length-bounds every other use of ptr (strncasecmp guards, errormsg manual NUL) but not this one.

evidence.reason:
input = ptr + url->timelimit_header_len (line 19) points into a buffer of only len bytes that is not NUL-terminated; the guard at line 18 only verifies input[len-2]=='' and input[len-1]=='
', and line 14 only bounds the strncasecmp prefix compare. Trigger: backend returns 'X-Timelimit: 
' (len=15, L=13): line 14 passes (15>13), line 18 passes (indices 13,14 are CRLF), then sscanf's %u skips the '
' at indices 13-14 and must read ptr[15] — past the 15-byte extent — to look for digits, continuing while it finds whitespace/digits because no NUL terminates the region. Root cause: missing bound/NUL-termination of input before sscanf.

assumptions: The signature (void *ptr, size_t size, size_t nmemb, void *stream) returning size*nmemb matches libcurl's CURLOPT_HEADERFUNCTION, whose documented contract is that ptr holds exactly size*nmemb bytes and is NOT NUL-terminated; the code's own manual NUL-termination at line 42 and length-guarded strncasecmp at lines 11/14/31 corroborate that ptr is a raw non-terminated buffer.
The auth backend's HTTP response is attacker/untrusted data across a network boundary.
limitations: The errormsg memcpy (lines 40-42) was fully verified safe: copy_len = len-24+1 ≥ 2 for len ≥ 25 (no underflow), the clamp at lines 35-37 caps the write at exactly sizeof(errormsg) at both bounds, and the source read peaks at index len-2 (unclamped) or len-3 (clamped), both in-bounds.
len = size*nmemb overflow is not instantiable here: the extents are libcurl-supplied and capped by its write-size limits; no quoted statement produces near-SIZE_MAX factors.
sscanf %u with a value exceeding UINT_MAX (e.g. '99999999999') is clamped by glibc to UINT_MAX and merely sets a far-future discon_time; no memory-safety impact demonstrated.

If an administrator configured auth_header as an empty string, strncasecmp(ptr, "", 0) == 0 would set client->authenticated = 1 for every header line; this requires admin-side misconfiguration, not an attacker-instantiable value.
Possible NULL of auth_user->client, client->auth, or auth->state would be a same-privilege crash at most; their producers are internal and not attacker-instantiable.

verdict.summary: controller::bookmark builds a debug log line from feed-controlled url/title/description/feed_title whose newlines are never sanitized (only single quotes are replaced with %27), allowing a feed author to forge log entries (CWE-117). The seemingly dangerous shell construction at lines 10/22/27-31 is guarded: the '%s' single-quote enclosure plus utils::replace_all(x,"'","%27") provably removes the only character capable of terminating a single-quoted POSIX sh string, so shell injection (CWE-78) was simulated and dismissed.

evidence.reason: Log-line construction from attacker-influenced content without newline/control-character encoding: feed-supplied title/description containing '\n' passes through utils::replace_all unchanged (it only replaces ' with %27) and is emitted verbatim into the log, letting the feed author forge additional log records with attacker-chosen apparent content. No statement on any path sanitizes newlines — the one missing guard.

Taint origin for the log sink: the four attacker-controlled feed fields are interpolated into the constructed string with only quote-removal applied (lines 12-15), so raw newlines and control characters from feed content flow unmodified into the string that line 17 writes to the log.

assumptions: The url/title/description/feed_title parameters are populated from remote feed (RSS/Atom) content when a user bookmarks an item, making the feed originator an attacker across a trust boundary; their full std::string domain (including '\n') is instantiable per the width-domain rule.
LOG is a characterizable logging macro that writes the formatted line (constant format, substituted argument) to log output without its own sanitization.
utils::replace_all replaces every occurrence of ' with %27, per its name and use as the code's own quoting guard.
limitations: CWE-78 shell injection was considered and dismissed after guard verification: in POSIX sh, only a single quote can terminate a single-quoted string, and lines 12-15 remove every single quote from all four fields before interpolation; the concrete payload `'; rm -rf ~; echo '` becomes the inert literal argument `%27; rm -rf ~; echo %27`. Backtick, $(), and ; are not special inside single quotes.

An embedded NUL byte in a field would truncate cmdline at c_str(), but any prefix of the fully-quoted command line is either a valid shorter command or an unterminated quote (sh syntax error); no out-of-quote command separator is reachable this way, and NUL is typically rejected by the XML feed parser.
The log-forging impact is confined to debug-level logging of a client-side reader, hence low severity; no memory-corruption, authorization, or resource-consumption defect exists in this function.

verdict.summary: jp2_decode, the JP2 intake point, contains two independent primary defects: (1) a BPCC box whose numcmpts is smaller than the code-stream component count only triggers a warning, after which the loop indexes dec->bpcc->data.bpcc.bpcs[i] for i up to the image component count, reading out of bounds; (2) the CMAP DIRECT branch stores the raw channel number (channo) into the channel-to-component LUT instead of the sanity-checked cmapent->cmptno, so a CMAP with numchans greater than the image component count puts out-of-domain component indices into the LUT that are later passed to jas_image_setcmpttype as component numbers.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds read: i is bounded only by jas_image_numcmpts(dec->image) (line 179), while bpcs is sized by dec->bpcc->data.bpcc.numcmpts at box parse; trigger: BPCC box with numcmpts=1 and a code stream with 3 mixed-dtype components makes i=1,2 read past the 1-entry array.

Origin of the defect: the only statement comparing bpcc->numcmpts with the image component count emits a warning and falls through instead of returning an error, so the mismatched count reaches the bpcs[i] indexing loop unguarded.

Stores the raw, unvalidated channel number instead of the sanity-checked cmapent->cmptno (validated at lines 240-241); the CMAP sanity loop never bounds channo against the image component count, so with cmap numchans=3 and 1 image component the LUT receives values 1 and 2, which are invalid component indices.

Sink of the CMAP defect: the out-of-domain LUT value (e.g. component index 1 or 2 for an image with 1 component) is passed as the component number to jas_image_setcmpttype; no statement between line 272 and this call bounds the stored value, giving an out-of-bounds component access driven entirely by CMAP box contents.

assumptions: Box parsing (jp2_box_get) allocates bpcc->bpcs with bpcc->numcmpts entries and cmap/pclr/cdef entry arrays sized by their respective numchans/numlutents fields, per standard box-decoder semantics.
jas_image_setcmpttype consumes its component-number argument as an index into the image's component array (out-of-range values access memory outside that array).
samedtype=false is attacker-controlled via code-stream component precisions.
limitations: Unchecked jas_alloc2 for lutents (line 274) followed by lutents[i] writes (line 276) could write through NULL on allocation failure, but the earlier PCLR parse already allocated numlutents*numchans LUT entries, so failure of the smaller numlutents*4 request is not instantiable from the shown statements.

jas_image_depalettize's return value is ignored (line 279); if it failed without adding the component, newcmptno would be an invalid index, but the failure conditions of the callee are not shown, so this remains speculative.
assert(dec->image->cmprof_) (line 212) is compiled out under NDEBUG, but the impact of a NULL cmprof_ depends on unshown consumers.
The OOB read in the BPCC loop only influences a warning message; the direct impact is the out-of-bounds read itself (potential crash/info exposure), not disclosure through output.

verdict.summary: pcl_status_read frees pcs->status.buffer when the status is drained but never clears the pointer, and the free is gated only by read_pos == write_pos, which re-fires at 0 == 0 on any subsequent call with empty status (count = 0); the second free operates on the already-freed pointer, a double free / use-after-free giving heap corruption reachable from a crafted PCL input stream.

Trigger: after a draining call frees the buffer and resets write_pos=read_pos=0, a subsequent call computes count = min(max_data, 0-0) = 0, skips the memcpy, and re-enters the branch because 0 == 0, executing gs_free_object on the dangling pointer — a double free of a heap block, i.e. use-after-free/heap corruption, driven entirely by two attacker-issued status reads with no intervening status write.

gs_free_object frees the supplied non-NULL pointer; freeing an already-freed dangling pointer is a double free, not a no-op.
pcl_status_read is a status-read handler in the PCL interpreter, so a crafted input file controls when reads occur (two reads with no intervening status write is attacker-arrangeable).
limitations: Candidate A (unsigned underflow at line 4: `pcs->status.write_pos - pcs->status.read_pos` wrapping when read_pos > write_pos, which would clamp count to max_data and make the memcpy read out of bounds at line 7) was not confirmed: no statement in this code can produce read_pos > write_pos — the invariant is preserved by line 8 — and the producing writer is not shown, so the triggering state could not be instantiated.

A second-order consequence of the same missing NULL-clear — the unseen pcl_status_write reusing the dangling `pcs->status.buffer` because it is non-NULL — was not counted as the primary finding since the writer is not shown; the in-function double free stands on its own.

verdict.summary: gem_transmit copies guest-derived descriptor data into the fixed-size stack array desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS] using a copy length of sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false), where gem_get_desc_len derives from the guest-writable GEM_DMACFG register. No statement in this function bounds that length to sizeof(desc), so a guest programming a descriptor length larger than DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS words makes address_space_read overwrite the stack frame past desc — guest-controlled out-of-bounds host memory corruption (up to and including return-address overwrite), at lines 28-30 and again at the re-read at lines 136-138.

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds stack write: the copy size `sizeof(uint32_t) * gem_get_desc_len(s, false)` is guest-controlled via the GEM_DMACFG register but is never checked against the declared capacity of `uint32_t desc[DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS]` (line 3). DESC_MAX_NUM_WORDS is the full capacity of the stack arrays desc and desc_first as declared.
limitations: The fragment gather into s->tx_packet is properly guarded by the quoted check at line 50 (`tx_desc_get_length(desc) > gem_get_max_buf_len(s, true) - (p - s->tx_packet)` breaks before the copy; operator `>` safely admits the exact fit), so that copy is not vulnerable.
A guest could construct a wrap/self-referential descriptor chain causing a long or unbounded descriptor walk; treated as guest self-inflicted resource consumption, not a primary finding.

`s->tx_desc_addr[q]` indexing depends on num_priority_queues, a host-configured device property not writable by the guest attacker in this code; any overflow there would require a host misconfiguration outside the trust model.

verdict.summary: Test-suite setup function registers a test group with a compile-time array length (OSSL_NELEM(name_fns)) and returns a constant. No attacker-controlled data is consumed and no security-relevant sink exists.

The mounted filesystem image is attacker-controlled data across a trust boundary (removable media / unprivileged mount).

Exact overflow byte count depends on the key struct layout not shown; the defect is the missing bounds check at the call site, which is provably absent from the code.

verdict.summary: The overflow guard underflows at add_len == SIZE_MAX: (SIZE_MAX - add_len - 1) wraps to SIZE_MAX, so with target->len == 0 the guard passes, target->len + add_len + 1 wraps to 0 at the growth test, the buffer is never enlarged, and memcpy(target->str + target->len, source, SIZE_MAX) performs a massive out-of-bounds heap write of attacker-controlled content and length.

Sink reached with add_len = SIZE_MAX and len = 0: line 13's 'target->len + add_len + 1 > target->size' evaluates the wrapped sum 0 and skips the realloc growth, so memcpy writes SIZE_MAX attacker-controlled bytes past the small initialized buffer — out-of-bounds heap write.

assumptions: simplestring_init_str initializes target->str to a small non-NULL buffer and target->len to 0 (the fresh/empty-string state that enables the trigger).
add_len is a parameter of an exported append API; its full size_t domain is treated as instantiable per the width-domain rule.
limitations: realloc-failure path (lines 26-28) leaks the original buffer but is safely gated by 'if(target->str)' — robustness issue only, not security.

A caller passing a corrupted/inconsistent target struct (str smaller than size) could also cause OOB writes, but requires an externally corrupted struct not produced by any statement in this code.

verdict.summary: mobi_buffer_move checks the upper bound (`buf->offset + aoffset + len > buf->maxlen`) only when offset >= 0. On the negative-offset path the sole guard is `buf->offset < aoffset`, which validates only the source lower edge; `len` is never compared against `buf->maxlen`, so memmove at the sink writes attacker-chosen `len` bytes at `buf->data + buf->offset` past the end of the heap buffer, and reads past the end from `source`.

evidence.reason: Sink: memmove copies `len` (attacker-controlled size_t, full domain) bytes into `buf->data + buf->offset`. On the negative-offset path no statement bounds `len` against `buf->maxlen`, so e.g. maxlen=100, buf->offset=50, offset=-10, len=200 passes the `buf->offset < aoffset` guard (50 < 10 is false) and memmove writes data[50..249] into a 100-byte heap buffer — a 150-byte out-of-bounds write (and out-of-bounds read from data[40..239]).

The missing `|| buf->offset + len > buf->maxlen` is the single anomaly enabling the overflow at the memmove sink.

assumptions: MOBIBuffer fields (data, offset, maxlen) are maintained by the surrounding parser; buf->offset <= buf->maxlen is taken as the internal invariant, and the defect holds even under it.
offset and len originate from parsed MOBI file content (attacker across trust boundary), so their surface is the full domain of int and size_t respectively.
limitations: Secondary integer-overflow candidate: on the positive path, `buf->offset + aoffset + len` can wrap size_t (e.g. len near 2^64) and pass the L5 check, reaching the same memmove sink with a huge length; same sink and CWE class as the primary defect, so not counted separately.
abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behavior and would produce a huge aoffset via the cast; not the deciding trigger.
buf->offset += len after the memmove desyncs the buffer cursor; consequence of the primary defect, not independent.

verdict.summary: In smtp_command_parse_parameters, the length passed to uni_utf8_get_char_n is computed with reversed operands: (size_t)(p - parser->end) is negative (loop guard guarantees p < end) and wraps to a huge size_t, so the callee's length bound is defeated and it reads up to several bytes past parser->end when an attacker-crafted SMTP command line ends in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, causing an out-of-bounds read.

parser->cur/parser->end bound a network-received SMTP command line, so the bytes at p and the effective distance to end are attacker-controlled.

The missing check for the incomplete-sequence sentinel (nch == 0 from uni_utf8_get_char_n, which would also leave ch uninitialized and stall p += 0) is masked by the wrapped size and is recorded only as a secondary robustness issue.

verdict.summary: The bounds checks in mobi_buffer_move use size_t addition (buf->offset + aoffset + len and buf->offset + len) which wraps for large attacker-controlled len, so the guard passes and memmove performs a massive out-of-bounds read/write past the heap buffer.
